BABY IN CHURCH. Aunt Nellie had fashioned a dainty thing, Of hamburg and ribbon and lace; And mamma had said, as she settled it round Our beautiful Baby's face, Where the dimples play and the laughter lies Like sunbeams hid in her violet eyes: "If the day is pleasant and Baby is good, She may go to church and wear her new hood." Then Ben, aged six, began to tell, In elder-brotherly way, How very, very good she must be If she went to church next day. He told of the church, the choir, and the crowd, And the man up in front who talked se loud; Bat she must not talk, nor laugh, nor sing, But jest sit as quiet as anything. And so, en a beautiful Sabbath in May, When the fruit-buds burst into flowers (There wasn't 'a blossom on bush or tree So fair as this blossom of ours), All in her white dress, dainty and new, Our Baby sat in the family pew. The grand, sweet music,reverent air, The solemn hush, and the voice of prayer Filled all her baby soul with awe, As she at in her little place; And the holy look that the angels wear Seemed pictured upon her face. And the sweet words uttered so long ago Came into my mind with a rythmic flow: "Of such is the kingdom of heaven," said He, And I knew that He spake of such as she. The sweet-voiced organ pealed forth again, The collection-box came round, And Baby dropped her penny in, And smiled at the clinking sound. Alone in the choir Aunt Nellie stood, Waiting the close of the soft prelude, To begin her solo. High and strong, Sne struck the first note; clear and long She held it, and all were charmed but one, Who, with all the might she had, Sprang to her little feet and cried Aunt Nellie, you's being bad!" The audience smiled, the minister coughed, The little boys in the corner laughed, The tenor-man shook like an aspen leaf, And hid his face in his handkerchief. • And poor Aunt Nellie never could tell How she finished that terrible strain, But says that nothing on earth would tempt Her to go through the scene again. SS we have decided perhaps 'tis best, For her sake, ours, and all the rest, That we wait, maybe, for a year or two, Ere our Baby re-enter the family pew. —lndependent (American).

div.p: Varittito.

OPPOSITION MAXIM.—" When ycju've no case, abuse Chamberlain."—Punch. "Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown." A head would be very uncomfortable without one. Madame Patti has determined to retire when she is forty. To avoid this, she is always going to be piano.—Punch. What is the difference between a minister and a school- master ?—One forms the views, and the other views the forms. An enterprising reporter, writing of a wreck at sea, stated that no less than fourteen of the unfortunate crew and .pas- sengers bit the dust. A Pennsylvanian boasts that he makes a soap that would "whitewash a politician's character as white as snow." There must be a good deal of "lye" about that soap. . CHICKETING QUESTION SENT UP TO COUNSEL.—What is the difference between a Westminster Senior briefly bowling a maiden over and a Temple Junior being bowled over by a maiden brief ?—Punch. Mrs. Ramsbottom has not quite made up her mind with regard to thought-reading, but she is inclined to think a good many of its extraordinary effects may be due to uncon- scious celebration.—Punch. Cicero sometimes got s good as he gave. Laberius, a knight, came late to the theatre, and looked about for a place when Cicero called out, "I would give you a place if I had room." "Why, everyone says you are used to sit on two stools," was the reply. An Mier boasted to a farmer of his ancient family, laying much stress upon his having descended from an illustrious man who lived several generations ago. "So much the worse for you," replied the farmer; " for we find the older the seed, the poorer the crop." ' A witty writer has observed with much truth that every man is, in a sense, three different men. In the first place, he is the man he thinks himself to be; in the second place, he is the man other persons think him to be; and finally, he is the man that he really is. Polho said of Augustus," It is difficult to wrift against a man who can proscribe." This remark has been ascribed to many, and no wonder, for it is very obvious. An amusing addition was made to it in reference to Frederick the Great —" It is difficult to argue with the owner of thirty legions and such very thick boots." ",In my:early days," remarked the old man ashe shovelled coal into the school-house cellar, "they did not use coal to keep us school young tins' warm, I kin tell you." A sad, far-away look seemed to pass over the old man's face as to the question by a boy, "What did they use?" he quietly responded, " Birch, my boy, birch." A foreigner, writing an account of his travels in England, expatiated in eloquent terms on the high respect shown there by young people to their parents. " A son, 'he alleged in proof of his assertion, "never names his father in the familiar terms common to other countries, but is careful always to speak of him under the dignified title of "gover- nor." The harassing reign of the domestic despot, the servant girl, is in no way better illustrated than in the conciliatory tone of advertisements for these household helps. One "ad." intimates that "the family is a gentleman's"— Bridget would not serve a common tradesman. Another pointedly speaks of "light work ;" a third of "washing put out ;" a fourth of "no children ;" a fifth of "easy access to town ;" A sixth of " train fares paid." This is the latest sign of submission.—American. No NAME.—In the early days of the Reign of Terror, a French gentleman of rank was brought before the revolu- tionary tribunal. "What is your name?" demanded the presiding judge. 0 Monsieur de Saint Cyr,":replied the aris- tocrat, with a grand air. "'Monsieur' is the title that exists no longer," said the judge sternly; "we are all citi- zens now." "De Saint Cyr, then." "' De' is an aristo- cratic prefix, and has been prohibited accordingly." "Well, Saint Cyr." "There are no saints now, the Church his been abolished." "Well, then, Cyr.""' Sire' is the title of the Bing, and he has been beheaded," growled the un- compromising official; and in this way poor M. de Saint Cyr was finally left with no name at all. Ting PHRASEOLOGY OF GARDENERS.--In a recent pamphlet we are informed that "Mr. Disraeli" is an ele- gant grower, and of most excellent habits ;" "Lord Elcho " is a "bold, fine sort, very suitable for exhibition ;" whilst the "Prince Alfred" is a "free sort, and must be well stopped when young." The ladies, too, often suffer from gardeners' nomenclature. One young lady is "inclined to Straggle, and must be sharply pinched ;" a celebrated ac- tress is libellously spoken of as a "blotchy, pale-coloured sort," and an eminent duchess not certainly in her first youth, as "very robust and Of great substance." 13nt at least the line should be drawn at flowers; when this license extends to fruits we find a celebrated lady (melon) described as "green flesh, tightly laced."—Sussex Daily News. An impertinent youth had been amusing himself by ex- hibiting the following lines to some of the ladies at Sara- toga : - -

Men scorn to kiss among themselves, And scarce would kiss a brother; But women want to kiss so bad, They kiss and kiss each other. • Whereupon a young lady at once pencilled this reply on the back of an envelope, and left it for the fool's instruction : Men do not kiss among themselves, And it's well that they refrain; The bitter dose would vex them so, They would never kiss again. As sometimes on poor woman's lip Is applied this nauseous lotion, We have to kiss among ourselves As a counteracting potion. THE " INTELLIGENT " COMPOSITOR.—This is Max Adeler's dedication to one of his books—" Out of the Hurly Burly" :—"My original intention was to dedicate this book to the friend of my boyhood, Azan ben Ghes, the Imatnn of Muscat, in memory of the happy days when together we played marbles in the Oman desert, and ducked each other in the Persian Gulf, and tortured inoffensive cats in the Island of 'Kishm. But I have changed my mind; I have resolved to dedicate my book to a humourist who has too little fame, to the most delicious, because the most uncon- scious humourist, to that widely-scattered and multitudinous comedian who may be expressed in the concrete as the intelligent compositor. To his faculty of penetrating felicitous absurdities I am indebted for 'laughter that is worth a hundred groans.' It MIS he, who putting into type an article of mine which contained the injunction, 'Do not cast your pearls before swine,' translated the phrase into Do not cart your pills before sunrise.' It was he who caused me to quote the poet's inquiry so that I propounded to the world the appalling conundrum, 'Where are, the dead, the varnished dead ?' And it was his glorious tendency to thake the sublime convulsively ridiculous that rejected a line in a poem of mine which declared that a comet swept o'er the heavens with its trailing skirts,' and substituted the idea that a 'count slept in a haymow in a travelling skirt.' The kind of talent that is here displayed deserves profound reverence. It is wonderful and awful, and thus I offer it as a token of my marvellous respect." THE LATE PROVESSOR WAY.—The death is announced of Mr. J. Thomas Way, who was at one time Professor of Chemistry to the Royal Agricultural Society, standing among the foremost and most useful of the English men of science engaged in agricultural research. MA.RXET GARDEN IMPROVEMENTS.—A deputation of market gardeners from Scotland have waited upon the Lord Advocate in order to urge the introduction of a clause into the Scotch Agricultural Holdings Bill to secure compensa- tion for unexhausted improvements in market gardens,given that improvements made by the tenant in gardens of this kind were on the same.footing as those made in holdings of a strictly agricultural character I JAM F.4.CTORY.—Lord Sudoley is building a large jam manufactory on his estate at Toddington, Gloucestershire. Two years ago he planted there 93,000 gooseberry trees, 167,000 black currant, 20,000 plum, 3,000 apple, 900 pear, 9,000 damson, 500 cherry, 10,000 red currant, 25,000 rasp- berry, and 100 cobnut, and 52 acres were planted with straw- berries. At the same time 100 Scotch firs and 10,000 pop- lars were planted for sheltering purposes. A HORSE IN SPECTACLE:L—An interesting experiment was not long since made in Berlin, upon the possibility of treating cases of nearsightedness in horses. It appears that a fine horse had become intractable inconsequence of defective eyesight. The animal was so valuable that its owner deter- mined to have a pair of spectacles specially made for it. This was done with the most satisfactory results, the horse becoming as docile as ever. • MR. GEORGE WHITFIELD, of Rougemont, Canada, has , leased his model farm to the Canadian Government. The terms of the lease is ten years. Mr. Whitfield retains the Istock on the farm as his private property. About 30 stu- dents will be on the farm to learn farming and the science of stock-raising and feeding. Professor Bernard is to have charge of the farming department, and Mr. William Watson of the cattle. • A VERMIN KILLER HEAVILY ElNED.—Joseph Turner, a vermin killer, residing at Hously, near Gresford, was sum- moned for illegally exposing poison on land at Newton-by- Tattenhall. It had been noticed in the neighbourhood of Tattenhall that several animals had been found dead. Ser- geant Morgan passing down a lane near the farm of Messrs. Saddler, Tattenhall, saw something which attracted his attention. It was a grainy substance, spread towards the rick, and was found to contain ten per cent. of arsenic. This grain was ascertained to be used by defendant for the poi- pose of killing rats on farms.—Defendant was fined £2 and costs amounting to about £ll. CAL AND MANURE.—In a lecture upon the volatile con- stituents :of coal recently delivered before the Society of Arts, by Mr. T. B. Lightfoot, M. Inst., O.E, he said it was evident: now that the guano deposits are becoming ex- hausted, the demand for artificially produced Manures would increase year by year. Then referring to a letter from Di. Angus Smith, he added that Mr. Smith stated that the am- monia from 1,000,000 tons of coal if used in manure as am- monium sulphate, would add about £533,000 worth of foods to the produce of the land; while if the ammonia from all the raw coal now burnt in this country was utilised in agriculture,we should add £50,000,000 worth of bread staffs, and might begin to export. BREEDERS' NAMES.—We speak of Shorthorn men, and Hereford men, and Sussex men as breeders, and it sounds all right, but when the Breeders' Gazette (Chicago) talks about " red hog men" it looks curious in type, and sounds very funny. We hAve not yet thought of talking about black polled men and red polled men, much less of large white breed men, small black breed men or middle breed men. It would be bad enough to speak of pig men or hog then in a general way, but when it comes to red hog men the advisability of drawing a „line somewhere becohies very apparent, because, if the term were to become adopted in this country the Tamworth breeders would certainly be offended. CHANGING A COW'S QUARTERS.—It is not a good plan to change the stabling place of cows just as they are about to drop their calves. Going into a strange place creates a feel- ing of anxiety and solicitude which has a debilitating ten- dency. If a chgnge is to be Made for such an occasion, it is bettor to make it while the animals are well, and long enough in advance to have got accustomed to it. If this cannot be done it is better to let them •remain well bedded in the stanchions till the event is over, if stanchions were what they were accustomed to. Keeping cows in stanchions upon.such occasions looks like rather rough treatment, but there are hundreds of dairymen who always do so, and have their cows get along favourably, but a roomy box stall, with a level and well-bedded floor, occupied long enough in ad- vance to:have the animals feel at home in it, is to be pre- ferred.

------- THE RECLAMATION OF MOSS LAND.—Mr. James Shields, Byers, near Bathgate, publishes in the Highland Society's "Transactions" an interesting account of moss laad recla- mation. It was a "quick bog" of 20 acres in extent which he reclaimed. Operations were commenced in 1872 by draining the moss and by carting spent shale to it. The draining cost nearly £7 ; the soiling, £4; delving and ploughing, £2 las., all per imperial acre. With interest at five per cent. this will represent the outlay. In all, the reclamation may be said to have cost, with interest, £l5 per acre, or say £3OO for the 20 acres. Mr. Shields does not say when his lease expires, but he does tell us that his pmprietor advanced £3OO at fire percent., which was repaid in seven years—and he gives us a particular account of all the whole produce of the field up to 1881, that is, for half of a nineteen years' lease. The result is encouraging to those who think that there is a field for the expenditure of more capital on Briti-h soil. Mr. Shields shows that, besides re- couping the whole of the capital charge of £3OO and pay- ments for all the labour, seed, and manure, there was a balance of a few pounds (£7) at the credit of the enterprise. Besides this there is, of course, an addition of 20 acres of useful arable' land, possibly worth 30s. per acre per annum to the landlord. - -

----- WHAT IS PERMANENT PASTURE ?-1111 arbitration in- quiry affecting this question has just been decided in North Devon, the parties to the case being Sir N. W. Throck- morton, Bart., on the one hand, and Mr. F. Dovell, the tenant of one of the former's farms at Killington, in the parish of Martinhoe. The facts of the case are very sim- ple. Previous to 1861 Mr. Dovell's father rented the farm on a lease of lives, and subsequently as a yearly tenant with- out agreement. During the ten years which succeeded 1861 Mr. Dovell, sen., laid down certain lands to pasture, and in 1871 his son, Mr. F. Dovell, succeeded as tenant. A short time ago some dispute arose between the landlord and the tenant, and the result was that it was understood Mr. Dovell would have to leave the farm. He thereupon asked for com- pensation for the pastures laid down by his father. This was refused, and the tenant then proceeded to plough the pasture, but stopped this on an injunction being applied for in the High Court of Justice. Negotiations followed, and it was decided to refer the matter to arbitration. The most interesting portions of the affidavit were those which dealt with the period after which land laid down to grass becomes "permanent" or " ancient" pasture. According to the affi- davits, there is much difference of opinion as to what is, by the custom of the country, permanent pasture. 'Mr. John Mortimore puts the period at 15 years; Mr. George Brown, 20years ; Mr. Pitts-Tuckers, 10 years; Mr. Thomas Ye 0,12 years, provided the tenant himself has not laid down the land to grass; Mr. John Hannaford, 14 years. After a visit to the farm the arbitrators disagreed, and referred the matter to the umpire, who has just given his decision in favour of Mr. Dowell. He allows his claim of £177 175., together with costs of the umpire. Each party is, how- ever, to pay his own arbitrator and counsel. ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY OF IRELAND.—CATTLE SHOW AT LIMERICX.—The Royal Agricultural Society's show is a comparative failure. The causes for this are various, and more than sufficiently account for the result. For some reason or other the show has been held much too early in the season. In many cases the withdrawal of stock from home at this season involves a heavy pecuniary loss— a loss which would hardly be ,recouped even by successful competition in the showyard. Another cause of the paucity of cattle exhibits may be found in the existence in various parts of the country of the foot-and-month disease. Coming to details, it may be stated that the total number of entries is 510. Of these the cattle number 90, the entries in the shorthorn classes being 29. The entries of sheep number 61, and there are only 26 entries of swine. The total ex- hibits of poultry of all classes are 112, and of batter 87 There are 112 entries in the various sections for horses. Cattle, although few in number, are of good average show quality, but there is little requiring special mention among the exhibits. The shorthorn bulls are pretty good useful animals, the younger ones being very good. The older ones include some who have been winners at other shows, and which now look rather aged. In the female shorthorns the exhibits generally are very good, and the same remark ap- plies to the Ayrshires, although in the latter class there may be said to be no competition, Lord Powerscourt being almost the only exhibitor. There is a really good show of Kerries and Dexters so far as quality is concerned, and the competition between Mr. Roberts, of Malahide, and Mr. Good was very keen. There are a few good Channel Island cattle, but the dairy cows are much fewer than might have been expected in a district famed for its milch cows. In sheep the Shropshires are of excellent quality, but the com- petition has been very much limited by the exclusion of those entered by Mr. Napier, of Loughcrew, and the Marquis of Hertford. Mr. Hannan shows some splendid Roscom- mons, and the Leicesters of Mr. Meade and Mr. Cooke are excellent. The show of swine is small. There is a good display of horses of all classes, including some old prize- winners. As an evidence of the lack of interest shown by the tenant farmers of the country in the exhibition, it may be stated that in the four cattle sections in which they have exclusive right for competition there are only five entries; audits the single section of sheep, in which the competition is likewise limited to tenant farmers, there are only two competitors, and in those sections for swine in which the ' competition is similarly restricted, there are no entries whatever.. The horses in the weight-carrying sections are of exceptional merit, and with these and the four-year-old geldings the judges expressed especial satisfaction. There was but a poor show of ponies, and there was nothing in the.entire class deserving of notice. The Croker Challenge Cup, for the best weight-carrying thoroghbred stallion, was awarded to Lord Dunr.aven, for his bay thoroughbred, Sam Chifney, a splendid animal, with a pedigree which includes St. Alban and Stockwell. Of course the first prize in the Class was awarded to the same animal. In shorthorns the first prize for bulls over three years old was carried off by Marcus, the property of Mr. J. M. Gumbleton, county Waterford, who also. took first prize for the best shorthorn bull calved if:1%1882. Mr. Henry B. Poe. of Solsborough, N'enagh, took first prize for shorthorn bulls calved in 1881, ith one of the finest animals in the yard. The show of

THE PRINTER'S DEVIL -VII.
[B Y Amoto-Scoirs.] (The 'eiyht of re publication is ;Tsui:ed.)

. _ " Audi alteram pattern." Let us now give the authors and " ink-slingers" a turn. Some Australian scholars (?) in a translation of Juvenal, speak of Drela!us as a " flying joiner." The same writers make Hannibal "skip over the Pyrenees," and translate "Candiduli divine tomaculi porci," as " a white porker's holy sausages." The " loose" style seemed to have spread to one of the compositors engaged on a review of the book, and an allusion to Cicero's jingling hexameters came out " bungling hexameters." The axe— with the invention of which tool the son of Eupalamus is credited,—had evidently no terrors for these worthies. I cannot confirm the assertion about Hannibal skipping over the Pyrenees, but it is quite evident the Printer's Devil can cross and recross the Channel at will, as witness the following taken from a recent issue of the Petit Joernal : "On nnonce l'arrivee, a Paris, de George Eliot. La to- mancli)re Anglaise bien connue eel accompagnee de Sir E. Scott, petit-file de l'auteur d'lvanhoa." The announce- ment suggests " Dobby " in more senses or applications than one. Some authors are continually sneering at" prin- ter's blunders:" but it would be well if some of these took the motes out of their own eyes. For a specimen of the " mixing process " the following by a Poet will take its place with anything the poor Printer can do : Take my soul, And set it in the tiar of thy brovi. Or clasp it oi the swelling of thy zone Dissolve ma in the amber haza of dews

That clothe thee round." A reviewer who bad been eet the task—for it is a task to review such stuff, and not a duty—says :—" The italics in the quotation are our own, and we willingly acknowledge that it is the first time, in our long experience of:poetasters, that we have encountered an aspiration on the part of a lover's soul to act eis a brooch." Considering that a " swell- ing " is spoken of, I am of opinion that the reviewer might have very appropriately applied the term " poultice " instead of" brooch" to such a metaphor. And this reminds me of an amusing adventure that once occurred to myself. I was standing at the wings of a Loudon Theatre, talking to the stage manager, an old friend, while a certaiu clever and deservedly popular opera-bouffe actress was performing a leading part in one of the brilliant spectacular and musical pieces for which the place was at that time famous. The lady was suffering from a severe cold, and while going through a brisk saltatory exercise, a plaister she had on her cheat shifted, and threatened if not replaced, to ludicrously interfere with the tout-ensemble of her pretty and picturesque costume. Coming up to where we stood, the lady said, in her charming manner," Now, I know you two are family men, and you must help me at once to refix this plaister, for if it should shake out while I am dancing in the next scene I shall get laughed at." Of course we performed the favour requested of us with gallant alacrity, as tenderly as we could, and of course, like "family men," said one or two pretty things while doing it, but wishing ourselves for the nonce stage jewels to be set in her theatrical bead-gear, or being metamorphosed into plaisters or poultices to be "clasped on the swelling of her z me, " were not of them. She would have boxed our ears if we had so offended, or clouted us with a supporting-iron. Nor can I 6onceive the class of woman Chat would feel flattered by such poetical tomfoolery being addressed to her, after having asked for and been granted delicate or tender assistance from the opposite sex in emergency or otherwise. But then I'm not a Masher. Take another instance. The orator who "saw in his mind's eye the vessel of the state floating on the brink of 'a volcano," must have been related to the persons who wrote about " Scan- del's dunghills flapping their wanton wings;" of the "raven ranging over destitute seas ;" of " delicious miseries ;" of "tasting the heaven of a woman's white skin," ate. The "vessel of state floating on the brink of a volcano" bangs into fits Punch's jocular prediction about our ironclads one of these days getting to Mount Ararat, a sarcasm aimed at the suppasel falling-off in shill and caution on the part of our navigating offic,rs, judged .from the fact of so many of our vessels being run aground some time ago. And a dunghill flapping its wines, wanton or otherwise, would be as interesting a sight or exhibition as a Newton tea-fight, or a lav-and-clergy slogging-match in the slush. But I presume, in face of the " hen and chicken " disaster, sarcastic at lueions to the ships of "the Queen's navee " will not be considered of a "lively " nature; nor, in view of recent tragic occurrences near Newton, will it be accorded wise or discreet to allude too pointedly to p,-euliar local customs. The compilers of books of referenc at times nod, or allow their pens to slip, as witness the following, tak,n ; from the third edition of the "Justice's Note B ok :"—" No person may part with, or cherish. the Celorado Beetle, alive, ix any stage of existence. Penalty for every offence of omission, or commission, £lO ; half to the inforanor." The person who succeeds in securing the half or whole of that penalty will deserve it. Perhaps the custodian of the Newton landing stage, having beaten the " assessors," will solve this problem. He put a poser to me in the Newton court-house, or Instice-room, or whatever it is called, on the last Saturday in April. Why he accosted me, for advice or sympathy, I cannot tell ; unless it was because, wearing serge at the time, he took me for a brother waterman. To conclude this instalment of the subject, surety the Pen or the P. D. is responsible for "fourth " being substituted for "first" in the following announcement in a births column : " Mrs. ,of twins, fourth tin.e." If the announce- ment is correct as it stands, " Deeonet " may well exclaim •in the Itcferee, "Ye gods! What a'Coned' of Errors ' for a new Shakespeare." - P.s.—Since the above was put in type I have received the following r ungent and sarcaetic reminder that we are all mortal, from a talent6el and amiable lady, after reading the last instalment of the " P.D. " :—" Do you remember our own absurd mistake in 'The Black Museum? Her sacred flesh ' for ' her scared flesh.'" With such a candid admis- sion on her part, it would be cowardly and ungallant in me to refuse an acknowledgment of my share in the blunder.
CLAIM AGAINST A HAYDOCK PUBLICAN.

At the Liverpool Court of Passage, on Wednesday, before Mr. T. IL Baylis, Q C., judge, an action was brought by a widow, named Mary Richards, residing in Bengel-street, against Joseph Ratcliffe, a licensed victualler, at Haydock, to recover the sum of £l3 123,, for board and lodging of an illegitimate child of which he was the reputed father, and for which the plaintiff contended the defendant had entered into an arrangement to pay. Mr. M'Connell represented the plaintiff, and Mr. Mulhollard appeared for the defendant. It was proved in evidence that the defendant had agreed to pay the plaintiff 84. it week, and that for the first year, from 1874, when the child was born, he paid the money regu- larly, but since then he had been very irregular in his pay- ments. The mother of the child was Elizabeth Orme, who was formerly in the defendant's service, and for some time subscquently she lived with him as his mistress. The defen- dant allowed the payments to fall into arrears to the amount now claimed, refusing .to make further payments on the the ground that he was not indebted to the plaintiff. —Elizabeth Chem, one of the witnesses examined, swore that the derendant was the father of the child. He agreed to pay the plaintiff 83. a week for his maintenance. The reason she had not taken pro- ceedings to affiliate the child upon the defendant, was that she had never been called upon to support it. Since its birth the defendant bad told her that he believed the child I was not his, but that was utterly untrae.—Mr. MulholLand I said after that evidence had been given he could not resist the claim. Since these proceedings were commenced the plaintiff had initiated a criminal action against the defen- dant for perjury, alleged to have been contained in an affi- davit filed by him it, reply to an an affidavit for judgment filed by Mrs. Richards. In that affidavit he swore he was not then' and never had been, indebted to the plaintiff, apd that he had never paid the defendant any money what- ever in respect of any indebtedness.—Tee defendant gave evidence. He said b e bad reason to believe the child was not his. He never made an agreement with Mrs. Richards. The agreement was made by Mrs. Orme, and he told her at the time that whatever she agreed to pay far the child he would give it to her.—The jury formally found for the plaintiff for the amount claimed.

ST HELENS COUNTY COURT.—At this court on Wednes- day the btpiness consisted of 171 cases, seven adjourned cases and 92 commitment cases. The remains of the Duke of Marlborough were interred at Blenheim on Tuesday. Sir Stafford Northcote was amongst the paThearers. At a meeting of the leading zitinns of Glasgow on Tues- day, a fund was started for the sufferers by the Clyde disaster. A sum of £9,000 was subscribed. £5,000 uf which was given by Messrs. Stephen and Sons. KEEP THE CHILDREN HAPPY.—lnvent every possible amusement to keep your boys at home, in the evenings. Never mind if they do scatter books and pictrires, coats, hats, and boots! Never mind if they do make a noise around you, with their whistling and hurrahing! We would stand aghast if we could have a vision of the young men gone to utter destruction for the very reason that, having cold, dis- agreeable, dull, stiff firesides at home, they sought amuse- ment elsewhere. The influence of a loving mother or sisters is incalculable. Like the circle formed by casting a stone into the water, it goes on and on through a man's whole life. Circumstances and worldly pleasures may weaken the re- membrance for a time, but each touch upon the chord of memory will awaken the old time music, and her face, her voice, and her loving words will come up before him like a revelation. The time will come, before you think, when you would give the world to have your house tumbled by the dear hands of those very boys • when your heart shall long for the noisy steps in the hall, and their ruddy cheeks laid up to yours; when you would rather have their jolly whistle than the songs of Neilson ; when you would gladly have dirty carpets, aye, live without carpets at all, but to have their bright,strong forms beside you once more. Then play with and pet them. Praise Johnny's drawing, Betty's music, and baby's first attempt at writing his name. Encour- age Dick to persevere in making his rabbit hutch. If one shows a talent for figures, tell him he is your famous mathe- matician: and if another loves geography, tell him he is sure to make a good traveller or foreign minister. Go with them to see their young rabbits, and chickens, and pigeons. Have them gather you mosses, and grasses, and flowers to decorate their room. Tne Earl of DERBY declined to renew the grant for the maintenance of the English church in Hong Kong, which was withdrawn by Lord Kimberley two years ago.—An in- teresting discussion 9,n the state of our military forces took place.—Lord WEMYSS called upon the Government to strengthen the militia, and a number of peers connected with the army commented on the shortcomings of the force. --Lord MO P.LRY pointed out that if we wanted a large army, every battalion of which should be fit for service, the force must be constituted on an entirely different footing from the present.—The Duke of CAMBRIDGE repeated his often. expressed opinion that a large and efficient army is merely a question of money, and Lord CRANBROOK defended his administration at the War Office.—The motion was carried. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MoNnax. THE haste MAIL INCIDENT.—Mr. B CRT called attention to the startling incident which occurred a few days ago on the Chester and Holyhead Railway, and asked if it was the fact that the drowsy driver and fireman had ben on Onty for 15 hours, and yet, notwithstanding this great strain, had been discharged.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said he had been informed by the railway company chat the men had mis- represented the duration of their labours, and they were dismissed for the falsehood. CHOLERA IN EGYPT.—Lord E. FITZ NIACRICE made a statement about the effective steps which are being taken in Egypt to prevent the spread of cholera, and also with rs. gard to the precautionary measures which are being adopted by Her Majesty's Government.—Mr. FAWCETT gave some particulars about the detention of the homeward mail from the East, and said the opinion was that it would be better fat. the next mail to proceed direct to England by sea. Every pare, he added, was being taken to die-infect the bags. MR. H. GLADSTONE'S UTTERANCES.—Mr. TOTTENHAM asked the Premier if the sentiments attributed to Mr. Her- bert Gladstone in a report of a recent secli expressed the opinion of the Government as to the desTrablenesS' amending the the Irish Land Act.—The PREMIER said the position taken by Mr. Herbert Gladstone was precisely the same as that taken by the Government—that there were certain points in the L.ead Act in respect to which the Go- vernment had always considered iriesirable that the House should give its attention. _ _

THE —BRADLAUGH INCIDENT.-Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE asked Mr. Gladstone what he proposed to do in reference to Mr. Bradlaugh's threat to take his seat iA the House.—Mr. GLADSTONE said the recommendations of the Government on this subject had not hitherto received the unanimous ap- proval of the House' and it rested with those whose advice had been accepted by the House to act on the information now laid before them.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE then moved that Mr. Bradlaugli should be excluded from the precincts of the House until he should engage not further tg disturb its pro- ceedings.—Mr. LARCH:THERE opposed the motion, but Mr. GLADSTONE applaled to him not to waste the time of the House by taking a division, as the motion was a necessary corollary to the steps taken on a former occision.—Sir W. LAWSON called for a division, and a vote was taken, with the result that Sir Stafford's Northcote's motion was.carried by 232 to 65.

TRH ORDER OF Bust.NEss.—Mr. GLADSTONE then made his statement relative to the business of the House and the work during (ha remainder of the session. Chief among the measures to be proceeded with are the bills which have gone through the Grand Committees, and the Corrupt Prac- tices and Tenants' Compensation Bills, and among those dropped are the Floods Prevention, Ballot Continuance and Amendment, Scotch Universities, Police Superannuation, and Irish Sunday Closing. After to-day the Government propose to ask for Tuesdays and Wednesdays till the end of the session.—Sir S. NORTIICOTE expressed the hope that in another week or two the Premier would have the courage to sacrifice a few more of his measures.—ln the discussion which followed, an appeal was made by Welsh members on behalf of the Welsh Intermediate Education Bill.—Mr. FORSTER hoped that the sabject of Irish emigration would not be lost sight of. He did not press for any special debate on South African affairs, though he thought there ought to be a discussion on the subject of the South African esti- mates.

THE CORRUPT PRACTICES BILL.—The House then resumed Committee on the Corrupt Practices Bill, which occupied the greater part of the sitting. On progress being reported, the Bankruptcy Bill was recommitted, and passed through that stage without opposition. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY.
THE COLONIES.7Viscunt Szumount suggested that the

Government should give the colonies some a—s-sistance in the matter of coast defence, and thought that naval pay officers at home might be allowed to join the colonial service with- out losing their chances of increased pay and promotion. Ile moved for copies of all correspondence with the colonies on the subject.-Earl DEnnv said it would be impossible to protect every part in our colonial empire. It was only at- tempted to do so in the case of a few of the most important points. The latter suggestion of the noble Viscount was a good one, but had not as yet been made to them by any of the colonies.—The motion was negatived. HOI.L':,E OF COMMONS—TUESDAY.

THE CHOLERA —At the afternoon sitting more questions were asked about precautions against cbolera.—Sir C. DUKE said it had never been found possible to enforce quarantine in England, and for many years it had been practically abolished, but this country had now the consent of most European nations for the system which was called medical inspection, and ever since 1873 England had been thoroughly

prepared for an invasion of cholera. —The House again went into committee on the Corrupt Practices Bill, and having got through the original clauses proceeded to discuss new clauses introduced by the Attorney-General. Foor-Awn-Mourn DISEASE.—In the evening Mr. CRAP- LIE called attention to the prevalence of foot-and-month disease, and moved a resolution in favour of prohibiting the landing in this country of foreign animals from any country the laws of which did not afford security against our imparting therefrom animals which were diseased.— Colonel ICINoscoTE having seconded the motion, Mr. I ARTHUR ARNOLD moved an amendment which, whilst de- precating fresh legislation, affirmed that the recent preva- lence of foot-and-mouth disease calls for the continued and vigilant exercise on the part of her Majesty'.3 Govern- ment of the powers entrusted to it, not only with reference to the movement of live animals at home, but in regard to their importation from abroad.— Mr. MUNDELLA, in a vigorous speech, full of plain facts and official statistics, showed that the adoption of the motion would be as disastrous for the producer as for the consumer. Within a few months of the passing of the resolution there would, he asserted, be a total prohibition of the importation of foreign meat. What that meant appeared from the state- ment that, not taking into account bacon and salted meats, one-sixth of the fresh meat consumed in this country came from abroad.—Mr. JAMES HOWARD supported the motion in a speech which concluded at ten minutes past one, and was marked by several lively interruptions suggesting the wish for greater broyity.—Sir H. SELIVIN-IBBETSON supported the motion.--Mr. DoDsoN, speaking at half-past one, was received with fresh signs of impatience. He said the Government were prepared to ac- cept either the amendment or a suggestion put forward by Mr. J. B rclay for the appointment of a Select Committee ; but they would not accept the motion.—After a vain attempt by Mr. Duckham to make a speech, Mr. ARNOLD withdrew his amendment, and Mr. BARCLAY moved the appointment of a Select Committee.—On a division, Mr. Chaplin'e motion was carried by 200 to 192 votes. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.
A SECOND SUEZ CAN&L.—In reply to Mr. Gourley, the PRIER MINISTER stated that he had received arommunica-

tion from a number of London shipowners embodying their views on the question of a supplementary Suez Canal, but he referred the questioner to the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer for information.—Mr. CHILDERS stated the nature of the provisional agreement arrived at on the previous day between the representatives of Her Majesty's Government Ltni M. de Lesseps, the President of the Suez Canal Corn. patty, for the construction of the second Suez Canal. The first paragraph in the agreement provided that the Company should construct a second cinal, as far as possible parallel with the existing one, to be completed by the year 1888. The dividend last year was 16 per cent., and this year it was expected to reach 19 per cent. It was agreed to reduce the future tolls and dues, the de- tails of the proposed reduction being given by the right hon. gentleman. There would be an increase of the English share in the management of the Canal ; and the IGovernment would use its influence for the purpose of ob- taining the necessary land for the formation of the new Canal. The Company was to pay 1 per cent. of the total I net profits to the Egyptian Government for ninety-nine years; and Her Majesty's Government proposed to lend to I the Company, by instalments, not more than £8,250,000 at 31, per cent., with a sinking fund calculated to repay the Icapital in 50 years, this sinking fund not to commence until after the complelon of the works. This agreement,--the ' Chancellor of the Exchequer added, would have no effect until it bad been sanctioned by Parliament. Some discus- sion followed, and ended with a promise to lay papers on the table.
THE FRENCH IN MADAGASCAR. OUTRAGES ON BRITISH SE/USIEN AND OFFICIALS.

ISir S. NORTHCOTE: I wish to put a question of which I have given private notice to the right hon. gentleman op. I posite. A report has reached me of some serious occurrence having taken place in Madagascar. I do not wish in the present state of my information to put the question in any form that would give colour to it. I therefore simply ask I the Government whether they have any information on the subject which they could communicate to the House. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. GLADSTONE : We have received within the last 24 hours telegraphic information from Zanzibar and from Madagascar with regard to occurrences in Mada- gascar. The House will be aware from informa- tion given by the Under Secretary of State that Tamatave was occupied by the French on the 14th of June, and a state of siege wasproclaimed there. The British Consul was unhappily at that time very ill, and the infor- mation we have received is to the effect that his illness was seriously aggravated by the political crisis. One incident of that crisis was that his secretary was Arrested in his presence. In these circumstances he received an order from the French admiral to quit the place within 24 hours. , Before the 24 hours had expired, in fact seven hours before the expiration of that term, he died. The French admiral subsequently invited the British to attend the funeral, and they did so attend in considerable numbers. A very con- siderable number of officers and men ef the Dryad, and several French officers, attended the funeral. 1 he French admiral stopped communication betneen the British man-of- war and the shore. The captain was allowedebut only al- lowed verbally—to protest against the proceedings. The flags all the foreign consuls, as we understand. have been hauled down in Tamatire. Besides that ,here is a portion of the

telegram affecting another person. In addition to the Con- sul's secretary, a British subject, a Mr. Shaw' who I be- lieve is a missionary of the London Missionary Society, was also arrested on the 16th, and remains in prison. The charge against him has not been made public, but it is sur- mised or presumed to be for correspondence with Vennerni, using what would be the French phrase under the circum- stances. Irquiry has been made with respect to him, but the only answer received is that "the law must take its course." (Sensation.) Ic announcing these grave aryl pain- ful occurrences, I have only now to say that we wait for further information as to the facts, and that we wait also for those communications from the Government of France which the case may require, and which we have intimated to the French Government that we anticipate, and which it would have been our duty to make under similar circum- stances. (Cheers.)—Sir G. CAMPBELL asked what was the nationality of the secretary arrested ?—Mr. GLADSTONE said, frem the name it would seem he was a native, but that was only surmise. _

MISCELLIOTEOI79.—The PREMIER, in accordance with nOtice, molted that f9r the rerriOnder of the session orders ih.. uãy have precedence of notices of motion on Tues- day, and that Government orders have priority on Wednes- days. After some discussion, the motion was agreed to, and the House then went into committee on Vile C37rupi Practices Bill, one of the new clauses of which was under discussion yhen by the standing orders the chairman had to leave the chair, and progress was reported. The order for going into committee on the Copyright Bill was discharged, and the House adjourned. _ _ HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIitIRSDAY.

THE MADAGASCAR INCIDENT.—The Marquis Of SALIS- BURY asked whether the Government could give any in- formation respecting the unhappy incident at Madagascar, and whether it was convenient for Her Majesty's Govern- tnent to state what measures had been taken to strengthen tier Majesty's navy in those waters.—Earl GRANVILLE replied that, with regard to the first part of the notice, no infotnl9ll had heed received except such as had been given In the House af Conmiod§. With regard to tbc latter part of the question, it would be better that he ihddid pot now make any announcement, especially as France was ready to render any satisfaction for any unjustifiable occurrenca in that dist-nit part ti the world. THE PAYMENT OF INTEREST OUT OF CAPITAL.—A motion to insert a clause in a railway bill authorising the payment of interest out of capital led to an attack upon Mr. Cham- berlain in respect of his speech on this subject in the other House.—Lord CAIRNS said that if he could not carry his colleagues with him on an important point affecting his own department Mr. Chamberlain ought not to be President of the Board of Trade.—Lord SALISBURY said too much stress could not be laid on the "divided action" of the President of the Board of Trade in this matter.—The LORD CHANCEL- LOR defended Mr. Chamberlain.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING,
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING,

TORNIPS.—If a sowing has not been made recently of these, one should be made at once, providing they are re- quired at the end of August or during September for exhi- bition purposes. A young, moderate sized turnip is superior to a large pithy or hollow one, a condition they frequently acquire at this season of the year if they have been growing too long. ONIONS.—These may be increased in size, if supplied with manure water, by making a shallow basin round each one, if far enough apart, if not, forming a low ridge on each side of the row, to prevent the water flowing away. Our prac- tice has been to select a sufficient number of the best formed and remove the others, so that the individual basin plan might be carried out, thick necked ones, as well as the ill- formed bulbs, being discarded. The necks of those remain- ing, unless very thin, may have an occasional pinch and be finally bent down. This checks the flow of sap, and that which would go to form tpp is retained to produce bulbs. The best stimulant we have used is guano water, using just sufficient guano to colour the water, or as much as can be held between the thumb and two forefingers, in a gallon of water, which should be well stirred, or the solution will be of unequal strength. The evening is the best time to water this as well as other crops at this time of the year. POTATOES.—The earliest of these will now be fit to take up. In doing so, where there are crops planted between the rows, we would advise the tops of the potatoes to be cut off level with the ground before any are dug up. We have seen the inexperienced getting almost bewildered when ex- ecuting this simple operation of potato digging. The haulm is almost too much for him. Now the fork is en- tangled in it, then some of the longest have dexterously twisted themselves round his ankles, or he has some ends under his feet, whilst his eyes are fixed on the other which he is straggling to raise, making his overthrow almost im- minent. As for the plants between the rows, some will have been dragged clean out of the ground, and the others trampled upon by the operator in his contest with the potato tops. It will be apparent to the most okAuse intel- lect that by a little forethought all this needless exertion is obviated by cutting as we advise. If the ground is levelled round each plant of the intermediate crop, they will have the most perfect earthing up that can be provided for them. We found planting amongst potatoes of great benefit this season. They acted as a welcome screen during the hot weather to our Cauliflowers, Kails, Broccoli, &c. So soon as they are likely to be smothered by the tops we shall turn these on one aide, drawing all their ends one way or towards the sun as far as practicable. Gnuns ON EARLY CALTLIFLOWERS.—Comptaints have reached us of the attacks of a white grub on these, and we have had a few cases ourselves. The grab we have examined is one-fourth of an inch long, white in colour, with occa- sionally a slight dab of brown on the head. We take it to be anthonya brassiere in the maggot state. They destroy the stein below the ground level, leaving it a mere shell. We have not heard of a better remedy than catching and killing them, and as they are numerous round each stem it involves much labour, or, at any rate, absorbs considerable time. We pondered for some time how to get rid of them; as far as they gave indications of their whereabouts. The flabby leaves are a sure sign of their presence or something as bad. Our first thought was to take a spade, lift plant and soil into a barrow, wheel into a convenient place, and light a fire on the top. This would have been more expeditious than hand picking. Just as we were muttering to ourselves in a grumbling mood at having to be thus inconvenienced, and how to undertake this unexpected labour, our soliloquy was interrupted by the quack of a duck. Providing our- selves with a few grains of corn, we succeeded in enticing it and its companions to the Cauliflower rows; dug a plant up and a spadeful of soil at the same time, threw the whole on the ground and partly spread it; a few grains of corn were thrown close to the maggots to draw the ducks' atten- tion. The moment they were seen they were greedily de- voured. Every bit of fresh turned up earth was carefully scrutinised by them. The holes were descended into and examined; so we feel sure they have cleaned them all so far. FRONT GARDEN.—SOiI should now be got ready and a few pegs made for layering Carnations. As a rule, the plants of these do not survive the winter, so that an annual propaga- tion is necessary. The best soil is loam and leaf soil, with an eighth of sand. The whole should be passed through a half-inch sieve and placed through the "stools," pressing well with the hand underneath the grass or future layers. All being in readiness, layering can be proceeded with any time after the middle of this month. PINKS are propagated by cuttings. They will do in a shady corner, but many of the pipings, as they are termed, perish. We would, therefore, advise the cottager to nail four boards together, having a depth of fin, and 121 n. and 18in., and procure a piece of glass to fit on the top. This will give space for a stock of pinks. THE WINDOW.—If the cottager has acted upon previous advice, this will be comparatively empty now. The Gera- niums that have been turned out will have got one-sided if they were not frequently turned whilst indoors. Every effort should be made to repair that fault, whether they are on the window ledge or plunged IR the ground, let the worst side front the most sun and Iltht. This applies as well to such 'plants as fuchsias, &c., especially if they are to be exhibited. Judges of flower shows have an ungovern- able curiosity to see all round the plants they are called to adjudicate upon.

The Home Circle—Walking round the room with the baby at night. • WORDS.-It is deplorable when a man uses words he does not understand, but it is more so when a lady makes slips in conversation. A gentlewoman at Dundee gave a party, which was kept up to a late hour. Next morning a young gentleman called for her two daughters, who, not having got up, requested their mother to say they were "indis- posed." The worthy matron, unaccustomed to learned phrase, informed the visitor that her daughters were ceased."—A lady in Fife being informed by a visitor that he was suffering from a cold, prescribed this: "Just take some hot gruel, sir, and get into bed, and you'll expire di- rectly 1" She no doubt meant "perspire."—A gentlewoman in Wigtonshire employed a house carpenter, who became an architect. She complained to a neighbour that he was-very much less attentive since he become an "artichoke."—An honest Scotch woman remirked to her master that she had seen all about a certain case in the Ulcerated—she meant the Illustrated—News.

THE AMAZONS OF DAHOMEY.—Perhaps the most extra- I ordinary feature in Dahoman economy is the corps of Ama- zons or female warriors. The word has got incorporatedl into the English language as expressing a masculine woman, but what the Amazons really are is not so generally known. Their origin dates from 1728, when the exigencies of war I compelled the then king to organise a regiment of women, with whom he attacked and defeated the old Whydahs. Since then they have been a marked feature in the military establishment of the Dahoman kingdom. Under Gezu the corps attained its maximum of greatness. With the acute- ness which distinguished him, he raised the Amazonian body from being merely a subordinate establishment to an equal level with the male soldiers, and created female officers, so that, by surrounding himself with a band of female viragos, bdpnd to him by all the ties of gratitude and interest, he could at once put a check on too ambitions subjects, and nip in the bud the first signs of rebellion. On a certain day —once in three years—every subject must present himself, with his daughters above a certain age, before the king. The most promising of those belonging to the higher classes he selects as officer, the poorer ones being chosen as soldiers; while the children of slaves become the servants of the Amazons who reside within the palace. This done, the other daughters are returned to their parents to be disposed of as they may find proper. Some of the selected girls are "dashed" or presented to the most meritorious soldiers as wives; while all the female children of these Amazonian wives are Amazons by birthright. With these exceptions. every Amazon is a celibate; bat as military discipline is not always equal to preserve the little god from his mischievous work, a fetish—the Demen—is erected over one of the palace gates, which by its power at once discovers any Amazon who is unfaithful to her military oath in the matter of celibacy. The informers also—who in these cases are generally jealous of the culprits—are never backward in causing the misdemeanour of the erring soldieress to reach the ears of the king, and her fears being worked on, she almost invariably confesses the name of her lover. The re- sult is that both are punished—he assuredly by a cruel death, and she in all likelihood by the hands of her com- rades. The King has several Amazons as concubines, under the name of "leopard-wives," who enjoy many privileges. Though the flower of the corps perished under the walls of Abeokeuta:in 1864, their number may be yet about 4,000. They are divided into three brigades, each of which has a peculiar head-dress or method of dressing the hair. Each of these brigades is commanded by female officers and sub- officers, and is again divided into Agbaraya, or Blunderbuss- women, the veterans of the army—only called into action in case of urgent need; the Gbeto, or elephant-huntresses, one of the most celebrated corps in the army, and who on hunt- ing expeditions are exposed to great danger front the infuri- ated animals; the:Nyekpleh-hentoh, or Razor Women, of whom there are only a few to each wing. Their special object of aversion is the King of the enemy, and the huge razor which they carry is especially intended for the decapi- tation of this Monarch. Lastly, there are the Gulonentoh, or Musketeers, and the Gohento, or Areheresses, who are all young girls, and more of a show corps, their weapons being of comparatively little use in. active warfare. In addition, there are 'troops of camp-followers, hewers of wood and drawers of water. Even they enjoy certain privileges. If met within the pathway, headed by a beldame ringing a bell, I every man—unless bearing the "King's stick," an insignium of rank—must instantly disappear to the right or left; to look upon them would be a crime. Acdordingly they are exceedingly important, and arrogantly jealous of their pre- rogatives. All the corps of Amazons—with the exception of the Archeresses—are armed with muskets or blunder- busses, kept scrupulously clean; but though these female warriors are brave to ferocity, yet they are poor marks- women,-eMr. Skertchly considering that hitting a hayetack would be about the sum of their accomplishments in this respect.—The Peoples of the World,for July.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TnuusDAy.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TnuusDAy.
THE MAILS—Mr. FAWCETT stated, in reply to a ques- tion. that the mail steamers arriving at Suez from India were now ordered to proceed direct to Plymouth through the Canal. •

THE AMBER OF AFGRANISTAN.—Mr. CROSS said the Government were not in a position to give any information as to contributions in money or arms Le the Ameer of Afghanistan. The relations of the Indian Government with the Ameer were very satisfactory. THE SUNDERLAND DISASTER. Mr. MUNDELLA, ques- tioned about the Sunderland disaster, said it was a scandal and a breach of good order that schools should be made the recruiting ground for itinerant conjurors or purveyors of entertainments, and he proposed to send out a circular to this tffect.

PRINCE LUCIEN BONAPARTE'S PENMON.—Mr. GLADSTONE defended in warm language the bestowal of a pEnsion on Prince Lucien Bonaparte, to whose services in the science of philology he paid a handsome tribute. THE SECOND SUEZ CANAL.—In reply to Mc Monk, Mr. GLADSTONE said no negotiations at present were in progress with the Egyptian Government respecting the proposed New Suez Canal, but in order to give effect to the provisional arrangement, if it was sanctioned by Parliament, negotia- tions would be commenced. M. de Lesseps was in posses- sion of a concession under which he could largely widen the present canal and afford additional accommodation to trade, so far as he might think fit, charging the same rates as were now chated. M. de Lesseps might make this large improvement in the crnal, but it was thought by the British Government that by far the best and most effectual improvement would be the construction of a parallel canal in the line of the present canal. It was not certain that the land he possessed was sufficient to enable him to make the second line of canal, I and that being so, the land being the property of the Egyp- tian Government, it would be nccessary for -him to acquire new land from the Egyptian Government for that purpose, and that would be the subject at the negotiations. The Government could not undertake to obtain a concession for making another canal, as M. de Lesseps was in possession of the exclusive right to make the canal so far as the Isth- mus of Suez was concerned.—Mr. BOURKE east doubt upon the existence of this exclusive right, but Mr. GLADSTONE said -it was a matter of public notoriety, and was the under- standing on which the money was subscribed, and it formed the basis of the Government arrangement. MR. BRADLAuGEL—The SPEAKER read the correspondence with Mr. Bradlaugh. A further letter had been received from Mr. Bradlaugh stating that he was advised that the resolution of the House was absolutely illegal, and that in obedience to the law he would endeavour to take his seat as duly-elected member for Northkmpton. The Speaker added, amid 'cheers from the Conservatives, that he had instructed the Sergeant-at-Arms? enforce the order of the House.

MISCELLANEOUS.—Lord E. FITZHAURICE, replying to a I question, announced that it had been decided to send out to Egypt a medical gentleman of high position to report on the cholera outbreak and to support Sir E. Malet in advising the Egyptian Government as to the proper measures to be taken.—ln reply to Sir M. Hicks-Beach, Mr. ASHLEY said that Dr. Jorrisen had been dismissed by the Transvaal Volksraad, but no reason was assigned. He had learned, too, that a resolution was on the way from the Volksraad con- demning the action of the Imperial Government in taking over Basutoland.—The House went into Committee on the Civil Servic,l Estimates. A number of votes having been agreed to, the House resumed and went into Committee on the Corrupt Practices Bill.
A COFFEE HOUSE FOR EARLESTOWN.
MEETING OF SHAREHOLDERS.

The first general meeting of the shareholders of the "Earlestown Coffee House Company" was held in the Mission lent, Legh-street, on Tuesday evening. There was a fair attendance, and Mr. E. J. Weaver presided. Among those present were—Messrs. John Clarke, A. Pimb- lett, Houghton, and Jameson. After the meeting had been opened with prayer, Mr. Weaver said he would give a short explanation as to why they had met that evening. For a long time past some of them had thought that a coffee- house for Earlestown was a very desirable thing, especially for the sake of those who had lately signed the pledge and joined the Blue Ribbon Army or any other temperance society in the town. In fact some of those persons had mentioned the matter to him—that there should be some place of resort where they could meet together to spend the evenings away from the influence of the public-houses and their old companions, and he and others had seriously thought the matter over for some time—as to the best plan to be adopted to carry out what had been suggested. They had decided that a coffee-house was just the thing that would meet the requirements—where the men could have a place to resort as they wished. They intended to have one room set apart for social gatherings, and would have newspapers, so that the men could meet together, con- verse together, and have little "free-and-easy " meetings. They would be at perfect liberty in such matters so long as they conducted themselves properly, and no restrictions would be placed upon their enjoying themselves in the best manner they could. In order to set the affair afloat, they had thought it would be as well to issue shares—the shares to be £1 each—and ss. to be paid for each share on allot- ment. They anticipated that that amount would be all the money required, and that they would not have occasion to , call on the shareholders to pay any more. They contemplated ; that they would have sufficient to open free from debt, and I that the proceeds would afterwards pay all expenses and be something towards the sharehollers besides. They were not merely taking the matter up in a financial spirit to make great profits, but in the linterests of the workingmen of Earlestown—to provide them a place of resort where they could spend their evenings away from the influence of the public-houses. Still, while they were doing that, they anticipated having a little return for the money they bad invested in it. He himself was very sanguine respecting the movement, and had not the least doubt it would be a great success. When he had seen the crowda about the Market Place on a Friday evening he thought, in fact he felt sure, that they should be able to draw sufficient that night alone to pay all the work- ing expenses of the week. He was happy to say that they had sufficient shares already taken up which gave them sufficient to start with at any time they thought proper. Two or three persons had recently been looking over several premises, and they had selected, as the most appropriate, the the new shop belonging Mr. Gerard Thorp, near the Market. He ( Mr. Weaver) thought they could not have a better stand or better premises in Earlestown. (Hear, hear.) It had been suggested that they should call the building a Coffee Palace, because they had gin palaces, and why should they not nave coffee palaces ? (Hear, hear, and applause.) He afterwards re- marked there were several business matters wanted attend- ing to at that meeting, the first of which was the payment of the 55. per share already taken up. At the close of this business he intimated that they bad been paid on 39 shares —which realized a sum considerably more than they needed at present. (Applause.)—Mr. E. J. Weaver was subse- quently appointed president; Mr. George Clarke, secretary' • and Mr. Adam Pimblett, treasurer. These three,along with Messrs John Clarke, W. Houghton, W. Jameson, and G. Thorp were afterwards elected as a committee.—The meet- ing shortly afterwards concluded. It is believed that the premises in question will be opened as a coffee palace in about a fortnight.

A FEMALE INVINCIBLE.-At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, a youth named Peter Hand, who did not ap• pear, and a young woman named Kate Ford, wereocharged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting with each other in Short-street, on the 2nd inst. The latter named defend nt denied that she had been fighting, but said that Hand used some disgraceful language regarding her, and among other things nailed her a ". - informer" and an " invir,cible." The Bench decided to dismiss the charge against her, and issue a warrant for Hand's appre- , heneion.

D COLERIDGE ON THE RIGHT OF BAIL.—The Lord Chief Justice, addressing the grand jury at Salisbury on Stturday, remarked upon the frequency with which persons of infericr position were refused bail, while persons in a lePerior position, even on serious charges, and who might be thought more likely to try to escape, were admitted to bail. Lie asked them to consider whether it was not advisable to give more extended use to the pewer of bailing. Men were soured and made bad citizens through this long im- prisonment. PANIC IN A THELTRE.—A panic, which might have bad very serious results, took place at the Amphi-theatre, Barrow, on Sunday evening, while General Booth was hold- ing a Salvationist meeting. The building was Crowded, about 2,000 people being present, when cries in the gallery - created alarm. Some thought lire had broken out, others ' that the gallery was falling, and at this time a sound like a Pistol shot caused a wild rash to be made for the doors. Fortunately, General Booth had presence of mind enough to as the band to strike up a tune, and the reassuring strains allayed the excitement. Several people, however, were injured. OPENING OF A NEW RAILWAY.— On Monday morning the new line of railway constructed by the London and orth-Western Company between Lancaster and Glasson Dock iris opened for passenger traffic. By the acquisition of this branch more direct communication with the ports of Liverpool, Whitehaven, Barrow, &c, is established. ,The line skirts the river Lune nearly the whole distance, about 5i ,Ineiles- The Port Commissioners have expended several euonsand pounds in the erection of a fine stone pier for the accommodation of vessels loading and unloading. Gleason Dock, being picturesquely situated at the mouth of the Lune, is also expected to attract visitors. BOARD OF TRADE Rernuss.—The Board of Trade returns e ',Ol. June show that the exports amounted to £204)34,942, a UeCrease of £83.308 as compared with June, 1882, but an in- crease of £1,229,945 as compared with June, 1881. For the SIX months the exports amounted to £116,966,905, a decrease of £1,311,625 as compared with the corresponding half of last year, but an increase of £7,658,430 as contrasted with 1881. The imports in June amounted to £36,740.030, an increase of £4,832292 as compared with June. 1882, and £5,874,148 in comparison with June, 1881. For the half Year the imports were £217,185,442, an increase of £lO 366,927, and £18371,806 in comparison with 1882 and 1881 respectively. The total of gold and silver imported amounted to £1,615,161, and that exported to £1,254,468. MURDER AND ATTEMPTED SmatoE.—Greet sensation was caused at Todmorden, on Tuesday, by the report that a Married woman, residing in Longfield-terrace, Todmorden, had cut a child's throat, and afterwards attempted suicide.l The rumour proved to be true. The woman is named uannah Uttley, aged 32 years, wife of Michael Uttleea weaver. About a week ago the woman was confined, and tbe had appeared to get on satisfactorily. Her mother-in- 'or, however, had occasion to go in her bedroom on Tuesday Morning, when she found the child covered over with clothes, and its head nearly cut off. She also found that thel child's mother had made a deep wound in her own throat. The beet was saturated with blood. The mother is still alive. though in a most precarious condition. A razor had been used by the woman who committed the rash act. • M. BRADLAUGH AT LEEDS.—On Saturday afternoon a edemonstration was held in Leeds, under the auspices of the Leeds Federation of Liberal Clubs, by way of protest against the continued exclusion of Mr. Bradlaugh from the House of Commons. The day being fine, there were many specta- tors. There were delegates from Manchester, Halifax, Brad- ford, Northampton, Sheffield, and otLer towns. Mr. Brad- laugh rode in a carriage in the procession, which proceeded to Woodhouse. where an open-air meeting was held. Here about 10,000 people heard the speeches which were delivered, and which %ere. receired with applause. Resolutions were Passed declaring the action of Parliament a gross breach of the constitutional law, and urging the House to allow Mr. Bradlaugh to take the oath or to affirm. Mr. Bradlaugh, in the course of his address, said he should in a few days again claim his seat. Eneueset PATENTS.
