The trial of the four Galway conspirators, who were in- dicted for having blown up a portion of Weston House, the residence of Sir William Mahon's agent, county Galway, was resumed and concluded en Saturday, at the Court- 'muse, Sligo, before Mr. Justice Murphy and a special jury. The prisoners were found guilty, and William Tansey, the leader, was sentenced to 14 years', Patrick Rogerson to 12 years', and Patrick Naughton to 8 years' penal servitude, and James Kelly to two years' imprisonment. The last- named prisoner thanked his Lordship, and the others cried "God save Ireland "on receiving sentence. It is estimated that under the Arrears Act the Irish Land Commission have already paid out to landlords over £620.000, and orders for further payments to the extent of £135,000 have been issued. About £50,000 more will clear off the remaining claims, bringing up the total sum dis- bursed to the landlords under the Arrears Act to something I over £BOO,OOO, which is very nearly the figure estimated I originally as the sum that would be Deeded under Section 1, which gave the relief to the small tenancies. The £BOO,OOO paid out represents between two and three mil- lions sterling of arrears due by Irish tenants. Over 90 per cant. of the claims were declared to be bond fide. The National League held its first meeting since Mona- ghan election in Dublin on Wednesday, and Mr. Sexton, M.P., was not unnaturally jubilant on that subject. He spoke of Mr. Gladstone as being "open to education," and said the right hon. gentleman could be " educated " to the point of complying with requests for State guarantee in purchasing the holdings of Ireland for the tLi..aut..-3. Mr. Sexton said the League would direct its whole strength to the carrying of seats in the North, and calculated Mr. Par- nell's following in the next Parliament at 75 or 80 members. The hon. member has omitted to take into account the probability of a redistribution of seats before the next election. DISAPPEARANCE OF " INVINCIBLES." Matthew Brady, the brother of the "Invincible" Joe Bradg, who was I executed for the Phcenix Park murders, has left Ireland. IHe found himself so continually watched by the police I after his liberation on bail for writing the threatening letter Ito the foreman of the jury who convicted his brother, that fhe thought it better to go away. Another notorious char- acter has also left the United Kingdom. Sylvester I Kingston, who was arrested some time ago near Liverpool I for being concerned in the plot to murder Poole, and who, according to informers, was one of the principal agents in the Fenian Vigilance Committee 'ire Dublin, has taken advantage of his renewed liberty and stolen away in a sailing vessel from Liverpool. Trig INFORMER CAREY.—II is stated that James Carey, the "Invincible" informer, was sent out of Ireland a few days ago without receiving a penny reward for his services. The Lord-Lieutenant positively refused to give him a written pardon. He was offered his choice to take his chance of safety on liberation or go to a distant colony, for which his wife and family had already set out, they having left Dublin several days betore. Carey was stunned at the news, and cursed and swore at the Government; but then sulkily consented to go, stating that his life would not be worth an hour's purchase in Dublin. His brother Peter got a reward. James Carey is said to have travelled from Dub- lin to Holyhead, and thence to London. For conveying his house property in Dublin to his nephew and mother-in-law without substantial consideration, while his debt to the Corporation for rates exceeded £lOO, Carey has been abju- dicated a bankrupt. This will relieve the Dublin City Council of all further trouble as to Carey's membership, but it leaves unsettled the interesting question as to whether the Council was justified in expelling the inf..roaer before he was declared a bankrupt. THE PEERS AND THE IRISH LAND ACT.—The fourth report of the Lords' Committee on the working of the Irish Land Act was issued on Tuesday. Their Lordships find that the emigration clauses of the Act have entirely failed, while the evidence taken shows that in some parts of Ire- land it is by emigration only that the prevalent suffering and discontent can be overcome. With respQct to the settle- ment of jualicial rents the Committee suggest several altera- tions in procedure, and regret that the duty of settling rents has been delegated to the Sul,-Commissionees, with the natural result of want of uniformity in decisions.' They do not see any probability of the reduced rents being better paid in times of difficulty or agitation than the old ones ; and,while the inclining tenants must pay an increased price for tenant right, the land is in the case of owners practically unsaleable. No inaney, say the Committee in conclusion, can be obtained on mortgage, and no capital will come into the country. Landlords, where they continue to reside, are largely reducing their elrpenditure, and many of those hitherto resident are ceasing to reside. The relations for- merly subsisting between landlords and tenants have been dislocated or destroyed the tenants have become de- moralized, and they readily lend themselves to hope of fresh agitation and a new L?nd Act.

MR. FIELD: FURTHER OUTRAGES. Mr. Field, the juror whose life was attempted by the Dub- lin Invincibles, Is still threatened. His wife and daughter are frequently insulted in the street, and threatening letters of the most violent character have been addressed to him. The life of, Mr. Quinn, his manager, is also threttened, and on Sunday night an attempt was made to farce an entrance into his house. He fired at the miscreants, whok.effected their escape. This is the second attempt of a siliailar kind, and there can be little doubt that the object was to intimi- date him by actual violence, If not to take his life. Ile was determined to leave the country, but. is unwilling to leave Mr. Field while he is endeavouring to dispose of his stock ' and tlic ;ri.terest in his house. The police have received in- formation of these outrages.

•EARLESTOWN MUSICAL SOCIETY. This society, which was establiehed in the autumn of 1881, and has been prominently before the public for two winter seasons, is undergoing a great change. Its origina- tor, Mr. John Hayes. has been obliged to resign the conduc- torship on account of professional duties taking him away from the neighbourhood, and as the ofil•-•.e has been entirely honorary, the members of the society desired to present Mr. Hayes with some testimonial of their great indebtedness to him. They met in the Wesleyan Infant school-room on Wednesday night last, and presented him with a clock of the Queen Anne style, the case being of oak, ebonised on the outside, giving it a very neat appearance. The chair was occupied by Mr. Haynes. The Chaitman called upon the secretary, Mr. J. H. Profit, to read the address which ac- companied the clock. The address was then read as follows : "The Earlestown 'Musical So dety t Mr. John Hayes.—lt Is with exceedingly great pleasure that we, 'be act've members of the above society, present the accompanying cl ck; which we ask you to accept as a t 'ken of our deep gratituie for your most valuable services as h morary conductor. As a society we owe our existence entirely to you energet"e efforts in promot- ing the cultivation of music. During the two sessions which have beel held since its formati in the s iciety has been a very great benefit both to us and to the pub le at large. Tharefore, It is with sincere regret that we receive your resignation, rendered necessary through your• leaving this neighbors, h sod. But we are assured that your-persistent and energetic efforts to promote the welfare of others. tied the spread of good musie; coupled with your unselfish, disinterested zeal, and with your c insistent moral life, will win for you hosts of friends and rewards in whatever sphere you may be placel. Wishing yiar much success and p osperity in all your undertakings, we are, on behalf of the members of the society, (Signed) H. E. RA:VNES. Vice-President; Jourt H. Peony, Honorary Seere- tary.—Es.rlestown, July 11th. 1S81" The presentation was afterwards made. Mr. Hayes, in re- sponse, expressed the great pleasure he bad had in conduct- ing the 84ciety, and hoped that the success which had attended the society's efforts in the past would in no ways diminish but rather increase in the future. He also impressed upon the members the necessity oilndividual effort to ensure the extensive puble patronage and saccess in musi- cal attainments, which, he thought, were quite within their reach.—The vacancy caused by Mr. Haves' resigna- tion will be filled by Mr. John T. Elliott, of St. Helene. At their meeting on Wednesday night the members bad placed before them the terms and conditions under which he would consent to accept the appointment of conductor. These were freely discuss-d and modified a little. Since then he has endorsed the alterations, so the society may still look for- ward to a very prosperous career. •

HONOUR TO A NEWTON GENTLEITAN.—A few dAys ago Mr. J. H. Nichols. of Sandfield Hall, N ' eliton received the pleasing intenigence that he had been elected a Fellow of the Royal Geolos.,rical Society of Loudon, to tint he now adds the letter! F R G.S. to hie name.

Thursday's returns show a decrease in the number of deaths which have taken place in Egypt from cholera. The Potts is endeavouring to obtain from the Ottomin Bank a loan of £60,000, for the payment of the salaries of public functionaries. A rich Italian, Signor Corpi, has been captnred by brigands near Ismid, and carried off to the mountains. The band, which numbers thirty men, demands a ransom of

£3OO. The trial of said Bey Khandeel, formerly prefect of Alex- andria, and the official instigator of the riots there, was con- chided on Tuesday. He was sentenced to penal servitude for seven years. The West African mail brings some unpleasant news from Gaboon, where the French commandant appears to have acted in a very arbitrary and offensive manner towards the English traders and American missionaries. A Cape Coast,Castle telegram says :—Captain Barrcw and the other special commissioner of the Gold Coast Govern- ment have returned from Coomassie. They succeeded be adverting war between the ex-liings Koffee and Mensah. There is a large party in Ashantee who desire the restora- tion of King Koffee Kalkalli. A Durban telegram reports a "great battle" in Zululand between the forces of Cetewayo and Oham. The latter chieftain was taken prisoner and conveyed to tlundi. The Transvaal Volksraad has "summarily dismissed" Dr. Jar- risen, the Attorney-General of the Republic, who has been in London for some time as the agent of the Government. It is reported from St. Petersburg that before the depar- ture from Russia of the Khan of Khiva and the son of the Emir of Bokhara, these Princ2s agreed with the Russian Government for the construction of a tramway 300 kilome- treskang, uniting Khiva with Turkestan. Ths tramway will traverse the sandy plain of Bokhara. The new treaty between Russia and Persia for the "recti- fication" of the frontiers of the former Power has not yet been ratified by the Shah, who is absent from the capital. An extraordinary clause in the Convention provides that protests which may be made by England against the treaty are to be referred to the Russian Government. By the" rec- tification" of her frontier under this treaty Russia virtually becomes the master of Merv. RIOT AT A BIILLFIGIIT.—A. riot broke out at Beziers, France, on Sunday, at a bullfight given by a Spanish toreador. The people, becoming enraged at the inferiority of the entertainment, and at the raised prices of seats' broke and threw into the arena all the benches and planks they could lay hands on, tore down the Presidential flag, and demolished the illuminations prepared for the National Fat!. Fortunately nobody was injured. It is reported from Varna that the inhabitants of Crete have refused, at the suggestion of their representatives in the National Assembly, to pay the taxes. Photiades Pasha, upon this refusal, has asked the Porte whether, if it be con- tinued, he should employ the troops to enforce the collec- tion. Great agitation prevails in the island. The relations between the Governor and the representatives are said to be completely interrupted. Two terrible tragedies are reported from the United States. On Wednesday a mob of masked men at Ilet Sulphur Springs, Colorado, fired upon four county commissioners and the county clerk, two of the persons attacked being killed, and others mortally wounded. The cause of this outrage is at present unknown. On the same day the con- victs in the Oregon State prison at Salem attacked the officers in the course of a desperate attempt to escape. Three of the convicts were killed, two were wounded, and eight others escaped. A GAMBLER'S ADVENTURES.—The Berlin correspondent of the Times telegraphs that on Tuesday a man, Reuter by name, moving in the upper classes of society, was tried for systematic gambling. Reuter was tried for "professional haz trd playing," of which he was found guilty, and for which he was sentenced to eight months' imprisonment, with a fine of 6,000 marks, bail to the extent of 40,000 marks being demanded of him. It formed an additional count in the indictment against him that when arrested in a fashion- able restaurant in Berlin he endeavoured to soften the heart of his cap•urer by slipping jet° his hand a thousand mark note; but Prussian officials, no matter of what grade, are the most incorruptible of human beings. Reuter lived in a fine West-end street in great style. He discounted bills at a high rate, went to all the chief watering-places, attended all the racecoursee, and enjoyed the services of an adroit confederate with whom he managed to fleece oppo- nents to the tune of as much as 200,000 marks at a sitting. He consorted much with officers and other aristocratic gamblers and with sporting men—and tell the Jewish youth and the jeunesse done of Berlin affect to be sporting men, hitherto an unknown race in Germany—and was a sort of peripatetic bank fur needy players at trente et quarante, roulette, make°, and similar games of hazard. Once be won from a companion 180,000 marks, and contented himself with the payment of less than a third of the sum. At last, however, his invariable good luck led his victims to suspect false play, and although this could not be clearly brought borne to him, he has now been made an example of.

THE STATE OF IRELAND. On Tuesday night, a rick of hay of over G'.) tons, the pro- perty of Mr.-Errington, M.P., was burned near Cashcd. Toe fire is attributed to malice. 'Patrick Hanlon, one of the nine men in cost r•dy at Mullin- gar for the murder of Mrs. Smythe in April, 1.832, has ill rued approver, and on his testimony eight more arrest have been

made. The appeal of the manager of the licery Schtl fte.? (Mr. Harrington) against the sentence cf the locti magistrate for the effonce of publishing threatening notic,..,s was before the County Court Judge atTralee on Tuesday. The sen- tence was confirmed, and Harrington will, therefore, be im-

prisoned for six months. A deputation of Irish members of Parliament and others interested in the furtherance of Sunday Closing in Ireland- waited upon Lord Spencer in London on '1 bursday, to ex- press regret at the proposed withdrawal of the Irish Sunday Closing Bill, and to ask the Government to rcconsider the decision. The proceedings were private. The Orangemen in the North of Ireland celt-brated " the Twelfth " with great demonstrations of loyalty to the Throne. At Belfast an immense procession was formed and a meeting held, at which resolutions denouncing the SO - called "National " party, and protesting agains: Any diplo- matic intercourse with .one were passed. The Dublin Freeman's JoaPnal says the Irish Divorce Court will shortly be engaged in a suit which will unfold sens.ttional incidents, with regard to which evidence to jus- tify a divorce is in process of investigation. The plaintiff is a military personage, well known and highly popular in fashionable circles, and he will seek a divorce from his wife , on the ground of her misconduct with a brother officer, a mems:er of an old and respected family in the north of Ire-

1 ind. It is already known that the dynamite party at Cork has been broken up. The police received information a- while ago of some of its criminal designs, and a number of arrests followed. They knew, too, of a large deposit of the explosive mat4.rial, and since the arrests a watch has ben kept on the spot where it was concealed—two miles onside the city of Cork—with the view of entrapping more of the assassins. No one, however, seemed anxious to possess the dynamite, which was in the shape of cartridges, and on Saturday night the police bad it dug up and removed into a place of safe
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. I RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD. 4

On Tuesday the fortnightly meting of Guardians was' held at Dutton Workhouse. There were present :—Revs. Canon Barclay (chairman), John Lockwood, and .1. W. N Tanner; Messts. T. Andrews, John Challoner, W. Jacksen, T. Norman, W. Handley, F. Fairhurst, P. Speakman, E. A. Wallington, J. G. Hamilton' H. Linaker (clerk), and R. J. Dansey (Local Government Board Inspector). • THE BOARD AND THE BALLOT. A letter was read from the Local Government Board acknowledging the receipt of the Board's memorial praying that the system of Guardians' election should be by bailor, and stating that the suggestions would receive the considera- tion of the Board. THE SALARY OF THE ASSISTANT MATRON. Mr. NORMAN moved that the salary of Miss Agnes Jones be increased from £lO to £l6. He stated that Miss Jones had acted as assistant matron for the past 10 years, and the services which she performed were eminently deserving of the increase now proposed.—The Rev. J. W. N. TANNER seconded the motion, and remarked that Miss Jones had given entire satisfaction, and the increase, which was a very reasonable one, was thoroughly deserved.—Mr. CHALLorrEre did pot think thc,l rpoyer and seconder of the motion were dealing honourably with Miss Jones. It she haa only been receiving £lO for 10 years, he did not know how they could for shame offer a rise to £l6. Why did they not increase the salary to £2O? (Hear, hear.)—Mr. • NORMAN said the matter had been discussed by the Visiting Committee, and it was thought that the Board would not agree to £2O. However, if it was the wish of the Board, he would gladly substitute £2O for £l6.—Mr. HAMILTON said the ratepayers whom he represented seemed to think an increase of 100 per cent, was too mcch, and he should, therefore, vote for the increase of £l6. Mr. CHALLONER said the ratepayers had nothing whatever to do with a thins of this sort. They had deputed the Guardians to do their work, and if the ratepayers could not trust them, let them come and de the work themselves. What did the ratepayers know about Miss Jones? They , would not know her if they met her, and did not know whether she was a man or a woman. (Laughter.)—Mr. FAIRHURST did not think any argument had been raised againet the increase. If for ten years she had been under- paid, it was quite time they increased the salary.—Mr. Nor- man withdrew his motion ; and, on the proposition of Mr. CHALLONER, seconded by Mr. FAIRHURST, it was decided that the salary should be increased from £lO to £2O per year.

MB. DANSEY AND THE noun. Mr. DANSEy said he had been over the Workhouse that morning, and was glad to see that everything inside was so satisfactory. The inmates were grateful for the treatment they received. He had visited the wards in the new hos- pital, and thought they were capital. The Guardians ought to be very well satisfied with them. He would, Uwe% er, suggest that two cupboards be provided for medicines, be- cause it was undesirable that patients should have the ha d- ling of them. He also drew attention to the fact that in the old lavatories there were a few pipes connected with the drains, which he recommended should be cut off.

THE DETENTION OF VAGRANTS. Mr. DANSEY said he had noticed that the Guardians had not thought it right to detain vagrants under the last Act. The Act of last Session said that all vagrants should be de- tained to the third thy after admission, unless the Guardians gave directions to the contrary; and they were empowered to give directions to the contrary as to any class or classes. At the house, however, as far as he could gather, a general direction was given to the master to discharge all vagrants on the second day. The effect of the detention in Shropshire and Herefordshire had been the diminution in the number of vagrants of rather more than 50 per cent. It seemed that at Dutton they had ample room for the detention of vagrants. They had seven cells, and the average number of vagrants were not more than 20 a fortnight. He was quite prepared to say that if they adopted the system of detention, their number of vagrants would be diminished. In one Union where the Guardians had a very limited accommodation and were afraid to use the power of detention, they had seven cells and 52 vagrants a fortnight: He recommended them to try the rule for a fort- night, and then, if they had not room, to modify it. They put the rule into operation, and instead of 52 vagrants the number came down to 19, and the average was now about 15 a fortnight. Although the Guardians of the Runcorn Union might be complying with the letter of the Act, they were not conforming to its spirit, and he thought they ought to give it their consideration.—Mr. HANDLEY moved, and Mr. SPEAKMAN seconded, that the matters mentioned by Mr. Dansey should be considered by the Visiting Committee; and the motion was carried.

FEARFUL ATTACK ON AN IRISHMAN AT RUNCORN. John and Mary Connor, man and wife, were brought before Mr. Wm. Benkes at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, to answer a charge of inflicting grievous bodily harm upon an Irish labourer namrd Martin Walsh.—Walsh was wounded so seriously that his appearance in court was itnpossible, and Dr. MacDougall informed his Worship that the injured man was so battered about the head that it was not unlikely that erysipelas would take place. In those circumstances the injuries might terminate fatally, and he recommended that the man's depositions should be taken. During an ex- perience extending over 14 years in Runcorn he had never seen a worse case of battery. - His Worship, accompanied by Mr. Ashton (the clerk), Mr. Johnson (the deputy clerk), and Superintendent Williamson subsequently adjohrnedt to n common lodging-house in Mersey-street, where• the injured man was lying. His depositions were then taken in the presence of the prisouera. The circumstances of the case are as follows :—Walsh and the prisoners lodged with an old man nimsd John McGarra at a house in Mersey-street. On Saturday afternoon Walsh went to Widnes, and returned home about 11 o'clock in a state of intoxication. It is alleged that he made use of a most disgusting remark to Mrs. Connor, which so exasperated her husband that he threw Walsh into the street. Walsh alighted on the kerbstone and injured his leg. He lay there for some time, and then Sergeants Walley and Meelichee] came upon the scene and took him inside the house. After the departure of the officers Walsh alleges that both the prisoners attacked him. With a blow on the eye Connor felled him to the ground, and then battered him about the face and bead with his lists, whilst Mrs. Connor picked up a poker, with which she several times struck him violently on the head. He was also savagely kicked about the body. At last he became insensibie through the ill-usage he had received, and the great quan- tity of blood he had lost from his wounds, his head being one mass of bruises. He re'rnembered nothing further until Sunday, when he found himself lying in bed. On that day Mrs. Connor, he alleged, was " going on like mad," and. threatened thet if he did not " clear out" she would. " chuck" him through the bedroom window. Subsequently, however, P.C. Bossons apprehended the prisoners, who, on the evidence of the pros?.cutor, were remanded until Monday next.—On the advice of Dr. MacDougall, Walsh was con- veyed to the workhouse hospital, where he would have care bestowed upon him. If he remained in the dirty hovel where he now was the doctor could hold out no hope of his re- covery.

J. W. N: TANNER seconded the motion, which was carried. THE COUNTY RATE BASIS. _

The CLERK read the following letter received in reply to the one written by the direction of the Board with reference to the revision of the county rate:—" Clerk of the Peace's ' Office, Chester, ith July, 1853.—Dear Sir,—County Rate Basis. Referring to your letter of the 27th ult., addressed to Mr. C. W. Potts, and which I show9d to Lord Egerton of Tattoo, the chairman of the Quarter Sessions, I am desired by his lordship to inform n you that he had already considered the desirability of a revision of the county rate basis, and had conferred with me about it before your letter was received. His lordship authorises me to say that he intends, at the next Michaelmas Quarter Sessions in October, to move for the appointment of a committee under the County Rate Act, for the purpose of making a new basis or standard of county rate for the whole county.—l am, yours truly, TROM&S ROBERTS."

RUNCORN hUR-AI, SANITARY AUTHORITY. The meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Work- house, on Tuesday. Present :—Mr. John Ashton (in the chair), the Revs. John Lockwood and J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. John Challoner. Thomes Andrews, E. A. Walling- ton. J. G. Hamilton, W. Jackson, H. Linaker (clerk), and J. Farrington (nuisance inspector.) Mr. R. J. Dansey (Local Government Board inspector) also attended, HALTON SEWERAGE The seal of the Board was attached to the contract for the construction of the main sewer at Halton. 'VITAL STATISTICS. Mr. J. G. BRIDE, medical officer, reported that during the quarter ended June 30th, the regietrar's returns recorded 153 births and 91 deaths in the three aistricts comprised in the Authority's district. Of the births, 93 were males and 60 females, the birth rate being 7 9 per 1,000. Of the deaths, 56 were males and 35 females, the death rate being 4.7 per 1,000. In the corresponding quarter of last year the births were 167, being 8.6 per 1,000; and 78 deaths, or 4.6 per 1,000. Of the deaths, 36 were under five years of age, 27 of these being under one year; and 55 were five years and upwards. Twelve deaths had resulted from bronchitis, three from 4i.errhoet, 1 from diphtheria, 2 from whooping coneh, and two from scarlatina. THE PUBLIC WELL AT etenfones. The Authority again c3nsidered the enclosure of the public well at Antrobus ; and it was decided that the solicitor to the Authority be instructed to take evidence on the matter, and to advise the Authority thereon. POLLUTION OF WATERCOURSES AT FRODSAM. The CLERK read a letter from Messrs. Heywood and Massie, of the Weaver Chemical Works, Frodsham Bridge, calling attention to the state of the water-courses from which they derived their supply of water. The brook had been polluted by the seWage from the houses in Water- street and those comprising Nwtown. On purchasing the Weaver works, the writers stated that they purchased all rights to the water-courses as hitherto enjoyed by the previous iiViners. The pollution was causing a serious detriment to their business, and on behalf of Mr. W. Haves, owner of the Salt Works Farm, and of Mr. James Andrews and Mr. John Priestner, who had requested Heywood and Massie to act for them, they stated that the brook was the only supply of their farms, at which their cattle drank, and the 'pollution was a source of injury to them. On behalf of them parties Messrs. Heywood and Massie petitioned for an abatement of the pollution.— Mr. FARRINGTON presented a report on the subject, in which, after stating that he inspected the brook, &c., on the Bth inst., he remarked :—The conrse of the brook, or water- course in question, commencing from the lower end, is froth the Salt Works Farm, under the railway, along the valley by Water-street and up to a pond below Towutield-lane, into which pond both water and sewage from premises higher up empties. The total number of houses from which sewage is carried into this stream either in a direct or indirect manner is 100. At the bottom end of such stream there is a lodge, or pond, which is intended to supply water to Messrs. Eleywood and Massie's works, and also to supply the cattle on Salt Works Farm with water. On the date of inspection, nothing WAS flowing into this lodge but crude sewage, which emanated from 55 houses in Newtown. New- town contains 66 houses, 53 of which (when all are occu- pied) discharge sewage direct into the stream; tiny are, it ;s true, drained into a small receptacle, but it is practically of no use, as the sewage simply runs through it, and I am of opinion that it has never been cleansed since it was made. From the point where the Newton sewage discharges, the course of the stream changes, and it runs. along and under the railway, ard opens out again into land in the occupation of Mr. James Andrews. Here the road water and the sewage from eleven houses situated in Bridge-lane empties. It is intercepted in a sump-bole, and then flows along again in open gutters in land. At the time of inspection nothing whatever was passing into the stream at this point, but in wet weatherit is bound to do so.-Weter- street contains twelve houses, the sewage from which flows direct into the stream. There is a large lodgment of stag- nant sewage matter at this point, and when rain comes it will be carried further down. From the lower end of Water- street to end of course nothing whatever was flowing; but the fact is that when the rain descends there will be, as into this length the road water, and the sewage from 25 houses, finds it way, either directly or indirectly, into thoebrook or watercourse. As previously -stated, the sewage from 100 houses goes into the stream, 67 directly, and 43 indirectly." A committee, consisting of the representatitives of Fred' sham Lorship, Sutton, and Newton, together with the er- officio members, was zippointee to investipte an report upon the matter.—There was no other business of public in- terest.

div.p: A CARELESS COLLIER.---James Baines, a collier, was charged at the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, with having had a tobacco pipe in his possession whilet in Re Havana Mine, Parr, contrary to the special rules. Mr. J. 0. Swift prosecuted on behalf of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., and stated that on the 25th June the officials at the colliery mentioned had the colliers searched in order to see if any of them had any article in their possession smell as matches, pipes, &c., which they were forbidden to have by the rules. None of the workmen, excepting defendant, had anything of the kind about them, but be had the pipe in question. Defendant pleaded guilty to the charge, but said he was not aware that the pipe was in his pocket. He was fined 10s and costs. A HALF-HEARTED CIALLANT.—Mary Chadwick, a young woman, who lives with her father in College-street, on Monday applied, through Mr. J. 0. Swift. for an order to be made out against a young man named Thomas Sumner, to contribute towards the support of her illegitimate child, of which she 4(1 he was the father. It was stated that defendant was the son of a well-Cc-do farmer at Scarisbrick, but at the time of his acquaintance with the complainant he had worked in St. Helens. He had assured her on several occasions he would marry her, and that he was not one of those sort who did not keep their word. Even since the birth of the child he had offered either to contribute a weekly sum towards its support or to marry her, and she had chosen the latter alternative, but he had drawn back again. Defeo- dant said he was not a farmer's son, but only the son of a farmer's son, and his father was engaged on his grand- father's farm.—An order for 5s per week was made. THREATENING A WITNESS: EXEMPLARY PUNISHMENT. John Burke, a middle-aged man, was charged at the St. Helens Police Court, on Tuesday, with haying stolen a Wit, of the value of Is 6d, the property of Alice Aspinall. —The prosecutrix, it appeared, was a widow, and kept a lodging house in Tontine-street. On Saturday night the prisoner and another man named John Wagstaffee took lod- gings with her, and left on Monday morning. As soon as they had left the house the prisoner said to Wegstaffe that be had got "eighteenpence worth on his back," and on being asked what be meant by that, said he had taken a shirt. He wanted Wagstaffe to get it washed for him, but the latter refused, and gave information to the police. Prisoner was apprehended, and the shirt he wore at the time was identified by Mrs. liepinall as her property.—Priaoner did not deni the charge, but, referring to Wagstaffe, said, "It's all through that bald-headed —, but I'll bald-head him when I come out. If he's in St. Helens I'll get at him, and I'll leave him a cripple if I serve leaven years .for it."—The Chairman (Mr. W. Pilkington) said the Bench thought pri- soner a dangerous customer, and judging from his behaviour en t then by constables. in the box, would be best in prison. He would have to go to gaol fer three months' hard labour.—Prlsoner : I am able againto d o into; ml:rm.encaend wtoci tiiitrheaetreen as aagnSyL reb u et l swe s talke PECULIAR EXCISE:TROSECUTION AT ST. It appeared that Mr. Sawyer, one of the excise officers in this district, had visited Messrs. They really looked upon him as a sort of jobbing gardener engaged between them. Mr. Rawlins also complained of not having further notice of the decision of the Revenue authorities befnre those pro- ceedings were taken.—Mr. Heal said defendant had been repeatedly called upon in the matter.—Mr. Rawlins said they had employed men for 25 years in the same way,, and they had never been required to take out a license.—Mr. Heal : That only shows Messrs. THE CRIMINAL ASSAULT AT RUNCORN.—Thomas Ball the young man charged with criminally assaulting a young girl named Elizabeth Doyle, daughter of a blacksmith re- siding in Brunswick-street, was again brought up before Mr. Bankes, on Tuesday, and committed to take his trial at the next Chester assizes. The circumstances of the case are of too revolting a character for publication. STONING THE SALVATION ARMY AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Bridget Mitchell, a woman with a baby in her arms was summoned on a charge of committing a breach of Le peace.—P.S. Strickland said that on the evening of the 2nd inst. the Salvation Army was marching through Marsh-street, when the defendant attempted to create a dieturbknce by shouting. He saw her go to the back of the procession and take up a- large stone, which she was about to throw when he seized her.—Defen- dant protested that she was only calling her son away from the crowd.—The Bench bound her over to keep the peace for three months, herself in £lO-and one surety in £5, or in default 14 days' imprisonment. THE ATMOSPHERE OF WIDNES —ln the list of judgment summonses before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, at the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, was that of "Young's Paraf- fin Light Company against T. Leggett, of Widnes." The amount of claim on which an order had previously been made was £6 5s for lamps sapplied.—Defendant, in reply to his honour as to how he could pay, said by 4s a month. Part of the lamps had been sold, but part remained, and he was giving up hisj shop.—The judge askcd if he could not arrange with plaintiffs (for whom Mr. Joseph Milnes ap- peared) to return some of the lamps as part payment of the debt.—Defendant said he isad offered to dothat.—Mr. Milnes said the reason that cffer had been declined was because the goods would be deteriorated in value after being in such an atmosphere as that existing at Widnes.—His honour said he was afraid that was so, and made an order for the full amount, payable at 44 a month.

CROP PROSPECTS IN LANCASHIRE.—The general fore- boding of a very light hay crop caused by the drought of May and June was reversed by the genial rains of the end of the latter month, which gave such a stimulus to the growth of grasses that gloomy apprehensions were greatly modiled, and quite an average crop was expected. Last week many farmers out their grass, but the weather has been so extremely unfavourable that very few crops have been housed, and those in inferior condition. Others, more wary, and perhaps wiser, are waiting for "set fair," and in the meantime their grass is improving ita weight, tilling up wonderfully at the bottom. Beans, oats, and potatoes are most luxuriant—the latter will be a remarkably heavy crop should nothing happen to injure their present appearance. Apples, pears, cherries, gooseberries, strawberries, and rasp- berries all promise fair aferage yield, but plums of all sort° will be a failure generally, and ettrrants will be shezt,

THE fourth report of the Lorr.ls' Committee on the Irish Land Act of 1881 was issued (Ili Tuesday, and we scarcely think it via.' awaken any surprise that this measure is ,111 that document very strongly condemnt That, indeed, was a foregone conclusion. Peers never liked the Act, they passed it Wit aprotest, and they have allowed no opporttl,,, nity to escape of showing their antipathy the beneficent legislation which it embodiew and to sneer at the good results which it has undoubtedly achieved. It had scarcely beestil passed twelve months before the very class of Irish landlords—recognising the incb that they could no longer harrass and r° their tenants—were clamouring for an invesn. tgation into its operation, in the hope 1;i." doubt of arousing sympathy on their behaL: and straightway the House of Lords, on Ow motion of Earl DONOUGHMoRE, appointed 3 Committee with instructions to "inquire int° the working of recent legislation in reference to land in Ireland, and its effect upon the. condition of the country." The course thus, resolved upon was at the time very generaWA deprecated, for the reason that the Act ha' not had a sufficiently loeg trial; and so satis; fled were the Government that if the Lords decision were carried out it would be prf; ductive of mischief, that, at the request of til; PRIME MINISTER, the House of Cominoni passed a hostile resolution, declaing Parliamentary inquiry at the present tone (February, rBBz,) into the working of t,he Irish Land Act tends to defeat the operation of that Act and must be •injurious to Of, interests of good government in Irelanclo*, This motion was carried by a majority of !I• of the people's representatives It was Of effect a formal protest against the action est the Peers, who, it was hoped, would 005 press the matter, but in spite of all that said and done the Committee was appointew and the inquiry entered upon. On ever/ hand, however, it was clear that investigatio.o could not under the circumstances result ni any good, and that the conclusions of thef Committee must be discredited. It was, (3), course, the interests of the landlords 00 that concerned the Peers, the grievances 0, the tenants they cared little if anything for: and hence the fifteen nob!e members conlf posing the Committee—in the selection ° whom the Government took no part—vieffie chosen from amongst those who were knoW' to sympathise with the landlords' view of the question. Nearly all were of one political oonld plexion and certainly all were avoW,e, opponents of the measure. This being tu,„" case, it appears to us it was bound we follow as a necesary consequence that th f Committee could not approve a piece °r legislation which they had already in anothe, capacity done their utmost to prevent beconit ing law. The Committee have issued 0114 reports. It may be remembered that in the fir',. a "startling propopl was madefor tenants to purchase their holdings at ti; public-expense ;" the second and third repol`; dealt with the evidence only ; but this, v.l,', fourth and last report, is much wider in scope, and it is very sweeping in its denuncl3 tion. In the opinion of the Committee there., is no portion of the Act which has not bee'i a failure. The emigration clauses are se denounced,; next complaint is made that toe settlement of rents has been delegated to alit Sub-Commissioners, "with the natural Ns° of want of uniformity in the decisionse' Through, this conflict of decisions, and .tble impossibility of ascertaining any prina upon which- the valuation has Pr,, ceeded there has been interposen, say the Committee, '• the most serionie difficulty in the way of making amicah's arrangements out of court." Reduction are stated to have been greatest Whef • tenants' improvements have been the leas and landlords who have been indulgent .0 their tenants have suffered much more thae. those who have got the credit of being severue The Committee, furthermore, complain of t'a legal Sub-Commissioner being reduced 00,, cypher, of the unsatisfactory mode of val,u„. ing, of the want of a proper record of iimie provements, of the failure to stille grounds for decisions, and of ' appellate functions of the Commissionepy. as little better than illusory. The C°the mittee do not see any probability reduced rents being better paid in ; of difficulty or agitation than the old they say the relations formerly subsiera between landlords and tenants have b_eve dislocated or destroyed, the tenants lrod become demoralised. and they readilY Jed a themselves to hopes of frolx agitation

Altw Land Act, Such are the conclusions of Committee, and it would be almost impos- tmle to conceive anything more gloomy or It_esponding; Some of the paragraphs in the !-erlurt are ridiculous in the extreme. If, for linsetance, the settlement of rents had not been "legated to the Sub Commissioners, how ~ould the Commissioners—of whom at first , 'nett were only three—have got through the 'Work ? Then again, every case has to be seittled on its merits, and that being so it is 40Surd to suppose that any central principle Which might be laid down as a guidance in s.ettling the rent could be applied in every Instance. There is one thing the Committee gave not discovered. It was thought by some af the Peers that between the Government and the Sub-Commissioners there was a secret lladerstanding that the latter should reduce rents totally regardless of the justice or otherwise of such reduction, but !there d9es not appear to have been any evidence 'lscovered of such a compact. If there had, We may rest assured we should have heard a Peat deal about it. We are therefore justi- ged in concluding that this secret under- standing is only another of the many bogeys c°njured up by LORD CAIRNS, and disclosed 48 suits his lordship's convenience. Our ex- perience of the state of Ireland, during the Rast six months at any rate, completely falsi- rs the conclusions at which the Committee 'lave arrived, for the peaceful condition of the 'Country must be ascribed to other than the Peration of repressive laws; but if every word the report contained were justified by the re- -311 Its, it would still be lacking in one essential -a remedy for the evils complained of. We gave now heard the very worst that can be .aid of the Act, and we doubt not that in the eyes of many that worst will be looked upon 18 an excellent rccpmmendation of the in- rrent worth of the greatest and most ueneficent measure passed by the present I)vernment. Some idea of the • state of rreland at the present time may be gathered ;rtorn the following extract from the letter of a üblin correspondent usually well informed: ,There is no longer a violent agitation in gle country. Landlords are not held up to .Itecration, their rights repudiated and their lives menaced. Intimidation has almost eeased, and there are signs of a better feeling tinging up among all classes. Mr. '-kitNELL'S speech at Cork was of a more Conciliatory tone, and the union of creeds and Parties has made the Cork ExhibitiGn suc- , cessful and memorable. These and other circumstances have contributed to remove ,Prejudice and diminish the distrust and ap- Prehension with which any proposal affecting Property would be naturally regarded if made tiluder different conditions. There is now at 'east a truce, if not a prospect of lasting Peace, between the contending forces; and any ts.cheme which offers a chance of reconcilia- 'on is viewed with satisfaction." The picture Would have been very different had the Land Act not been passed.

131C-NIC TO WHAVERHAN.—We would again draw the at- tention of the public to the pic-nic of the Runcorn Y.M.C.A., which takes place to-day. If the weather be fine the sail will be a delightful one, but ample provision has been made should rain prevail. Tea will be provided. RUNCORN CONSERVATIVES AND THE REGISTER.—From an advertisement in another column it will be seen that Conservatives who are not on the register and are paying an annual rental of £l2 and upwards, are requested to lodge all necessary particulars with Mr. Lightburn, Con- servative agent. Applications must be made not later than Wednesday next. BRUNSWICK WESLEYAN' SIII.IDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN Large congregations assembled in St. Paul's Chanel on Sunday morning and evening, when the Rev. R. P. Downes, of London, preached the two sermons on the occasion of the school anniversary. Special music was sung by the chil- dren in an admirable manner. Mr. Downes also preached to a crowded congregation on Monday evening in the same place of worship. The total collections amounted to £57. Ruscoas GOOD TESIPLARS PIC-NIC.—A pleasant pic•nic in connection with the Hope of Runcorn CiJod Templar Lodge took place on Monday. About 47 members started from Runcorn at 7 o'clock in three large waggonettes sup• plied by Mr. Peck, their destination being Chester. The drive was much enjoyed, and having breakfasted in the city, the party was conveyed in two barges to Eaton Hall. Seve- ral hours were spent in the beautiful gardens at this place, and on returning to the city the many places of historic in- terest were visited. Brother John Faulkner super- intended the arrangements, which were very successfully carried out. -

PUNCORN TEACITER.--Abont forty teachers and friends of the Holy Trinity Ragged School had a pic-nic on Saturday, when they were driven to Hels- by in conveyances provided by Mr. Peck. Tea was partaken of in the Hill-side House, and a pleasant afternoon was spent in rambling over the picturesque hills. Before departing, Mr. W. J. Cunningham, the superintendent of the school, presented Mrs. Dan'sebin (nee Miss Horsefield) with a hand- some album in commemoration of her recent, marriage, and Ire recognition of her devoted labours in connection with the school. The gift was suitably acknowledged, and the party etarted for home, Runcorn being reached about 10 o'clock. WIDNES ATHLETIC CLUB SPORTS —The most important m.eting of athletes in the northern counties will take place on the show field, Farnworth, on Friday next, and also on the following day. Friday night's proceedings include the local events only, and the open events, 19 in number, will be c )mp.ted for on Saturday. Prizes to the value of £2OO will be off,.red, and will include many elegant articles in silver, and the club's gold medal. Mr. F. H. Goss-ige is president of the club, and Mr. J. L. Muspratt, vice-president. Mr. Walter Platt will act as handicapper and referee, and Mr. T. Wilkinson, of Sheffield, will be the starter. The ralway companies offer special facilities for travellers, and the sports promise to be as successful as on former occa- sions. Entries sent by to-night's post will be accepted.

ZION UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH SCHOOL, WIDNES.—On Saturday the children and teachers attending this school had their annual treat. Assembling in the school-room at half-past one, they were formed into proces- sional order, and, headed by the Mill-brow Brass Band, Runcorn, who had kindly given their services, marched to tie Central station, where they left by the 2-23 train for Hough Green. On arrival they marched to a field lent by Mr. Longten, of Ditchfield Farm, and spent the afternoon in a vtriety of pleasant ways. The scholars, numbering 220, were regaled with tea, bread and butter, and sweet stuffs, while for 100 friends, who bad made the journey, an excel- lmt tea was provided, Mr. Longton having put all conveni- ences at the disposal of the School Committee. Before leaving the fieldq the scholars assembled in front of Mr. Longton's residence, and sang a number of hymns, after- wards returning by train to Widnes, which was reached at half-past nine.

DESTITUTE FAMILIES AT W I DNEs.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, George Barnett was brought up, on remand, charged with neglecting to maintain his family. Mr. Scannel, the relieving officer for the Whines district, said the prisoner deserted his wife and children or. the 25f h June. He visited them, and found them in a very destitute condition, having no food whatever in the hcuse. For the last three weeks he had only given his wife 43., although he had been receiving 21s. per week as a labourer at Weston. The prisoner was remanded for a week to give him an op- portunity of paying the money due to the Guardians. It amounted to £2 2s. 6d.—At the same court, John Connolly was brought up, in custody, under a similar charge. Mr. Scannel said previous to the date of the offence the prisoner and his wife and children lived at St. Helens. The prisoner was employed at the Globe Alkali Works, where he was getting decent wages. For some reason or other he left his employment and the town, and the woman and her children found their way to Widnes. They were in a most destitute condition—they were absolutely naked. he ap- plied on the 3rd May for relief,and he sent the family to the workhouse, where they had since been. The prisoner at frequently deserted his family. For this year alone his family had cost the Guardians upwards of £l6 The amount owing to the Guardians at present was £8 163 6d and costs. I The visener had recently worked for Meeirs . Muspratt at I Flint under an assumed name. He was a turnaceman, i could easily obtain work, and was always in receipt of large wages. This was a very bad case, and he was instructed by I the Guardians to press for a heavy penalty.—The prisoner was committed to gaol for two months' hard labour.

HALTON FEMALE FRIENDLY SOCIETY.—The annual gathering of the members of the Halton Female Friendly Society took place on Manday. 're members met at their clubroom, which stands amid the picturesque ruins of the fortress of the De Lecey's, to the number of 219. They were joined by Lady Brooke (to whom the society is in- debted for much of its success), as well as Mr. C. Reynolds, J P., Mr. William Chrimes (the' society's former secretary), add tie° present hardworking secretary, Mr. Thomas Wright. Being arranged in processional order, the members walked to the Parish Church, where a shorten-d form of service was introduced by the vicar, and a sermon preached by the Rev. Robert Salthouse, F.R.G.S., incumbent of St. James's, West Derby, Liytrpool. Quitting the churoi, the proces- sion passed down the slope to the Green lanes of the villaee. The members were joined by the Revs. John Lockwool and R. Salthouse, and the procession marched to the strains of the Halton Brass Band to the gates of Norton Priory. Here a short pause was made, and then the procession haying paraded the other portion of the village, returned to the Castle grounds. According to a time-honoured custom, the members marched three times around the green, the grey, crumbling walls which once resounded with the shouts of soldiery now echoing with the gay chatter of female voices. I One member of the order trod the greensward for the 67th I time, and as she took her place with the rest en Mond4y I her foot seemed to have lost none of its pristine sprightliness. I In a large tent adjoining the green tea was provided by Mr. Phillips, after which several speeches were made, including I one by Lady Brooke, which charmed all present as much I by its gracefulness of diction as by its apt and interesting allusions. The evening was spent in dancing and other , amnsements.
A meeting of this Board was held on Thursday. Present: Messrs. T. S. Timmis (chairman), Father Clarke, J. H. Davis, John Brock, W. Hartland,.R. Shaw, Dr. O'Keeffe, H. Brunner.

DISTRICT EDUCATION. The District Education Committee reported that during the month of June (two weeks) the numbers of cases sum- moned before the committee were 40 applications for pay- ment of fees, of which 37 were recommended to be paid. For contravention of the Education Act 147 persons appeared before the committee; and 37 were convicted by the magis- trates.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Father CLARKE.

;THE EXTENSION AT SIMI'S CROSS. The Sites and Building Committee made the following recommendations—That the returns prepared by the Sites and Building Committee for the estimated loan required for the additional accommodation at Sionm's Cross schools be adopted and forwarded to the Educational Thpartment for approval ; that the contract drawn up for the due execu- tion of the work in connection with the Simm's Cross schools, and approved by the committee, and also that the sureties offered by Mr. Thomas Sadler (Messrs. John Taylor, contractor, Koludah-terrace, Widnes, and Benjamin Brown, ironfottnder, Widnes), be accepted ; that the countorpart of the contract or agreement with Mr. T'nomas Sadler, be sealed in due course ; also that the chairmen or vice-chair- man be authorised on behalf of the Board to complete the contract with Mr. Thomas Sadler for the additional accom- modation at the Simm's Cross schools on receiving the Edu- cation Department's sanction of the tender proposed to be ac- cepted, also the sureties' bond ; that the seal of the Board be affixed to the agreement for the hire of the Oakland-st. schoolroom if approved by the Education Department.— Mr. Bnocx, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the committee bad succeeded in obtaining a contract for the lump sum of £2,500. But they would also have to pay architect's commission, and would probably want a further sum for new benches and desks in the school. The corn' mittee, therefore thought it would not be advisable to ask the Education Department for a less sum than £3,000. The architects fees would be about £l5O, and £250 was the usual sum put down for contingencies, so that the sum he had named would not be much in excess of what would be re- quired. Of course the committee would not spend more than was absolutely necessary. Owing probably to some red tapeism on the part of the department, the returns for the estimated loan had not been received. It the Board thought it right to give the chairman and vice-chairman of the Board power to fill up these returns, they would do so, and submit them to the Board at the next meeting to show that they had carried out their instructions. If they did not get that privilege from the Board, the whole matter would have to lie over for six weeks. The committee was very sorry about it, but it was not their fault.—The CHAIR- MAN thought the Board ought to put the trust in the com- mittee that was asked for.—Mr. HARTLAND observed that the summer would be over before the work was commenced if any further delay occurred.—The minutes were passed.
THE EXAMINER, S.ATETRDAY,-JULY 14, 1883 RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMIS- SIONtRS.

IMPORTANT MEE TING YESTERDAY. A sp:11 meeting of Runcorn Board of Co oininioners was held yosterday afternoon, for the purpo-e of rr.ceiving recommeolat:ons from the Waterloo Mouse C gniiiFtee, and considering the payment of the costs in the action Beasky v. the Comsnisoioners. Mr. Meadowcroft and there were a..kso present Messrs. Norman. 1) hon. J. J. Speakman, P. Speak.nan. F. A. Lake, Wilharns. Dr. Mac- Dougall, Fisher, W. H. Linaker (law-clerk), W. 11rookes (secretary), and M. Barker (surveyor). TIM WATERLOG HOUSE QUESTION. The first business was the submission of severe; resolu- tions pabsed by the Waterloo House Committee.—Mr. &Law moved the first: that the Commisoners let to the corerseers of the poor two rooms in Waterloo House, numbered 1 and 3on the right side of the entrance, at a yearly rental of £35, rates, coals, gas, and cleaning free, the occupancy to be determined at 12 months' notice.—Mr. FisitEß seconded the motion.—Dr. MACDOUGALL pointed out that the rate- payers had decided that the overseers move to Waterloo House at an annual rental of £3O, and he asked if it was competent for the committee now to bring forward the reso- lution, and how far it would be binding on the ratepayers.— Mr. Straw replied that the ratepayers were under a misap- prehension when they passed the resolution referred to, and he believed that the Local Government Board would give their sanction to the overseers taking the rooms at a rent of £35. The extra rental would go to the credit of the Library Committee, so that it was immaterial to the Cool- tnissioners whether the overseers paid £3O or £3s.—Mr. LAKE said he might be rather dense, but he did not quite understand how credit was going to accrue to the Library.— The CHAIRMAN explained that a certain sum was fixed as rent for the Library Committee, and deductions would be made from that sum as the other rooms were let.-Mr. LAKE: Do I understand that the Library Committee would get, credit for the difference between £3O and £3s.—The CnAIR- MAN: Yes, certainly.—The motion was carried.—Mr. SHAW then moved that the Commissioners set apart for the Library rooms 4,5.6, on terms and condition same as stated in the committee's previous report. These terms were to the effect that the fixed rent was to be £25, to be reduced as the other public bodies occupied their offices.—Mr. Fisher seconded the motion.—A discussion took place as to whether the Commissioners could charge rent, and the Law Clerk, at the instance of Dr. MACDouGALL, read a section from the Free Libraries Act, which seemed to sho s, that the Commissioners could erect a building with all conveniences for a free library or a museum.—Mr. LAKE moved an amendment to the resolution that the words after "plan" be omitted, observing that it was a great pity that the Board should in any way cripple the resources of the Library Committee.—The amendment was seconded by Dr. MACDOUGA.LL and lost.—Dr. MAC- DoUGALL then moved that the discussion be adjourned until Tuesday, but this was also lost.—The original motion was then carried.—The following resolution was also passed : "That the Waterloo House Committee be empowered to obtain from the surveyor an estimate and other information required by section 174 of the Public Health Act, 1875 and advertise for tenders for the requisite alterations for painting and otherwise preparing Waterloo House for occupation by the Commissioners, the overseers and the library, and also for the furnishing of the Commissioners' rooms. THE BEASLF.Y LITIGATION: EXECUTION ISSUED AGALNS COMMISSIONERS—SHE RIFF'S OFFICER ON THE SCENE. The LAW CLERK said on the 4th inst. the taxing master proceeded with the taxation of Mr. Beasley's bill, but it was adjourned until Friday the 6th far the purpose of adding up the costs, and closing the taxation, which was done last Saturday, when there was given an allocatur for amount of costs, being £lOl is. 71 On Monday he received the following letter :-- 1, Bedfori-row, L mdon, W. 0., 7th July, 1883.—Dear Sir,— Beasley v Tee Rune irn Cmimissioners The allocatur has been taken for the amount as follows : Bill £521 15s. 8,1., taxed off £125 is.; £396 14s Bd. ; 'axing fee, £1 9s. 6d. ; total £4Ol 149. 24 Au error in the Bill reduces the actual allocatur to £4Ol Is. 7d. We do not know if plaintiff's agent was sgious, but he stitsd that he might be instructed to issue execution alga-nat the Commissioners.—Yours truly, for Partner and self, THOMAS RAWLE.

On the same morning he (Mr. Linaker) handed it to the secretary of the Board, and on Tuesday the sheriff's officer turned up at his office with a writ of elegit against the Commissioners' property. He had an interview with him, and explained how the matter was. The consequence was the officer consented to put the matter off until that day. The officer was at present in the town waiting to see him. On the 7th instant, Messrs. Jones and Pride wrote to him as follows:- 86, Queen-street, Cheapside, E.C., July 7, 1883 —Dear Sir,— Beasley v. Runcorn Commissioners. I have to-lay taken the Masters' Allocatur herein for £lOl Is 7d. I have to ask for im- mediate payment of £176 104 81 arrived at as follows, as well as interest on the £lOl Is 7d from this date :—Amount of taxed Casts, Liul Is 7d; anviunt of damages, 15 ss; interest fnon 10th Auft.ust, 1887, 4s Id; additional costs as agreed. t2O ; t• tat, £126 103 8d —Yours truly, LERIS PASS —Messrs. Gregory and Co. In that letter there was no intimation of proceedings being taken, but on Monday execution was nevertheless issued Mr. NORMAN: And now there is teething left but to pay the ! bill, or else go to prison. (Laughter.)—Mr. LINAKER said ' the plaintiff's solicitor was acting within his strict legal rights in issuing execution immediately they obtained alio- catur, but the qaestioa was whether, considering the security the plaintiff had for the costs, it was a proper course to have taken.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN said the matter had as- sinned a serious aspect, and he moved that a committee, consisting of Mr. Briscoe, Dr. Steele, and Mr. Shaw be ap- pointed to consider the accounts of Mr. Beasley, and also the accounts of the law clerk in connection with the litigation and report to the Board.—The CHAIR- MAN ruled this motion out of order.—The LAW CLERK dis• claimed any feeling in the matter, and suggested that the committee should be appointed when his b;11 was taxed so that they could attend if thought necessary.—Mr. SPEAK- MAN did not wish to place the Board in a dilemma. The inevitable must be borne, but before the clerk's bill was taxed, a committee ought to put the matter in such a shape that it could come properly before the Board and the nub- I lic.—The CHAIRMAN: Will someone move that this bill be ' paid ?—Mr. SHAW: I think the doctor ought to move that the bill be paid. He knows as much as anybody about it. (Hear.)- Dr. MacDounatr. should hue to know what these individuals meant by these insinuations. Did they think the doctor was not man enough that he was unable to stand on his own acts? In saying that the doctor knew more about that bill than anyone else they were strictly not within what were their rights, but there would be no revelation of cowar- dice on his pert in that bill.—Mr. SPEAKMAN: I have no I hesitation in saying that if it had not been for the part Dr. MacDougall took in the action, we should not have had the bill at all. (Mr. SHAW: Hear, hear. )—Mr. Dossoer: That lie a very serious charge.—Dr. MACDOUGALL said I he had not expected anything different "from them," but the time would come when his action would be explained. He invited them to make any statement they thought fit. He had a distinct answer to make to them. He took it that the bill would be produced and the items discussed at some future time, and then every person would be shown in his true light awl in his true colours. At that time he should be prepared.—No member offering to move a resolution, the CHAIRMAN said : I am waiting for some one to move that this cheque be signed. Under the circumstances we can do nothing else.—Dr. MAC- DOUGALL said he would take the responsibility of moving I the payment. He was not running away from his duties, and had never done so. At the proper time he should dis- cuss it elsewhere, and he should attack an Individual on that Board principally on evidence contained in that bill, of which he should take a fair copy and make whatever use he might think proper. —Mr. NORMAN seconded the motion.—Mr. SHAW said the Bill contained very serious items which had been brought about by some means or other, which a number of the mem- bers were entirely ignorant of, and therefore they should like to know more than they did at present. The Board was in a fix; those that got them into that fix ought to come forward either now or at some other time and tell them why they did it. If there was any credit due to them, he was sure the Board would he willing to give it.—Mr. LA.KE said if there was anything in the insinuations which bad ! been flying about the town for the last year, the ratepayers would have to pay for what had been an aggrava- tion of private feeling. (Hear, hear.) If there was no trut'e in these insinuations there ought to be a complete answer to them. The 60th section in the Commissioners' Clauses Act simply applied to proceedings on powers which the Board might exercise lawfully. Here the Board had admitted by counsel that they had acted unlawfully; that they had committed a serious trespass on Mr. Beasley. He thought that if the members of that Board, or an individual member, or any particular party, had been the cause of this, these were the people who ought to pay, and not the innocent ratepayers who had no voice in the matter whatever. (Hear, hear.) It was a serious matter to charge the ratepayers sd. in the £ extra simply because of an unfortunate piece of business with Mr. Beasley; and he entered his protest against it, but he could not see what other course was open to the Board but to pay these costs.—Mr. DOBSON : Why are we called upon to pay this? Is it for scandali.;no Mr. Beasley? The : AIRM AN (laughing) : IrJa had better ask the law clerk.—Dr. MACDOUGALL pointed out that any action that was taken was taken by the direction of the Board, and said he should he prepared to defend his actions at the proper time.—The resolution which was to the effect that the plaintiff's taxed costs and the expenses of the writ of elegit amounting to £440 10s. 6d., and other expenses be paid, was then passed, Mr. P. S. Speakman leaving the room.— Mr. Shaw, Mr. Fisher, Mr. Lake, Mr. Dobson, and Mr. J. J. Speakman voted for the resolution under protest, the other members voting without remark.—The CHAIRMAN remarked ! that he was not present at any of the meetings that had to deal with this matter, but in at once passing this bill the Board would be saving the ratepayers expenses and paying due attention to their interest. This concluded the business.

ACCIDENT TO A CARTER AT ST. HELENS. - On Thurs- day last week a carter named John McHugh, employed by the Corporation, was driving a horse and cart across Hard- shaw Fields when he accidentally lost his balance and fell out of the cart. Owl of the wheels passed over his left arm and broke it between the elbow and shoulder. FortunitAy Police-sergeant Gilligan trippened to be near, and hal the injured man removed to Dr. O'Keeffe's surgery, where his arm was dressed. He was afterwards taken hone, and is progressing favourably.

FORNIATION OF ei COUNCIL OF EDUCATION AT WIDNES.

A meeting was held yesterday afternoon in the officers' room of the Drill Hall, Widnes, for the purpose of forming a Council of Education on the lines of that established in Liverpool. Mr. T. S. Titnmis presided, and there were also present the Revs. J. Wright William., George Bond, T. Finegan, Me&rs. H. W. Deacon, S. K Muspratt, Dr. O'Keefe, John Hough, Dr. McLennan, G H. Danhy, R. S. Davies, F. Cave, James White, J. Morrison, and B. Brown. —Th- CHAIRMAN read the scheme, as follows: Title.—" Ph., Widaes Councit of Eduaation:"

Object —To peomote and encourage Elementary Education by every availab'e means, by gene al co-opreation with the managers and teachers of all public elementary schools and others interested in the practical work of education In Widnes; but without interference with the intemal econ my or management of any individual school. _i/eans.-1. By encouraginz a more general and increased t—gulatity of children's at,tendenee and by discus ag ng their migration from soh rol to echo )1. 2 By stimulat.ng both parents and children by ajudie ens dist ibution of priz s, re- wards, and certificates of merit. 3. By establishing (as funds permit ) scholar ships, c oeneetin e the public element ary schools with any "second grade" schools, which the c 'mien of the Association may approve, with the view not only to foster in- dividual talent, industry and character, but, above all, to rake the general standard of elementary trainirg and aLtainmnits. 4 By founding (as funds permit) a system of prizes and cer- tificates of me, it for pupil teachers who shall be distinguish-d by superior industry, intellig snce, attainment,, anti good coti- duct. 4 By the public distributi la of such sch larships, prizes, and other rewards in the manner m )st likely ,o attract the greatest mea,ure of attention and sympathy CONSTIRIVION: Menzbershi p.-1.. The qualification for life membership of the association shell be the feuodation of a re-holarship, or a donation of not less than £2l; for ordiaary membership an annual subscription if not less th an 1036,1 Counel —2. The association shall be governed by a council of not less than 12. ner more than 18 directors, who shall anisu ally elect a president and vice-president from among their number. 3. The directors sh all be elected by a majority of the members present at the annual meetin of the association. A third of those so eleoted shall retire at the end of each yeas; the retire- ment in the first two years being regulated by ballot and after- wards by rota' ion. such directors being e igible fir re electiou. 4 The members of the assoc:ation shall a-nually e'ect from the members of the council an honorary treasurer and an h ,norery secretary. 5. The council shall appoint an executive committee comprised of five directors' which committee shall rep rrt its preceding to the council from time to time as o-casion may require. IS. The council shall make an annual report of •its proceedings at a meeting of the members of the association, to be duly summoned for that purpose. T. No alteration shall be made in the c onstitution or general principles of the assoelation, except by a resolution of two-thirds of the members of the as- s ,elation present, passed at a special meetin4 c onvene I for the purpose, up in the requisition of not less tnan five members. Trustees.-8. The funds of the association shall be invected in the name. of three trustees, to be appoirred by the council. Mr. DEACON expressed the hope that the Council would see their way to found at least one scholarship, as the competitive examination was a great beneat to the scholars. —A long discussion took place. Most of the gentlemen present were apparently in favour of giving prizes as at pre- sent, rather than establishing a scholarship.—The CHAIR- MAN moved, and the Rev. Father FINEGAN seconded, that the draft scheme for the propose I Council of Education presented by the committee he adopted.—lt was also re- solved, on the proposition of Mr. MusPnArr, seconded by Mr..Monnisorr, that in order to carry out the foregoing re- solution the committee already appointed be requested to obtain promises of support and call;a meeting of subscribers. The CHAIRMAN said it was quite open to the committee to elect a council and then get to work.—ln reply to some re— marks by Mr. B. Brown, Mr. TIMM'S said Mr. Gossage and himself would be glad to give £5O each towards the general echeme.—A vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman, on the motion of Mr. B. Bnowa, seconded by Mr. JOHN Hunan, and the meeting concluded.

SMALLPDX NEAR ST. HELENS.—A young person named Burns, who lives at Portico, Eccleston, near St. Helens, has been stricken with this dreadful disease. Dr. O'Hara, who has been for some time acting for Dr. Hall, surgeon to the workhouse, considered the case to be of so serious a nature that the patient was on Tuesday removed to tlw, Prescot Workhouse Hospital.
