div.head: PROVIDING FOR MXPENNY TELZGUIMS,
div.p: PROVIDING FOR MXPENNY TELZGUIMS,

A communication was reed stating that the Postmaster- G-eneral is about to erict a line of telegraph from Londbn to Liverpool, and applying for the Board's consent to the erection of poles and wires along the highroad between Stockton Quay and Acton Bridge, the making good of any damage done iu the execution and maintenance of the work being undertaken by the Postmaster-General. A subsequent, letter, replying to one from the clerk, stated that the new line of wires is intended to enable the department to pro- vide for sixpenny telegrams, and that the poles would be erected to the satisfaction of the Board's surveyor.—The consent asked for was given.

div.head: GAAPPENHALL PINFOLD.
div.p: GAAPPENHALL PINFOLD.

At the request of the Chairman of the Beard (Mr. Edwd. Greenall) the surveyor had prepared a report, which stated that the pinfold at Grappenhall, which was situate on the off side bank of the Bridgewater Navigation Company's canal, had been removed by some of the employ6l of the company. That the pinfold had existed in this situation for a great number of years there was no doubt, and that it was used as a putalic pound down to a recent date was readily proved. He had been informed that the pinfold ani the land upon which it stood belonged to the Bridgewater Navigation Company, and that the company had ordered its removal. The drain or sewer which pissed through the pinfold had also been interfered with by the outlet being made narrower. —The CLICRK said the Board had nothing to do with the pinfold, but if the drain had been interfered with, then that was another matter.—No action was taken in the matter.

div.head: TIIE PROPOSED. OOGSRALL BROOK BRIDGE.
div.p: TIIE PROPOSED. OOGSRALL BROOK BRIDGE.

A plan of proposed Cogsball Brook Bridge, the cost of which is estimated at £3OO, was laid on the table, and the SUR- 9EYOR said he estimated the cost of the approaches at £3OO. One-third of the cost of the bridge being borne by the County Authority, thus leaves the sum of £5OO to be pro. vided for the carrying out of the work proposed.—The CHAIRMAN suggested, now that they were in possession of plans and estimates, that the Clerk should write to the Clerk of the Peace for the county and to the landowners having land abutting on the road to the proposed bridge, informing them of the estimated cost of the proposed work, and asking them if they would give the Board any help in the matter. Mr. BENNETT thought it was a question for the Board whether they were prepared to spend £soo.—The CHAIRMAN felt confident the land owners would meet the Board in a generous spirit. He had known Cogshall Brook Ford for 50 years, and it had always been a nuisance. He would travel three miles round before he would go through the brook, and there were persons who would open half a dozen gates, go through his yard, and round that way, befoie they would go through. He hoped the Board would look upon the proposed work in a favourable light.—Mr. BENNETT thought it was very unreasonable to expect the Board to expend anything like the money mentioned. It was a very large undertaking for that Board. There was no doubt the erection of a bridge would be a great improvement, and he believed it would greatly enhance the value of the farms in the district sur- rounding it, but he considered that before they went any further they should first see whether the Board were in a position to spend any money, and if so how much. They had not a word from the landlords to lead them to expect support from that quarter.—The CHAIRMAN tkouzht Mr. Bennett had not quite understood what be (the chairman) said. What he suggested was that the Board first ascertain what assistance they might expect to receive. They were now in possession of the plans and estimates, and now was the time to make applications for help in the quarters he had referred to. They could not reasonably expect people to say how much they would give until they knew what was going to be done, and what the work would cost. If the County Authority and the landowners would not assist them, then he would say let the matter drop.—The suggestion of the Chairman was then embodied in a resolution, and passed on the motion of Mr. MCINTYRE, seconded by Mr. HANDLEY. —The CLERK remarked that the resolution would not bind the Board to anything, so that they would be left in exactly the same position as they were in before. There was no other business of public importance.

div.head: MANCHESTER ROYAL EVE HOSPITAL. AN APPEAL.
div.p: MANCHESTER ROYAL EVE HOSPITAL. AN APPEAL.

_ The Board of Management of this excellent Institution have issued an appeal for subscriptions to enable them to erect a new building, and in it they say The Hospital has been in existence for nearly seventy years. For a long time its progress was a steady and gradually improving one, and when, sixteen years ago, the present building was erected, it was thought, judging by past experience, that sufficient provision had been made for any increase that might reasonably be expected for a lengthened period. The demands on the Hospital have, however, increased far beyond expectation, and in the annual report for the past year the committee pointed out the gradations by which the present number of patients has been attained. After an exiAenca of thirty-eight years—in 1852 the patients treated numbered 2,284, in 1862 3.765, in 1872 7,673, in 1852 14,601. Th nturbAas still continue to increase, and up to the Ist May in the present year 492 more patients have been admitted than were admitted in the I corresponding period of 1832 The committee pointed out I also that the in-patients now approach in numbers to those of Moorfields, and c insiderably surpass any other ophthalmic linstigation either in London or the provinces. These con- stant increases occasioned them the deepest anxiety; indeed the chief burden of their annual reports for some three or four years has been the reiterated statement that the ques- tion 9f increased accommodation was daily staring them in the flee, and an enlarged hospital was fast becoming, in spite of themselves, an absolute necessity. Over and over again they had to point out that the hospital was inadequate for the accommodation of the out-patients, and still more CO for the necessary proportion of in-patiants, who, after being operated on, require, to conduce to recovery, properly ven- tilated wards, and that supervision that special knowledge, nursing, and appliances can alone secure. The average daily attendance of out-patients last year was 220, but on some daye the numbers reached 300 and even 400 For the reception of these there is only one room, and before the day's work is over the atmosphere has become thoroughly vitiated. For in-patients the present building provides 65 beds. This number has been found to be inadequate for the accommodation of patients requiring operations, and it has been necessary sometimes to make room for very urgent cases by discharging patients who would have probibly benefited by a longer stay in the hospital. The foregoing facts show the absolute necessity for enlarged premises, and the Board of Management appeal with con- fidence to the public for the necessary funds to enable them to erect a new hospital in whic's there shall be room for one hundred beds, and proper accommodation for out-patients. They estimate that the sum of £20,000 will be required for a site and building such as will enable them to do justice to the requirements of the district, and to give those afflicted with eye disease all the advantages developed by modern science. They are emboldened to make this appeal by the consciousness that they have made good use of the funds entrusted to them in the past. Last year, which was no exceptional one in this respect, the expenditure on 14,661 patients, including 1,265 in-patients, was only £2,524 14s 10.1—an economical administration which is generally admitted to be without parallel. The Board claim substantial help from the surrounding districts. Great numbers of the patients are from the surrounding towns, and the committee feel they are consequently entitled to expect substantial aid from the neighbouring municipal bodies, from local boards, boards of guardians, and all employers of labour, from the nobility and gentry of the district, and from all ratepayers. The charity cmn truly plead that by its means hundreds of children are rescued from blindness at the very outeet of life. Sight is restored in hundreds of cases of cataract. Proper treatment, rest, and good food have been the means of restoring and preserving vision in hundreds of cases which otherwise would have been condemned to life-long poverty, misery, and blindness. The board of management earnestly call attention to the above statement, and invite generous aid and support.

A GOOD REASON.—Solomon Coates, a farmer at Parr, was summoned before the St. Helens bench on Friday for keeping a greyhound without a license.—P.C. Hargreaves spoke to having seen the dog in defendant's house on the 213,h nit, and to the fact that defendant was unable to show a license.—Mr. Coates, in defence, said the dog was not his but was one which strayed about the neighbourhood owner- less. He had no use for a greyhound, he said, and could not see what the use of a greyhound would be to a farmer in Parr. There were no hares or rabbits there.—He was, however, fined 5s and costs. ASCAULTING A FOREMAN AT Sr. HELENS.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Saturday, a young man named Richard Mills, who is employed at Messrs. Pilkington's sheet-glass works, was charged with having assaulted James Jones, a foreman, on Thursday morning. Mr. J. O. Swift prosecuted. It seemed that the prisoner early on Thursday morning, during the night shift had been illtreating a lad named Gutridge, who complained to Jones. Jones went to the prisoner and remonstrated with him for what he had done, when the latter's temper apparently getting the better of him, he made a rush at Jones with a blow pipe with which he was working, and at the end of which was a lump of molten metal about two pounds in weight. Jones ran out of the way, hut did not quite escape as this piece of hot metal caught him on the hip and burned his trousers. On the sub-manager, Mr. Scott, being brought prisoner made another attack on Jones with a blow pipe, he, however, managing to get out on to a verandah without receiving any injury. Prisoner was sent to gaol for one month.

Reports from Egypt !ndicate that the deaths from cholera are on the decrease.
The Eton and Harrow erieket match commenced at Lords yesterday. The former made 231 in the first innings, aud Harrow 120.

The Princess Beatrice departs for the Continent on Thee- iay to take sulphur baths; her Royal Highness having lately suffered from rheumatism. It is stated in the Dztblin• Express that the informer Carey has made an attempt to communicate with Mr. Gladstone,. in the way of a complaint agtinst the Irish authorities, bur, his letter was stopped. A bulletin issued at fonr o'clock yesterday, stated that the. Bishop of Peterborough was no worse. Local inflammation was not subdued, but showed no tendency to spread. The patient passed a fair night, and maintained his general strength.

The Metropolitan Board of Works decided yesterday to apply neKt session for powers to construct bridges across the names and other improvements, at a cost of ten millions, to meet which coal and wine duties will be re- tained.

Mr. John Ferguson, of Glasgow,. having written to tie Rev. Isaac Nelson, M.P., advising him to resign his seat in Parliament, owing to his desertion of the Parnellite party, a telegram has been forwarded by an elector stating that the men of Mayo are able to mind their own county.

div.head: DISASTROUS FLOODS IN CANADA.
div.p: THE DISASTROUS FLOODS IN CANADA.
Twelve persons have been drowned in the floods. The damage to property is estimated at a million dollars. A TOWN ON FIRE.

At Rostoff, on the Don, a terrible fire broke out on Thurs- day night. A large part of the city is in dames, and it has been found impossible to master them. The whole of the city is threatened with destruction. STRIKE OF WEAVERS.

Yesterday at Harot Mills, neAr Ashton-under-Lyne, two thousand power-loom weavers came out on strike against the introduction by the employers of the Blackburne scale, which the men urge is equivalent to a considerable reduc- tion of wages.
TliE TRIPLE CHILD MURDERS AT MACCLESFIELD.

Mary Ann Davenport, who for some time has 4een incar- cerated in Chester Castle, awaiting her trial for having murdered her three children, at Bollington, near Maccles- field, by drowning them in a pit near her residence, has been removed to'Broadmoor Criminal Lunatic Asylum by order of the Secretary of State, the medical authorities and the visiting justices having pronounced her insane. THE IRONWORKERS' STRIKE: EXPECTED SUBMISSION OF viE MEN.

Yesterday, a delegates' meeting representing all the iron works in Wolverhampton, was held to decide whether work shall be resumed on the masters' terms. The opinion of the majority of works not being obtained for or against, the meeting was adjourned until to-day. Very many mititnen are anxious to resume work at the drop. A large number of orders have been lost to the district, and the wages drawings at banks amounts to mtny thousands of pounds less than before the strike. The strike in Wednesbury, Darlaston, and Cradley Reath portion of South Staffordshire district, is now practically ended, and it is expected that work will be resumed at the whole of the works in these districts on Monday.

div.head: LOVER'S REVENGE.
div.p: A LOVER'S REVENGE.

A remarkable case was heard on Thursday even- ing before the Caergwria (Flintshire) magistrates, when George Jones, farm labourer, was summoned for shooting at David Roberts, with intent to do him grievous bodily harm. Prosecutor had been keeping company with Miss Sidney Jones, neice of a tenant farmer, and the birth of a child resulted from the intimacy. Miss Jones afterwards dPclined to renew the engagement, and the prosecutor then went about the village declaring that• he was still keeping company with her, and making disparaging observations about her. Miss Jones sent for the prosecutor to her uncle's, and while there she threw a bucketful of liquid manure over him, and a gun was also discharged in unpleasant proximity to his ears. The prosecutor now indicted George J ,nes for shooting at him with intent, but as the prisoner declared he only exploded the gun to frighten the prosecutor from pursuing his scandalous conduct, the magistrates dismissed t 3 case.

THE DIFFICULTY WITH FRANCE. REPORTED FURTHER ARRESTS IN MADAGASCAR. Nothing further is yet known respecting the attitude assum,d by the French admiral towards Her Majesty's sub- jects in Madagascar. It is thought, however, that the arrest of Mr. Shaw has been followed up by that of others. The Society for the Propogation of the Gospel supports eight clerie.d missionaries in the island, besides a large number of catechists, all these bing under the ecclesiastical super- vision of the Anglican Bishop of Madagascar (Dr. Cornish), and fears are expressed by:the officials of the society that the Rev. James Coles, one of their missionaries, and a very energetic worker may be among those arrestee. The society's missionaries have hitherto met with very un- satisfactory treatment at the hands of the French in Mada- gascar, numerous obstacles being placed in the way of their labours. The last report sent by the bishop, however, stated that English influence was increasing at the capital (Anta- Rmarivo), and much was hoped from the appointment of the new governor, who had already withdrawn the opposi- tion formerly shown in educational matters, and was loolted upon as a fair-minded man.
SHIPOWNERS AND THE NEW SUEZ
CANAL.

A large meeting of underwriters, shipowners, and others was held in Lloyds underwriters'-room yesterday, under the presidency of Mr. Leonard Wakefield, to discuss the Suez Canal question. The Chairman said the committee had de- parted from their ugual rule of discussing only matters con- nected with underwritirig by reason of the disastrous results which would result to commerce and to shipping if the pro- posals respecting the second Suez Canal were made binding by the Government. Mr. Wills moved the first resolution, , which declared tbat the meeting had seen, with extreme regret and disappointment, particulars of the proposed ar- rangement, and strongly disapproved of it as regarded 1. The advance of so large an amount of British capital to be spent by the board of a foreign company, which would not even consent to have a domicile in England ; 2. The slight and remote chlracter of the proposed reduction in the dues ; 3. The inadequate proportion of British directors ; 4. The fact that the arrangement will so heavily tax the commerce between Europe and Asia to the end of next cmtury ; 5. It affords no security to the Imperial interests which this country is bound to regard. In moving this the speaker disclaimed the idea of the meeting being in any sense a party one. Other speeches having followed in con- demnation of the proposed arrangement, the resolution was carried with two dissentients and ordered to be forwarded to her Majesty's Government.

—TEE NEW-PON, Ll-17-DOCR, AND GOLBOYNE BUILDING SOCIETY. Sir,—Seeing a report of the annual meeting of the above eociaty in your issue of the 7th inst. containing remarks re- enacting myself, and wishing to reply to them, I shall be • extremely obliged by your publishing the following. In the - election of officers of the above society I was proposed as • iecretary in my ilbsence, and without my knowledge or con- sent. A discussion ensued, and Mr. Glover is reported by you to have said, 'lf Mr. Simpson is elected secretary, I will not sit as chairman." I have been at a loss to unaer- stand why Mr. Glover should villify me in this manner. I have come to the conclusion that he is still suffering from the effects of the dressing c own he received at the hands of • the sub-committee (of which I was a member) about 12 months ago. Mr. Glover may possibly adopt some other reason to justify his ungentlemanly language. It matters little to me what /hr. Glover does in that respect, for I am convinced on one point, viz, my connection with the New- ton Building Society has been perfectly consistent and honourable. And Mr. Glover may rest assured lam not anxious for his company neither on the Building Club Com- mittee or anywhere else, as my spare time can be more pro- fitably employed. Before I conclude I must remind Mr. Glover this is not the first time he has threatened to resign the chairmanship. By inserting this you will confer a per- • sonal favour, and oblige yours truly, J. SIMPSON. High-street, Newton-le-Willows, July, 1883. OUR NATIONAL CHURCH. • Sir,—lt is one of the chief features in polemical strife that antagonism of ideas must be calculated upon. Anyone setting out with ever so brilliant an idea must be prepared to meet opponents. Not one important measure, having special reference to the wants of the people, has ever been passed by the House of Commons without meeting with strenuous opposition. Before the era of Radicals, or the advent of Liberals, the divine right of kings, upheld by a superstitious people, enabled them to demand and receive from the people nearly all the fruits of the earth, meeting with scarce a dissatisfied murmur. This is altered now. The politicians ranging themselves under various banners, and following favourite leaders, determine, as opportunity offers, what questions they will support and which oppose. And this only holds good in a somewhat limited sense. We are now getting used to one party, the Tories, constantly for- swearing themselves. What they are prepared to support one day they are equally prepared to oppose the following day. And more than this, questions upon which we are all individually agreed and which we know are within mea- surable distance of becoming law, for mere obstructive pur- poses are seized hold of, and the nation's wants laughed to scorn. There is not one of us who is not perfectly satisfied with the happy results of the disestablishment of the Irish Churcb, yet what an ignoble and degrading stand the neutral clergy took upon that question. Five months elapsed from the introduction of the bill before it became law. Daring that precious interval the Church lengthened her cords and strengthened her stakes. Her bishops "laid hands suddenly" on every youth who could be persuaded to accept holy orders. When the bill was passed the curates of the Church had increased from five hundred to fully nine hundred, and the incomes of very many of her clergy had undergone a sudden and unprece- dented augmentation. Such will be the course adopted by the Church party in England when her turn comes. To gather into herself all that belongs to the people will be no. crime. The Church has in all ages used her opportunities for her own aggrandieement. Before the Reformation her wealth, forced from dying and superstitions miscreants, did double duties. Supporting. first, a degrading and immoral system of monkery, it was next allowed to go in driblets amongst the people, being in every sense a huge pauperiLing, institution. Su wealthy did they become that the clergy in the reign of tient-a li. were considered to possess one- third of the land of England, had become vicious in their lives, and idle and corrupt in character. No consideration for the people led the eighlh Henry to interfere, but a cavet- ous and inordinate desire for power led this "defender of the faith "to seize upon all that came within his clutches. From that day to this the clergy and royalty have made common cause. At various times we find in church history that her clergy have sided with the people ; so also we find Oat royalty and the aristocracy have jained , issue with the people against the Church. Whenever this has happened the cause has been , jealousy, and the people, as usual, have had to fight the battles of their pastors and masters. How long this will continue we can hardly tell, but of one thing we may be sure: the days of the Church as established by law are numbered What is the Tory party unless it represents national feeling? A myth. What is the National Church unless it draws within its fold the people? A sham and a mockery. Does it do this? The answer might be brief—a plain "No ;" but a more satis- factory and less laconic style of argument may be adopted towards so respectable and 90 ancient an excrescence. I have before me a large quantity of figures compiled from the religious census raurns, the totals of which prove, even to those who do not like to admit it, that a large major- ity of the religious world do not attend church; but this I hold to be insufficient for my purpose. • Warrington, with a population of 40,960, provides sittings as follow :—Estab- lished Church 4,880, Free Church 9,170; larg•-st attendance. Fstablished Church 2 279, Free Church 4,695. per cent 17 0. , Thus we see, if we allow a liberal percentage for various causes why people (lid not attend church and chapel on this particular day, and say in round numbers that 7,000 did so attend, there remains sill 33,960, or say, 30,000 allowing a fair margin for babydom, that are outside the pale of the Church. The Free Church people not being State recipients of the people's money have a free and independent course before them. They may either claim or disclaim a share in the endowments when disendowrnent day arrives. But what of the 30,000 inhabitants of this town owing allegiance to none of the churches? Now, sir, I think I have proved that • the Established Church is not a National Church. Let U 3 take another view, quite within the reach of anyone. Go any Sunday, and watch at the gates of the Parish Church, take notice of the class of people who attend the ministra- tions of this place, and you will find that ninety per cent. are made up of the upper and petty tradesman class. Nay, more; get into conversation with them, and you will find two most noticeable features : 'First, a complete absence of knowledge as to what the sermon was about, and next a freedom of conversation on matters not usually connected with a place of worship. Again, make inquiry on School- brow, Church-street, or in Howley-lane, as to the respect in which the rector is held; also as to the number of visits received from that good, easy man, and the answers will prove conclusive that the Church has no hold on the people, and the sooner her funds are turzled to better uses the better. • In another letter I may have mere-to-say on this important subject. CLIFFORD DIX. Warrington, July, 1883.

DISTRICT NEWS.

ASEITON. CAVE-BROWNE PROTESTANT INSTITUTE. During the past week Mrs. Gibbon, of Laburnam-vills, Lymm (late of Earlestown), very kindly presented to the committee of the Cave- Browne Protestant Institute, Heath-lane, Ashton, seven new flags or banners for the use of the scholars on gala-days or other demonstrations. The gift has been appropriately acknowledged. I THE ASHTON CHURCH ASSOCIATION.—In accordance with the wish and suggestion of the Council of the Church Association (London), that an united prayer meeting,, amongst all the branches and members of the Chur,ch Association throughout the country, should be he1,;.1 en Thursday last—the "glorious 12th July "—a special service for the purpose of offering thanksgivir4 for past mercies, was held in the Cave-Browne ProtestrAnt Institute, Heath-lane, Ashton, on that day. There was a fair atten- dance, and the meeting was conducted by Mr. B. Hodgkin- son. After meditation and prayer the hymn 'Oh God our help in ages past" was sung. The proceedings were im- pressive and earnest, and concluded with the singing of the Old Hundredth Psalm." SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT PARK-LANE : A FEMALE TRAMPLED UPON BY Cows.—An extraordinary, and we regret to say, a most serious accident happened to Mrs. Wilcock, 68 years of age, residing at a place known as Doeriding's farm, Park-lane, Ashton, on Friday evening last. About six o'clock Mrs. Wilcock proceeded to the shippon for the purpose of milking the cows, and it is sup- posed that one of the beasts became restive and knocked her down, rendering her unconscious. The cow or cows would then seem to have trampled upon her to such an extent that she received very serious injury. Two of her sons were employed mowing the grass in a neighbouring field, but were totally unconscious of what was taking place in the shippon until the continuous barking of the dog at- tracted their attention. On going to see what was the matter, they found their mother lying on the floor of the shippon in an insensible condition, her face and head be- smeared with blood and dirt, and she had evidently been much hurt. Her face and head were cut in several places, while her body was also cut and bruised. She was carried into the house,*and Dr. Anderson, of Billings, was immedi- ately sent for. Ile has since been attending upon her. - BOLD. DOMESTIC SQUABBLES AT BOLD —Henry Jackson and Jane Jacks,m, his daughter, were summoned before the St. Helens county magistrates, on Monday, by Ellen Jackson, for alleged assault on the 4th inst. Mr. Swift appeared on behalf of the complainant, and applied for a separation order. It appeared that the zomplainant acme three years ago married the male defendant, who was then a widower with nine children. Their short conjugal experience, how- ever, seems to have been of a very unpleasant description, and a short time ago the complainant went back to live with her mother at Sutton. On the day in question she returned to Jackson's house for the purpose of getting some spoonsl she said she had left, and whilst there an altercation ensued, during which she alleged both of the defendants assaulted her. This, however the defendant denied, and called several neighbours Who spoke to the violent behaviour of the complainant. They stated that she had broken the windows with stones and nearly hit some of the children, I besides using very discreditable language—After hearing .be case, the Chairman said the Bench did not feel disposed o convict in that case, and wntrld dismiss it. BURTON WOOD. .

BuRTONWOOD WE;LEYLN SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVER- SARY.—The anhiversary services in connection with the Burtonwood Wesleyan Sunday School were held on Sunday last. The morning and evening preacher was the Rev. John Tucker, of Liverpool, whose sermons were earnest and im- pressive. In the afternoon Mr. John Prescott, of Earles- town delivered a practical interesting address to the parents, teachers, and scholars. A. nice selection of hymns were especially sung by the school children. The collections amounted in the aggregate to £l2 2s. 101, a sum exceeding by £2 that collected last year. It is a pleasure to learn also that during the past year there has been an increase in the number of scholars attending the school. DITTON. NEW WORKS AT DITTON.—We have pleasure in stating that the Broughton Copper Company, Limited, an extensive Manchester establishment, have taken land near Ditton Station, on the %Varrington and Garston line, where they intend t 9 carry out on a small scale a portion of the opera- tions connected with the production of copper and brass tubing, as well as the general manufacture of copper and brass articles for a variety of industrial purposes, for which the company have long had a high reputation. Should success follow their first efforts, there is a reasonable chance that the whole of the company's extensive works may be removed to Ditton, and thus a new and important industry will add to the commercial prosperity of Widnes and district. "OnANon" Rows AT DITTON.—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Wednesday, three cases were. beard which had arisen from disputes about Orangeism.—Susan Campion, wife of Robert Campion, of Ditton, summoned John Faza- kerley on a charge of assault. Mr. Husband appeared for \the complainant, and it appeared thikt on the 2nd instant whilst Mrs. Campion was standing at her own door the I defendant and his wife came up, and a squabble took place ' about "Papists" and Orangern.n, during which it was alleged that the defendant struck the complainant. Wit- nesses were called on both sides, and the Bench went on to consider a charge against Robert Campion of assaulting Ellen Fazlkerley. Mr. Husband defended in this case. It was alleged that Mrs. Fazikerley went into the New Inn to obtain a drink. Defendant was in, and called her a "Papist —," picked up a glass of beer, and sent it at her. Had she not moved her head, she would not have been there to give evidence, but doing so the glass hit the wall and smashed. She produced the pieces. She called Mrs. Wright, who was serving in the bar at the time, and this witness stated both complainant and defendant were calling each other, and that the former sent a quantity of beer in the face of the latter. The Bench dismissed the summons —Job. Cliberin was then charged with assaulting Mrs. Fazakerley, who alleged that he entered her house on bunday, the Bth inst., and, without any provoc ttion, used vile language to her, and attempted to strike her with a poker. On the other hand, it was alleged that the defendant was passing the complainant's house with an orange lily in his hat, he hav- ing taken part in the procession to Farnworth in the morning. She knocked his bat oil and took the lily, and the defendant, under the impression that her sons were after him, ran and fetched a poker, which, however, he never used. The Bench dismissed this case also. ‘
FRODSHAM.

FIVE CROSSES SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.—The an- nual sermons at the Five Crosses Chapel were preached on Sunday by the Rev. Frederick Haines, of Northwich, when ! the chapel was crowded, aild the collections amounted to the sum of £l7 is. ed. FRoLsRAM NATIONAL SCROOLS.—It has become necessary to provide additional accommodation at both the boys' and the girls' school in this parish. The managers have, there- fore, decided to build two classrooms for the girls' school, , and one for the boys' school. The cost of these three rooms is estimated at about £450, of which sum Mr. E. A. Wright, , of Castle Park, Frodsham, has generously offered to contri- hute £250. Such liberality will, we trust, stimulate others who have an interest in the parish to do their part in pro- moting so good and so necessary an object. Lord Choi- mondeley has promised £3O, so that less than £2OO is needed to enable the managers to effect what will be of the greatest benefit to the whole parish.—Parish Magazine. THE RAILWAY ACCOMMODATION AT FRODSHAM —Adad- journed meeting in the above matter was held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Tuesday evening, when there were present Mr. E. A. Wright, J.P., irohe chair, Messrs. W. H. Pickering, John Ashton, Henry They, Thomas Riley, Thos. Davies, F. P. Weaver, Samuel Spencer, Peter Herron, and Charles E. Linaker, hon. sec. The committee appointed to consider the matter reported that they bad bad an interview at the station on Saturday with Mr. Patchett of Shrewsbury, Mr. Shaw of Liverpool, and Mr. Woods of Chester, superin- tendents of the joint lines, and the proposals of the commit- tee were very favourably entertained. As the matter would have to be submitted to the directors, it was decided to ad- journ the meeting to a day to be fixed by the bon. secretary, when the decision of the railway companies has been re- ceived. LIVERPOOL GEOLOGICAL ASSOCIATION AT FRODSHAM.— On Saturday the members of this association held a field meeting at Frodsham. Mr. Charles E. Miles conducted the excursion, and explained the physical and geological features which were presented en route. In the road lead- ing from Frodsham to Overton a section was inspec!ed, in which the Lower Kenner candstone is seen, with a well- defined band of rock regularly jointed, resembling tnasoney ; and at a little distance further on another section was visited, in which the waterstoaes are seen .reposing on the Kenner basement beds. The party then proceeded to a quarry, where an "open fissure" occurs. Here Mr. Plea gave an interesting account of .the rock formations of the locality, which, it appears, has recently been re-surveyed by Mr. Aubrey Strahan F.G.S. In another quarry, near to Five Lane-ends, the building stones of the Lower Kenper are well exposed. Near the top of the section occurs a bed of sandy shale, on the under surface of which tnpressions of reptilian footprints, ripple marks, and sun cracks are found. Good examples of the latter were obtained Lly „several of the party. The occurrence of drift, with boulders of foreign rocks ,im- bedded in stratified sand, was pointed out be Mr. T, Mellor(' Leads, F.G.S. The appearance of drift at so high an ati- Witt is worthy of remark. After tea the members walked to Dunsdale Hollow, where a fine section shows the Kenper basement beds resting on the Bunter formation. The view.; frore this point in exceedingly picturesque, and the scenery 'd of the route was another enjoyable feature of the excursion. occasion wecaCsaioennooFtche Csellietrmilennopernoinng Got-nu GA.RSTON. was the ste"oNe.w— S Churchund a v of St. Francis of Assiei, Chapel-road, Garston. The building pp to a few years ago was occupied b • the Congregational sect, since which time it had not been used, and as the great I want of a Catholic place of worship for this portion of Garaton had been long felt, it wag, with that object in view, bought for .ELGOO. The chief point of alteration in the premises, which will seat about '2OO persons, is the taking away of one of the galleries, and erecting a serviceable altar in its plaee, and also the addition of vestry. A portion of land surrounding the church has been purchased, and it is hoped, when the Catholic community increase, to eiect a larger church and a new school. The mission will be in tbs charge of the Rev. Father Smith. On Sunday morning High Mass was celebrated by the Right Rev. Monsignor Fisher. D.D V.G., who was assisted by the Rev. Canon Holden and Father Cahill. The Rev. Father Gillow acted as wader of the caremonies, itud Can.= Carr WU in the Banc-

Wary. The Bishop of -11.'verpoot was advertised to preac but his health w.'401(1 not permit of him visiting Garston. In his absent, an eloquent seroken was preached by the Rev. Father Murphy, of St. Antleany'e, Liverpool, from Matthew xxx, 18-20. In the e ..ourso of hit sermon, the rev, gentleman replied to the arg rament that the Catholic Church had en- deavoured to cr.ash the intellect of the people, and said that on every pa,- of English history was written the admiration she had 1-ad for, and the aid given to, the progress of learn- ing atVa to the development of every branch of science and art. They would find that in all times wherever churches ware erected there followed schools, colleges, and universi- ties. At the evening service the preacher was the Very Rev. Canon Carr, and, as in the morning, the church was crowded. The music at mass was rendered by members of St. Anthony's choir, Liverpool. GOLBORNE. SERMONS AT GOLBORNE PARISH CHITRCH.—The annual sermons in aid of the Curates' Augmentation Fund were preached in St. Thomas's Church, Golborne, on Sunday last. The morning and afternoon preacher was the Rev. Hewitt Linton, vicar of Abram, and the evening preacher the Rev. James Carson, curate of Winwick. The choir very effectively sang as an anthem the collect for the day, "Lord of all power and might," and in the evening gave Mac- fadyen's "Hear me when I call." Mr. Duddle, the organist of the church, presided at the organ with his accustomed ability. The collections amounted to £lO 12s. 101 GOLBORNE PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE: MONTHLY MEET- ING.—The members of the Goltorne Parochial Committee held a monthly meeting at Messrs. Brewis's office on Wed- nesday afternoon, when there were present Messrs. W. Mit- chell, J. Davies, John Lowe, William Garton, Thomas Mitchell, and C. S. Bennie (surveyor).—The Supply of Water: The Surveyor read a letter from Mr. Nichols, of the Legh Arms Hotel, respecting the water supply to his property, and asking for a reduction in the price charged. It was agreed that the charge should be that already fixed. Mr. Bennie then read a letter from the secretary of the Liberal Association on the same subject, asking that the. water supplied to the club premises be cut off altogether, as they had no use for it. The Committee decided that the letter in question should be considered a three months' notice, to terminate on the 29th of September next--The Recent Water Case at Newton Sessions: Further Proceedings: The Surveyor read a letter from Messrs Moore and Sons, solicitors, Warrington, respecting the. case against Martha Harrison at the Newton Petty Sessions, and reported in this paper lest week. Mr. Moore advised that Mrs. Harrison (the tenant) and Mr. Garton (the owner of the property) had rendered themselves liable to penalties under the Public Health Act of 1875 for disobeying the order of the Newton magistrates to close the well for all domestic purposes.—The Surveyor was instructed by the committee to take out summonses against Mrs. Harrison and Mr. Garton.—Proposed Improvements: A plan and section of certain improvements intended to be made in High-street were submitted by the Surveyor and passed.—Letter from the Local Government Board: The following letter was read :—" Local Government Board, Whitehall, S.W., 9th June, 1883.—Sir,—I am directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 25th ultimo, and to state that they woul I not be prepared to invest the Rural Sanitary Authority with any further urbin powers in respect to the township of Gelborne, which the circumstances of the township at the present time do sot render it essential they should possess. I am to request that the Board may be furnished with a statement showing precisely the sections of the Public Health Act, 1875, the powers of which the Rural Sanitary Authority desire should be con- ferred upon them, and • the reasons which in their opinion render such powers necessary. I am direc- ted to add, however, that the Board have not in any in- stance invested a rural sanitary authority with urban powers to enable them to purchase existing gas works or to erect new works to supply gas, and the Board are not at present aware of any grounds for making an exception in the pre- sent case.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, WALTER F. SENDALL, assistant secretary."—lt was resolved that a letter be sent to the Local Government Board again making ap- plication under sections 162, and 2nd and 3rd paragraphs of section 161, of the Public Health Act, 1875. —This was the only business and the meeting concluded. HALE. .
This being the second time the cup haa been won by Ell',son, it becomes his own proptqty. KNOWSLEY.

KNOWSLEY SUNDA.Y Scnoor, SICK CLUB—Toe members of this society made their annual demonstrati.on on Wednes- day afternoon. The society was founded r,beut forty years ago, and is in a gratifying state of prosperity. Paying its ' way year by year almost, it has an accumulated capital of nearly £7,000. Last year it was able to set aside £BO after paying all expenses and claims. The scholars met at the .schools, and then attended divine service at the Parish Church, the sermon, which was preached by the Bev. Mr. Willis, taking the form of a practical address to the young people. After the service the children and their friends re- paired to a field adjoining the parsonage, where a very pleasant afternoon was spent. Tea was provided by Mrs. Reichardt, and there were marquees for occasional refresh- ment.. A bazaar was also held on behalf of the Church Missionary Society, and proved very profitable. Several hundreds of people joined in the festivities. KNITTSFORD.

CONSERVATIVE PICNIC AT TATTON PARK —The members of the Manchester Working Men's Conservative Association and the Oldham Working Men's Conservative League had a picnic on Saturday afternoon in Tatton Park, Knutsford About 800 persons were present from Manchester and 200 from Oldham. At the close of the afternoon a meeting was 'held, presided over by Mr. E. G. Simpson, who explained that Mr. T. Nash had promised to deliver a speech to them, but had been unable to remain for the meeting in conse- quence of the sudden illness of Mrs. Nash. Mr. P. Went- worth moved the adoption of the following resolution "That this assembly hereby records its solemn and deliberate opinion that the present Government has by its vacillation and feebleness, occasioned by the essential dis- union of its Cabinet, proved itself incapable of domestic legislation and the management of the House of (.;omtnons, and has trifled with the honour of the country abroad, and is therefore unworthy of the continued confidence of the people; and this assembly further pledges itself on the first opportunity to displace this Government of pretence and excuse, and to return to power a constitutional Govern- ment determined to secure the permanent prosperity of the country and the integrity of the empire."—Mr. O'Gorman seconded the resolution, which was supported by Mr. J. H. IBottomley (Oldham), and adopted.—Mr. Chas. Kenwortby p-oposed a vote of thanks to Lord Egerton for the use of the park, which was seconded by Mr. G. H. Massey, and carried. LEIGH.

HOW TO SPREAD SWINE FEVER. - At the Leigh Petty Sessions, John Royle, a pig dealer, has been summoned on rive charges, for contravening an Order in Council issued to prevent the spread of swine fever.—Mr. Jackson, superin- tendent of police, stated that in consequence of several out- breaks of this disease, in which the animals had to he slaughtered, he caused inquiries to be made as to where the pigs came from, and it was found that Boyle had sold them immediately after purchasing them in Warrington. By the order in council he ought tr have kept them 14 days on his own premies. It was also ascertained that the man was hawking the pigs through the streets. Nearly the whole of the animals disposed of suffered from the disease. The bench inflicted a penalty of 20s in each case,the amount of fine and costs being £ll as 31.—A beerhouse keeper, for allow- ing some of the pigs to be sold on his premises, was tined 103 and costs.

div.head: LYMlif.
div.p: LYMlif.

John Kerrigan, Labourer, of Leigh, who had been nine times previously convicted, was on Monday charged at Lymm Police Court with being drunk and disorderly in Lymm at one o'clock on Sunday morning, and was tined 5s and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment. RAINFORD. _ .

PITCH IND Toss AT RAINFORD.—At the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, on Monday, Michael Duffy and Michael McCann were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs for having played pitch and toss at Red Cat, Rainford, on the 24th Ult. DRUNKENNESS AT RAINFORD.—OR Monday, at the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, James Ashurst was fined ss. and costs for having been drunk in Chapel-lane, Rainford, on the 3rd inst —Samuel Smith was fined 7s. 61. and costs for a similar offence, on the 22nd ult., in Pasture-lane, Rain- ford.—Joseph Waring was fined ss. and costs for having I been drunk and disorderly in Pasture-lane, Rainford, on the 22nd June.—Peter Haves was fined 7s. 6d. and costs for a like offence, at Rainford, on the 25th ult.—A similar charge against Walter Smith was dismissed. STACK FIRE NEAR RAINFORD.—On Saturday afternoon last a stack of straw belonging to Mr. John Farritnond, a farmer at Moss Nook, near Rtinford, was destroyed by fire. It is stated that the fire was caused by a son of Mr. Kari- : mond's, a child four years of age, haying been playing near ; it with matches, one of which accidentally ignited the straw. lUnsuccessful attempts were made by Mr. Farrirnond and some of his neighbours hy throwing bucketsful of water upon them to suppress the II tmes,the stack being ultimately I completely destroyed. The damage done amounted to about £7 10i. PECULIAR SUICIDE AT RIINFORD• On Tuesday last a i suicide of a peculiar nature was committed at Red Cat, near Rainford. A collier nam,d John Mather, aged 41, who lived with his wife at Red Cat had for some time been suffering from bowel complaint, the pain of which seems to have affected his mind. At about four o'clock, on Tuesday afternoon, he and hie wife had tea together in their own house, and she at that time noticed something peculiar about her hu,band's appearance and conduct. Tea having i been concluded be went out and was afterwards seen by a I man who spoke to him. About six o'clock, however, !another man named John Grayson, whilst in his garden, ob- s•.,rve,l that some stones had been rolled away from the mouth of his well, and on looking .down saw a cap floating on the surface of the water. He then obtained the assist- ance of a man named named Tinsley, and together they scorched the well, and there found Mother's body. At an inquest, held on the following day by Mr. T. W. Barker, a verdict of suicide, whilst in a state of temporary insanity, , was return. d. ___---

PICNIC OF TOXTETH TORIES.—Tho members of the South Toxteth Working Men's Conservative Association held their 12th annual picnic on 1 uesday, at Hale. About 200 persons —men, women, and children—were conveyed to Hale in waggonettes, and, after participating in various amusements in the beautiful grounds of Col. Ireland Blackburne, they assembled to tea at the Childe of Hale Hotel. Mr. G. W. Hunter, secretary of the association, presided, and he wag supp'rted by Councillor Joseph Ball, Messrs. George Simpson, John Long, R. Bennett, C. Gerrard, W. Halton, T. H. W. Walker, William Lloyd, &c. A number of speeches of a congratulatory character were delivered. Mr. Ball afterwards proposed "Success to the South Toxteth Work- ing Men's Conservative Association," and Mr. George Simpson and Mr. Huiton responded. HAYDOCK. . ANOTHER ACCIDENT AT HANDOCK —On Thursday morn- ing Michael Martin, a day-wage man employed at the No. 2 Ram Pit, New Boston, Haydock, and living in a cottage off Lodge-lane, Ashton, was seriously injured while following his employment. There appears to be some little doubt as to how its received his injuries, but it is said to have been in connection uith one of the "cages," which commencel to move upwards unawares. He was either caught by it or he was upon it, and he fell off. He was badly injured about the head and back. and had to be removed home in an un- conscious state. He was afterwards taken to the Cott4ge Hospital at Eiaydock, where he is being attended by Dr. Hayward. ACCIDENT AT A HAVDOCE. HtryDOCE WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE SOCIETY.—The annual demonstration in connection with the Haydock Wes- leyan Methodist Band of Hope and Temperance Society was held on Saturday afternoon last. The scholars as- sembled at the schoolroom shortly before twe o'clock, and were formed in processional order. First came the large banner belonging to the school, beneath which walked Mr. Jehn Fairhurst (president af the society), and Mr. Baxen- dale (vice-president). Then came the Haydock Brass Band, -conducted by Mr. Mclntyre, and the members of the committee, who were succeeded by nearly 300 members and friends. The procession left the school about a quarter past two, and on reaching the toll-bar near Blackbrook, returned through the village to New Boston. Here they again turned back, and subsequently entered a field near the chapel, very kindly lent by Mrs. Evans,of " The Heves." Those present afterwards partook of a most excellent tea, and were thus invigorated and refreshed prior to spending the evening in various games and amusements. Everyone appeared to thoroughly enjoy themselvas, and the company separated about dusk. THE HavDocK LOCAL BOARD: SPECIAL MEETING.—A special meeting of the members of the Haydock Local Board was held at the Board offices, on Monday afternoon, when there were present Mr. Charles Pilkington (in the chair), Alker, Caod, Greenall, Cunliffe, Balharry, and Turn- bull (clerk).—The Chairman read the notice convening the meeting, which had been called for the purpose of again considering the scale of charges and regulations for water supply, and to fix a scale of charges for shops, warehouses, works schools, places of worship, and public,houses. After some discussion, it was decided, on the motion of Mr. Alker, that schools be charged ss. per quarter and that places of worship be supplied free.—Mr. Balharry moved that public-houses be charged at the rate of is. pert On the rateable value up to £2O, and dd. in the £ on every £ above £2o.—Mr. talker seconded the motion. —As an amendment Mr. Cunliffe moved and Mr. Greenall seconded that it be 3d. in the £ above £2o. On being put to the vote, two members voted for the amondment and four for the motion, the latter thus being carried.—The clerk was afterwards instructed to get Mr. Cawley (the assistant surveyor) to clean out the pipes more than once a week.. Mr. Turnbull remarked that Mr. Goldsworth (the surveyor) has asked him to say that at the next meeting he would give a full report of the works and the water supply generally. —This was the only business. HUTTON. Harrow CONGEDGATIONAL Curincu.—The interior arrangements of. the Congregational Church, Huyton Park, are being improved by the reversal of the position of the organ. It may not be generally known that an interesting ornament of this church is the study chair of the venerable doctor of divinity, Isaac Watts. The chair is of oak, elegantly carved. It was presented to the church about twenty years ago by the late Mr. Pack, and is set apart for the communion service. Huireute Bovemeee Ceee. WHISTON PARISH CHURCIL—On Saturday last sermons were preached in this church on behalf of the choir, by the Rev. Thomas Chambers, rector of Halewood. UNITED METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOLS, WHISTON.—One of the most successful gatherings that have taken place in Whiston for a number of years took place on Monday. The scholars fermed in proceasion at the schools at half-past one. At the head of the procession was carried a handsome new banner, made by Keesey, of Birmingham. It was of blee silk, and bore a represeutation of an °nen Bible, with figures of angels and the name of the schools in black let- ters on a back ground of gold, and won the praise of every- one in the village. The Hey. J. Sarvent, of St. Helens, and Mr. Roylance headed the procession, followed by the newly- organised Brass band of the schools, the children, who were marshalled by their teachers, numbering about 200. From the school the procession marched to the residence of Mr. J. Leatherbirrow, guardian of the township, where the band played a selection of music and the scholars sang a hymn. After leaving Roper's farm the scholars and their friends proceeded by the Union Workhouse to a field adjoining Stony Lane, kindly lent by Mr. Leatherbarrow, where the young people amused themselves with .cricket, foot races, three-legged race-, wheelbarrow races, and ether sports, the Prizes for the successful competitors being given by Mr. Leatherbarrow and Mr. Storey, the band playing at intervals. At half-past four o'clock about 200 scholars sat down to an excellent tea, being waited upon with much assiduity and kindliness by Mrs. Seddon, Mrs. Storey, Mrs. Heyes, Mr. Storey, Mr. Read, Mr. Leatherbarrow, the teachers and others The childred having been thus refreshed, the teachers and friends to the number of about 150 also had tea. Occasional refreshment was provided at a stall erected by Mrs. Travis. The presence of the band gave an of nortunity for dancing, which was freely embraced, two old dames from the alms houses, aged respectively 68 and 73, particularly diatinguishing themselves. The fun and frolic were kept up till half-past eight, when the ptocession was reformed and returned to the schools. On the way stoppages were made at the residences of Miss Williss Sandfield, and Mr. D. Seddon, Lane Ends, where hymns were sung. On again reaching Roper's Farm, another halt was made, a hymn was sung, and, on the motion of Mr. Storey, seconded by Mr. J. T. Stott, a vote of thanks was enthusiastically passed to Mr. Leatherbarrow for the kindness and liberality which he had displayed on that as on many other similar occasions, and Mr. Leatherharrow suitably acknowledged the compli- ment. The children then went to the chapel where each was presented with a bag of nuts and cakes, the festivities continuing till about ten o'clock. The arrangements were successfully carried out by Messrs. Jahn Mallinson, Samuel Davies, and J. T. star (general secretary). The weather was floe, and between seven and eight hundred people partook of the amusements in the field. The per- formances of the band were very favourably commented upon, and much credit was given to Mr. Corns for the effi- cient state into which he has brought the band in so short a time.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

SALVATION ARMY.—",General " Booth did n6t come on Friday any more than on the Tuesday previous. He had sent his son, Mr. Bollington Booth, and two of his " Majors," Taylor and Corbridge with fair promises for some future day. These explained how the enemy had been pressing the "General "and wanting to make him still use Eagle Tavern hr a spirit shop, and had carried on the trial to his detriment. They encouraged the army in their work, and predicted much success to their efforts. Singing, prayer, and reading the Bible, varied by experience of many of the rank and file, filled up the programme. ODDFELLOWS OF WINSFORD.—The Royal Weaver Lodge of the United Order of aldfellows, Winsford, headed by the Weaver brass band, under Mr. Robinson, its leader, proces- stoned the streets on Saturday last. Their hand and banner were not less attractive to gazers than the 80 out of its 156 members. After cce aliin on Messrs. W. H. Verdin, J.P., Highfield House ; J. D.'Kaye J.P., Winsford Lodge; Dr. O'Kell, Over Lodge; and R. Kaye, Fein Villa, they ad- journed to the Cocoa Rooms for dinner. There they did credit to Mr. Mark Atherton's able catering. The subscrip- tions got from some of the visited ones will go to swell the fonds of this benefit society which already amount to £1,050. GATHERINGS AT WOODFORD BALL —The residence of Mr. Slater, Mayor of Over, has twice within the week been visited by public bodies from Winsford. The first to avail themselves of Mr. Slater's kindness was the Sunday school, Zia., of the Free Methodists. Nearly 500 scholars, teachers, and friends went for the annual tea meeting. There was

div.head: sATURDAY', JuLY 14. iBsg.
div.p: sATURDAY', JuLY 14. iBsg.

only one drawback; it was a wet day, or the number would have been larger and the enjoyment much grel3.l.ee. As it was the tea and the sports had to take place in the large barn, and though the rain was peering, it did not hinder the flow of fun and affection. Hearty cheering for Mr. and Mrs. Slater clostel the progranune.—The second gathering was on Saturday, when the fire brigade of Winsford, by invitation, aasembled at the hall to hold their monthly drill and to par- take of Mr. Slater's hospitality. They had four men drill, single man drill, and eight man drill, all of which redounded to their credit. In the one man drill Ashley stood lust, as he generally does; he turned down the levers, took out the pole, removed the swing trees, ran out 23 yards of hose, and made ready the engine in 4S seconds. Baker did the same in 55 seconds, and the fireman Clutterbuck did it in 59 seconds. After the eight Men set to work they did the same, with the addition of 50 yards more hose, with water pumped through, in 50 seconds. Their work over, the Mayor and Mayoress entertained °them with a substantial repast, to which they turned with evident gusto from their previous labours. After ample justice had been done, Superintendent Hulse' for the brigade, tendered their, best thanks to the host anq hostess' who was the only one of the Lecal Board who had invited them in such a manner. He adverted to the small supply of water at farm houses generally, very different to that of Woodford Hall, and the street supply of Winsford. Superintendent Dodd was pleased the Mayor had invited them, and hoped they would never have to visit his house under more disagreeable cir- cums'ances. He was sure the brigade would agree with him that their best thanks were due to Mrs. Slater. The Mayor thanked them on behalf of Mrs. Slater, and said how pleased he had been to see their efficiency. Much de- pended on their despatch and ease. He was glad they had had a fine day.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARIj-OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARIj-OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Thursday. Present—Mr. W. Tyrer (chairman), Revs. T Chambers, J. Barnacle, and 'l'. Finegan; Messrs. Meadows, Leatherbarrow, Hall, Jacksrm, Birchall, Gerrard, Dobell, M4tthews, Penketh, Sadler, Syder, Lowe, lienwright, W. B. Longton, Gilbody, Huhne, Griffith. and Hartley (clerk). MASTER'S REPORT.

The Master renorteCrthaTtire-r-e- -were 454 inmates in the workhouse as against 422 in the corresponding month last year. During the week 34 vagrants had been relieved as compared with 137 in the corresponding month of last year. rle also reported that Mr. Edward Broome, Rainhill, had sent another present of flowers for the hospital. Thanks were voted to Mr. Broome, and also to the Rev. T. Cham- bers for a present of roses. He also reported that the fever hospital was full of smallpox cases, and asked if he was to refuse further admissions.—The CLERK stated that the last subject would be dealt with by the Visiting Committee.'

div.head: EMIGRATION OF CHILDREN.
div.p: EMIGRATION OF CHILDREN.

The clerk produced two letters from the Local Govern- ment Board with respect to the proposal to send children to Canada. The Board put obstacles in the way and wanted certain information.—The letters were referred to the special committee appointed to deal with the subject.

div.head: SUPERANNUATION ALLOWANCE.
div.p: SUPERANNUATION ALLOWANCE.
The Local Government Board wrote approving of a super- annuation allowance of £2O a years to Mr. George Lorrimer, late clerk to the master of the workhouse. VACCINATION.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board requesting the Guardians to caution Mr. Pendleton, vaccina- tion officer for Huyton, as to the way he discharged his duties, and to appoint a committee to see to the proper carrying out of the vaccination laws.--:NIr. DOBELL : How many cautions has he had ?—The CLERK: At least hal f-a- dozen:—Mr. DOBELL : It struck me sp.., and we may go on cautioning.—The matter was referred 11 the Finacce Com- mittee.

div.head: SCHOOL AT rENDANCH.
div.p: SCHOOL AT rENDANCH.

The CLERK stated that he had reported to the Local Government Board the action of the Guardians in appoint- ing an additional school attendance officer and urged them to sanction the appointment. In reply, the Local Govern- ment Board asked for further information and particulars as to the present and the proposed arrangements. He would send the particulars, the letter having only arrived yester- day.

APPOINTMENT OF NURSE. At a special meeting of the Guaqedians on the 10th inst., 13 applications for the post of nurse in the infectious diseases hospital were considered and three candidates selected, who were to attend on Thursday.—The CLERK stated that two of the candidates had written to say they could not attend and only one was in attendance, Martha J. Robins, of West Derby Union. He was told that her testi- monials were the best and that she was the most likely candidate.—Miss Robins having had an interview with the. board she was appointed, on the motion of Mr. HALL, seconded by Mr. LEATIIEBARROW. VAGRANT WARDS FOR ST. HELENS. A letter was read from Mr. Brewis, the town clerk of St. Helens, asking what the Board proposed to do with refer- ence to establishing vagrant wards at St. Helens.—The CLERK remarked that it was not a question for the Board seeing that the number of vagrants ead been reduced from 137 to 34.—Mr. LEATHERBARROW asked if it would not be desirable that a small committee should be formed to meet a committee of the St. Helens Town Council and discuss the matter and show them how the number of tramps was being materially reduced. A very few words of explanation might settle the whole in Itter.—Mr. HALL said the Town Council had never shown them their Case and they "ought not to give them inform ition. The Guardians said that no wards were required because they had reduced the vagrancy to such en extent that it was now really a nominal tigure. —Mr. LEATHERBA.RROW : We have not given them that in- formation.—Mr. HALL : It is in the papers every week.— Mr.LEA:rnEunAnaow: But that is not MEcial information. I , move that the matter be referred to a committee.—Mr. Du- BELL : I second the motion —Rev. T. FINEGAN : That is the way they have of shelving things in the House o f Commons.—The motion was carried, and the following committee was appointed—Rev. T. Chambers, Messrs. Meadows, Hall, DJbell, Birchall, 'idler, Jackson, and Leathet barrow. THE EGRESS FROM THE WORKHOUSE.
On the recommendation of the Vtsiting Committee, Mr. Henry Sumners, architect, Liverpool, was appointed to re- port upon the means of egress from the Workhouse.

div.head: FINANCE COMMIT FEE
div.p: FINANCE COMMIT FEE

The Finance Committee's minutes recommended that the application of Mr. Bullock, relieving officer, for an increase of salary ha deferred for three months. ,They also recom- mended that non-resident and non-settled relief be discon- tinued except in existing cases. Ihe committee's attention having been drawn to the large amount paid for water, they had ordered a return to be prepared. This return was now produced, showing that the amount in 1880 was £222 ; in 1881, £130; in 1882, £129. and in 1883, £l2B.—The min- utes were confirmed.
MR. STUART'S SALARY.

Mr. LEATRERBARROW, as chairman of the Finance Com- mittee, made the motion of which he had given notice, that the salary of Mr. Stuart, relieving officer, St. Helens, be increased from £lOO to £l2O per annum. The motkon was made on the unanimous recommendation of the Finanee Committee.— Mr. HALL seconded the resolution. He believed Mr. Stuart was a very valuable officer, and had reduced the cost of re- lief cowiderably.—Mr. BIRCHALL supported the motion on the same grounds.—The Rev. J. BARNACLE supported the motion for the reason that. from the half-year ending March 1882, to the half-year ending March, 1883, he had reduced the expenditure £lOO ; and even in the last quarter, ending 24th June, the expenditure was £2O less than in the pre- vious quarter. Mr. Stuart had done very substantial work, and deserved the support of the guardians.—The Rev. T. FINEGAN did not rise to oppose the increase of Mr. Stuart's salary, but he rose to say a few words against the reasons brought forward in favour of it. He never considered that it was a recommen- dation for a relieving officer to get his salary increased that he reduced the expenditure. The expenses depended so much upon circumstances that be should be sorry to let it go forth from the Board that they increased the relieving officer's salary because he had reduced the expenses. He fincied thaf Mr. btuart had sufficient to recommend him without that. It might work badly. It might appear to the other officers that they had merely to reduce the ex- penses in order to obtain an increase of salary. He did not object to the increase, but he objected to the reasons given for it by the Guardians who had spoken.—The motion was agreed to.

PRESCOT PARISH Cunacat.---The parishioners of Prescot are suffering a serious deprivation by the absence of ,the familiar faces of the Parish Church clock. The deprivation is, however, only temporary and preparatory to the bestowal of a great benefit, the clock having been sent to Coventry to receive at the hands of that master of an unappreciated art, Mr. G. Worden, the necessary additions for the attachment of Cambridge chimes. The extensive alterations to the vicarage are nearly completed, and the Vicar, who has been absent on his holidays for the last three weeks, is expected to return next week. TIIE SUNDERLAND DISASTER: VERDICT OF THE SECOND JURY.—The inquest upon the children who resided at Monk- wearmouth and were killed in the disaster at the Victoria Hall, Sunderland, was concluded on Tuesday. The jury, after an hour's consultation, found that the deceased came to their deaths by suffocation through the partial closing of a door on the landing, fixed in its position by a bolt, but by whom the bolt was fixed there was no evidence to show. The jury further found in answer to a series of questions sabmitted by the Coroner, that upon Messrs. Fay and Coates rested the legal responsibility of taking proper pre- c iutions for the preservation of the lives of the children, that the particular neglect of duty which led to the loss of life was in otnmitting to provide a sufficient staff of atten- dants to preserve order within the gallery and during the departure of the children; and that the staff provided was not sufficient for the purpose even if the fatal door had not existed. The caretaker's omission to inform Fay and his assistants of the existence of the door was neglect of duty, and the directors of the Victoria Hall Company were not justified in erecting such an unusual door, with such pecu- liar fastenings, without instructing the caretaker to call the special attention of strangers taking the hall to it. They were of opinion thatparents Cr relatives were not justified in allowinechildren of tender age to go alone to crowded public entertainments without first satisfying themselves that some grown-up persons were intending to take entire charge of them • and that the masters of the various schools were not justified in allowing children under their charge to be can- vassed by Fay and their attendance secured without provi- sion being made for their proper supervision and control by their teachers. The jury finally recommended that statu- tory provision should be made for enforcing the entrance and exit of buildings bein7, made to open outwards, and for inspection of public buildings.
WOUNDED BY A SAUCEPAN AT WIDNES. THE PRISONER COMMITTED FOR TRIAL.

-Before Mr. H. S. Hall and Mr. J. Brock, at Widnes Polioe Court, on Monday, Harriet Burns, a married woman, living in. Alfred-street, was brought up on remand charged with unlawfully and maliciously wounding Emily Lightfoot, wife of Thomas Lightfoot, labourer, of 16, Alfred-street. The prosecutrix, a delicate-looking young woman, who ap— peared to be in a weak condition. was accommodated with a chain—Dr. Cooper deposed that he .was called ,to see the prosecutrix, at half-past five, on the 2nd inst. He examined her and found her suffering from a severe wound on the front of the head, and a slight one at the back. The former wound was about an inch in length, the scalp beiog cut throhgh to the bone; and it might have been attended with danger. such wounds were always dangerous until they were healed. Mrs. Lightfoot was weak and excited, and had been confined to her bed for several days. She was still very weak and not fit to follow her employment; and probably would not be well for seven or eight days. A blow from the iron pen.(produced) would cause such Wounds as he had described, and if the pan was unbroken at the time the Wow was given it would require a good deal of force to inflict such a wound. The wound was a dangerous one if followed by erysipelas, suppuration or sloughing of the skin, or any inflammation of the Crain or its membranes. The prosecutrix was progressing favourably at• present. prosecutrix was then , sworn, - and said about four o'clock on Monday, the 2nd instant, she passed by the prisoner's house on her way home, and the prisoner followed her. As she was entering the house the prisoner struck her with her list and called her afoul name. She then got inside the house. The prisoner followed her, struck her in the stomach with ber fist, knocking her down. She felt backwards, but immediately got up and ordered the prisoner to leave the house. Prisener refused, tind a woman named Elizabeth Partington, who had come in, pushed the prisoner out and shut the door, but she must in again. Mrs. Lightfoot attempted te escape through the back kitchen, but the prisoner felled ker with the saucepan produced, and she became unconscious. She , only regained consciousness when the doctor was dressing her wounds. She felt very weak, and went to bed, where she remained until the following Filthy. She had been weak and ill since the eccurreuce, and was still suffering from her injuries. She had never given the prisoner any provocation to ieriee her.—By Inspector - Barnett: The saucepan was her's (the prosecutrix's), and was perfectly sound before the affray. She could not say how it came to be broken—whether from the blow or otherwise.—The prisoner, in cross-examining witness, said she had a poker in her hand.—Mrs. Partingtom of 2, Alfred-street, gave cor- roborative evidence, and P.C. McDonald deposed to appre- hending the prisoner.—After being cautioned in the usual way, the prisoner said "I intended to hit the woman with the pot that hit me with the poker, and not Mrs. Lightfoot. I did not want to do anything to her."—The prisoner was committed to the quarter sessiene for trial.

div.p: CRICKET. oat _ tecretar!es of Cricket Clubs are requested to note tteel Its of matches played on Saturday must be sent to rtbead Office, Bewsey-street, Warringto—, not later than ten Qc. on Wednesday morning.

1 PROSECUTION OF A " SHAKER " Felt MANSLAUGHTER:. HeurT Osborne, chief elder of Mrs, (killing's Shaker com- munitY, was charged ai Lyrdingion on Tuesday with caus- ing the death of his daughter, for whom, during her illness, he provided no medical assistance. The doctor, who made the post-mortem examination of the deceased failed to at- tend the magisterial proceedings, and the police were conse- quently unable to complete their case, Osborne having to appear at Winchester assizes on Thursday to answer the in- dictment for manslaughter on the coroner's warrant. The case therefore fell through. Mrs. Girling, who was in court with a large number of her followers, said no one was satis- fied with the verdict of the jury, and the coroner and doctors were satisfied with the treatment of the deceased girl. DARING ADVENTURE OF A BANFFSHIRE FISHERMAN.—On Sunday afternoon a herring fishing boat of 52 feet keel, be- longing to one of the smaller fishing villages on the Banff- shire coast, arrived at Peterhead from Stornoway in charge of one man only—the skipper—who is also owner, the boat having been a week on her passage. It appears that the man had been in financial difficulties, and had engaged an entire crew of hired men, along with whom he prosecuted the fishing from Stornoway. He was unsuccessful, fishing only a few crans. At the close of the fishing a fortnight ago , he was unable to pay his men, and the boat was arrested in payment of the wages. The attachment was made in the usual way by carrying off the rudder and some oars. The skipper, however, had entered upon an engagement to fish at Peterhead, and had been paid his £4O bounty. Getting the sail hoisted he started from Stornoway Harbour at two a.m. on Saturday, June 30, with oars, nets, d;c., but without a rudder. He says he pulled five minutes alternately on either side until the wind caught the sail, and then, steering the boat by means of an oar, he held on his way. The first two days were calm, and he managed to get an occasional sleep, but afterwards had to keep awake. Two days after he left he filled a pan with water wherewith to bell some fish he had caught, but forgot to plug the barrel, so that when be returned for a drink he found the contents gone. For three days he had no water, and had to run for Cullen harbour, on Saturday, where he got a fresh supply.

HIGHWLY COMMITTEE.

This committee had received a letter from the London and North-Western Riilway Company saying that the bridge at Bradlsy footpath would be made 7ft. flin. instead of 6ft. as at first arranged. A statement was presented showirg the cost of each horse employed by the committee to be .£2 Is. 7d. per week. Mr. Midwood reported result of interview with Me. Worthington, re Lugsdale-road, which was considered satisfactory. The surveyor was instructed to prepare a plan of the Board's requirements, which Mr. Worthington undertook to submit to his directors. A letter I was read from Mr. Swale, calling attention to the crossings at junctions of Midwood and Travis-streets with Widnes- road, and to the flioding of cellars. The committee recom- mended that two sett crossings be put in, and that Mr. Swale be informed that it is the owner's duty to drain the cellars. The Health Committee's rzquest to join in the expense of Halton-view drainage was considered. Thh committee did not see their way to agree to their request. Plans for St. Paul's Church were submitted and pas,:d subject to the Health Committee's approval.—Mr. MIDWOOD moved, and Mr. SADLER seconded the confirmation of the minutes.— Mr. WEBSTER said the crossings at Widnes-road were not worse than other crossings in the neighbourhood, and he thought if Mr. Midwood began to put settings in one cross- ing be should put them in all.—Mr. MARTLEY remarked tuat there had been several applications with regard to the making of Irwell-street ny the trustees of Hartland Chapel and as he supposed they were willicg to nay, he did not see why the Board did not do the work. With regard to the coat of horses, the minute did not say whether the amount stated included the driver's wages.—Mr. WRIGHT said Mr. Midwood had been preaching very hard at the Gas Com- mittee about economy, and sparing the ratepayers' money, and he saw that this committee had given instructions to the surveyor to obtain estimates for a new water cart barrel to contain 250 gallons to be fixed on an old frame. The summer was almost gone, and perhaps by the time they had orected the barrel on the cart winter would be here, and the cart would not be needed until April. (Laughter.)— In reply to Mr. Webster, Mr. MIDWOOD explained that there was an understanding with the late Board that the crossings should be made, and land had been given to the Board for the purpose, and in all fairness the Board was bound to carry out the arrangement. Matters were in pro- gress with regard to Irwell-street, and he hoped would be concluded by the next meeting.—Mr. WEBSTER wished to see the agreement with regard to the crossings. He had had to pay for flagging himself —Mr. MiDwocm : The Board has taken the land.—Mr. WEBSTER moved that the recom- mendation be referred back, so that the agreement could be produced.—Dr. O'KEEFFE : On the same principle as the Netherley building I will second the motion.—Mr. SA.DLER : In this case the Board has had the land given to them; at Netherley they bought it.—The amendment was lost, and the minutes were passed.
