On Thursday, in the House of Commons, on the consi- Aeration of the iNianchester Ship Canal Bill, Sir Charles Forster moved that standing orders 223 and 243 be sus- pended and the Bill read a third time, the Queen's consent on behalf of the Crown and the Duchy ef Lancaster being signihed.—Mr. Whitley said he wished to put a question to the president of the Board of Trade of very great itnpor- tance. The Conservators of the Mersey were looked noon as the protectors of the interests of that river. The people of Liverpool had the greatest confidence in Admiral Sprat t, who was the acting conservator of the Mersey, and was well acquainted with alt the sloals and difficulties of the river; but it had been stated that Sir John Coode had been appointed in some capacity or other, as they understo:d, to assist the conservators of the river. He wished to know what was the scope and object of Sir John Code's employ- ment. If it was simply to advise the conservator of the river, there could be no possible objection; but if his evi- dence was to be given before the House of Lords, to enable the promoters to obtain their bill, it was felt that the in- terest of the Mersey might in some degree be jeopardised. Therefore he wished to know from the right hon. gentleman who, by virtue of his office, was a conservator of the Mersey, what was the scope and object of Sir John Coode's employment, and by whom he was employed.— Mr. CiIAMBERLAIN said the hon. gentleman would be aware that the Mersey Conservancy consisted of the First Lord of the Admiralty, the President of the Board of l Trade, and the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, and they were assisted by Admiral Spratt, the acting conserva- tor. When the bill was first promoted the promoters sought

HEALTU COIIIIITTEE.—FEVErt AND TIM SEnitiNG ov HALTON VIEW. The MEDICAL OFFICER reported to this committee that during the mon,h of June ttiere 'were 87 births, or 41.76 per 1000; and 34 deaths, or 16 32 per 1000. Of the latter eight were children under one year. and 11 children between one and five years. Zvmotic diseases caused one death. The nuisance inspector's report for June stated: "The small-pox case in Widnes-road is progressing favourably ; the shop is still closed and the children still away. A case of fever is reported at Elieibeth-street, New- town; on account of poverty the relieving officer requested me to provide nursing, dic. After consultation with Dr. O'Reeffe and the medical officer, I declined to interfere, ex- cept to disinfect, which has been done. The patient is re- covering. Five cases of scarlet fever (children) have been reported; one at Crowwood, two at Moeshank, and two at No. 42, Charlotte-street; all are recovering." Plans were submitted to the committee for the drainage of Halton View at an estimated cost of £165 ; and it was recommended that the work be done, provided the owners of the property there agreed to pay one half of the cost. The building plans of St. Paul's Church were approved subject to the surveyor's suggested alterations respecting drainage and sanitary arrangements being adopted.—Dr. O'KEEFFE pro- posed the adoption of the minutes.—The motion was seconded.-Mr Manwooo asked whether theproposed drainage at Halton View was pert of the main sewerage scheme. Ir. SADLER objected to the recommendation, because it appeared to him to make flesh of one and fish of another. There were scores of houses in the particular state that was de- scribed at Halton View, and if it was intended to drain that particular district, other people might fairly ask for similar work to be carried out.—Dr. O'KEEFFE replied that some years ago there was a comprehensive scheme drawn up for the drainage of Halton View, and one of more than double the expense of the present one. It. was postponed from time to time, and since then additional cellars bad been built. They would all bear in mind that a short time ago a case of malignant scarlatina broke out there, and the patient died. This called the the committee's attention to the necessity of providing against the recurrence of any outbreak of a similar kind there, because if scarlatina once spread through the town- aship.and became epidemical, it would put the Board as a sanitary authority to an expense far greater than they pro- posed to expend upon this drainage. This sewer would be a portion of the main sewerage scheme, and would drain the cellars in the neighbourhood for the nest 50 years. He had interviews with the owners, and had no doubt they would contribute fully one half of the cost.—Mr. SADLER said the doctor had failed to show why Halton View should have precedence over places established longer. There were houses and shops in Widnes that had been flooded for years, and no doubt the owners of this property would contribute towards the cost of drainage if they were approached in the same way as the owners of Halton View had been. Dr. O'KEEFFE replied that Halton View offered greater facilities for drainage than other parts of the town —Mr. SADLER said he had heard it stated that the 'Board was not compelled to drain cellars.—Dr. O'KEEPFE replied that unless drainage existed previous to the cellars being built, the owner was obliged to provide drainage for them.—Mr. CAREY explained that one of the reasons why they proposed to drain Halton View was because they wanted surface drainage for road purposes and for the cottages that were being built there, and the other was that there was a good number of cellars clustered to- gether which were becoming a danger to the neiehbourhood for want of the proposed accommodation. He believed there were nine cellars in that one spot. —Mr. SADLER: I could take you in a street to-day where there are 29 cellars flooded. He mentioned Anne-street.—Mr. CAREY said there were drains there but they were not low enough.— Mr. MIDWOOD then seconded Mr. Sadler's amendment, which was however lost, and the minutes were then passed.

That clause had been agreed to, and it was in accordance with its provisions that the Conservators of the Mersey had appointed Sir John Coode, as an engineer of very wide ex- perience in similar matters, to advise them and assist Admiral Spratt He was not at all connected with the pro- moters or the promotion of the bill, aud was only being employed in a consultative capacity on behalf of the Con- servators of the Mersey.—Mr. Whitley said the explanation was perfectly satisfactory.—The bill was then read a third time. div.head: MR. MIDWOOD ON SPECULATION.
div.p: MR. MIDWOOD ON SPECULATION.

Mr. MIDWOOD thought the Board had better give the Gas Committee a new name, and call it the speculation com- mittee. Within the past few months they had been trying • speculations,, and they had not properly tried one project before they entered into another, The committee recom- mended an expenditnre of £135 on a washer, which seemed to be a new thing ; and one or two other things which had been very expensive had been tried. I hey might answer, he hoped they would, but there was too much speculation in the committee's actions, and he thought that before th'ev • entered into any further speculation with the ratepayers' money they ought to test what they had already got. The -committee was now recommending a plan for a new build- ing at Netherley, to be erected over an engine which was doing nothipg, and might be wanted perhaps once in seven years. There was at the present time &wooden erection over the engine, which bad been there for some years, and in his opinion would be adequate for all purposes for the , next ten years. It might be urged by the chairman of the , committee that they were bound by an agreement to ,erect this building, but before he was agreeable for the minutes to be passed he should want him to produce that document and seeif the Board's seal was attached. If it was not he ahnuld let the present erection stand as it was. He understood list week that the estimated cast of the new building eras £BOO, but the Chairman now stated it was Seeing that they had a loss of £l,lOO on water in ,1881, and a lots of _saw last year, he was puzzled.to know .bow the committre Were goingto give an extra five percent. -discount. ,It might be urged that they would sell a Larger -quantity. They would have to sell a very much Icrger luantity..becazse the extra. five per cent, would reduce the -income a great 'gel), and ae.ding that rOuction to the losaes Auring the past few years. he could. not really find out where they would get it. Vie committee might be better Jiltaancier2 than he was—he hoped they were—hut at the same time he felt that the Gas and Water Committee were going in for speculatian rather than for spending the town- ship's money with economy. (Hear, hear.):—Mr. B. Dirrrom was very much astounded at the tespection when he saw the plant the Board had for making gas, and also for raising water. He certainly thought the ratepayers had cause to be proud of such plant. They were now at the prime condition of the plant; everything should be in the very best order. He ob4erved when at the gasworks that certain new retorts were being put down, that experiments were going to begin in order to economise, if possible, in the ..manufacture of gas, and it was only natural that the rate- I anyers shonld expect the Board to make some reduction in the price of gas. Mr. WEBS—TER then moved the resolution of which he had given notice, that all the officials of the Board shoald r,- side within the rateable district of Widnes. At the present time, in connection with Widnes Local Board there were, he said, three foreigners who took about £650 out of the town. lie thougtt persons corning from another town ought not to take money out of the town; they ought to reside within the ratable district of Widnes. They received their money from the rates, and he thought they ought to be ready to contribute towards the rates of the town. Therefore he moved the resolution.—Mr. SADLER : Mr. Chairman, I think he ought to be called upon to withdraw that word foreigners.—After a pause the CHAIRMAN said Mr. Webster's motion fell to the ground for want of a seconder. Mr. WEBSTER: It may fall to the ground how, but it will be brought forward in the future. The ratepayers of Widnes agree with me on the question, and at the nt-xt election it will be made a cry.—At a later stage Mr. WEBSTER gave notice that at tne next meeting he would move that Mr. Allen's (the clerk's) salary be reduced .£lOO, and Mr. Cope. land's (the resident engineer's) £5O unless they agreed to reside within the township

div.head: PROPOSED NEW PUBLIC OFFICES.
div.p: PROPOSED NEW PUBLIC OFFICES.

Mr. MIDWO-0-;;;;Id he wished to bring under their notice the offices the Bo ird at present occupied. In 1879 they leased the present premises for £7O per annum, being £55 for the accountants' department, and £l5 for the surveyor's office. That lease would should shortly run out; it expired next year; and he thought, looking at the many disadvantages in connection with the present building, that the Board could not under present circumstances be the tenants of the premises. In the first place, the cellar was nearly always flooded with water, the sine/1 from which ascending into the office, the clerks at times could scarcely breathe. Mr. Allen's office scarzely ever get any daylight; it was damp all round, and altogether a most miserable room. The Board-room, as the chairman no doubt knew, was a very cold, draughty place in the winter. He got a stiff neck on several occasions last winter when he had to stay in that room for hours The room overhead had become a most disagreeable thing. The members could scarcely ever hold a meeting, without being interrupted with singing, music, dancing, and barrels of beer or barrels of some other spirit being rolled down the steps. Frequently some of the Board's officials had to go out and ask the people above if they would please be quiet until the Board bad finished their business, and this was a most disagreeable thing for a public body to do, con- sidering the price they paid for the premises. The School Bo ad paid about £4O per annum, for their offices, the over- seers about £2O per annu.n, and laoking at two or three circumstances, he thought the time had .come when the Baerd ought to have a building of their own, at a cost of about £2 000 or £2,500. In time, this sum would be paid off, out of the rent which these public bodies were paying, and the property would become the property of the ratepayers, whereas now the Board might go on paying as long as they lived for these miserable offices, for beginning at the cellar and going to the top, there was not a worse place in the township at present. The Board might borrow £2,500 at 31 per cent. for 30 years, and the rent being paid by the public bodies he had named, wbo might be induced to take offices in a new building erected by the Board, would soon wipe out the debt. They had land on the other side of the way that cost £9OO, which could be utilised, and would thus reduce the present outgo of the market. The Board, he thought ought to take the matter into serious consideration whether it would not be wise to build public offices at a cost of the sum he had named. He begged to move that the Finance Committee take the subject into serious considera- tion.—Mr. ekREY said he should be glad to support Mr. Mid- wood in his proposition. There was no doubt that these offic:e were inconvenient and not at all suitable for the pur- pose. He was sure they could not be very healthy for the clerks who were in the building continually. If it could be shown that they could put up a new building without costing the ratepayers any more than the present offices cost them, he thought it would be a very desirable thing.—Mr. WEB- STER said Mr. Midwood seemed to be a very wonderful man and seemed to change colour very often. (Hear hear.) He had taken the Gas Committee to task for wanting to erect a building they were told was wanted, but he could see his way to spending money there where it was not wanted. He (Mr. Webster) could not say they would be doing a good thing by building a town hail at present. If they could .convert the market into a place for the offices and the Board room, it would be bettter than building a town hall.—Mr. MZDWOOD thought Mr. Webster's argument would not hold water. (" Nonsense.") There was ac much difference between the Gas Committee's recommendation and his (Mr. Miderood'e) proposal as there was between chalk and cheese. The Loud would not derive one penny from simply pulling down the engine shed at Netherley and erecting another in its place, but the building be proposed would wipe off the debt incurred by the rent that was being paid now by public boards in the town. The School Board would be able to use the Board room, which would be a great convenience. [A MEMBER: You must get them diet.] They could get them. He forgot to say in his opening remarks that the landlord of the present offices had intimated that when the lease ran out the Board vieould have to pay a higher rent. He thought they ought to take all things into consideration.—Mr. CAREY said be should like to remind Mr. Webster that the proposi- tion was not for the erection of a town hall. It was to con- sider whether they ought to have a building of their own to transact public business. He seconded Mr. Midwood's proposition, which was adopted, Mr. Webster not voting.

div.p: GOSSIP OF THE LONDON CORRESPON-

Owing to the unbrotherly relations of the new Duke of Marlborough and Lord R. Churchill, it is deemed probtble in political circles that Lord Randolph will change his mind and not attempt to stand for Woodstock. In that event he may be glad to fall back upon the offer of the Manchester

Tories. aLord Derby is not supposed to be given to joking, bu he is credited with the following witty observation to a brother peer, who was complaining of the coldness of the House of Lords whenever he addressed it : " I am becom- ing accustomed to it; but at first I felt like speaking to gravestones in a cemetery." It appears from some proceedings which have taken place in the Court of Session, that the special trains (the " Mes- senger" trains, as they are called), which run daily between Aberdeen and Ballater while the Queen is at Balmoral, are not paid for by her Majesty,as is generally supposed, but by the Home Office. These trains cost nearly £7O a week, and during the last ten years the amount paid to the company has been £9,300. The vacant deanery of Exeter is one of the nine most valuable in the gift of the Crown. The stated emoluments of that dignified offica are £2,000, the same as those of the deaneries of You., Canterbury, London, Rochester, West- minster, Oxford, and Lincoln. Only the Dean of Durham, in fact, whoso salary is £3,000 per annum, will be the superior in a pecuniary sense of the new dean of Exeter, whoever he may be. Lord Derby's success with regard to the finances of Cyprus is even greater than was stated yesterday, and his Lordship has now informed the Treasury that the estimate of £45,000 which stands to be voted by Parliament will not be required, and that ho is prepared to accept a reduction of £15,000. The consequence is that when the vote comes on, which will probibly not be until August, Mr. Courtney will apply for £30,000 only, being one-third of the vote of last year. Mr. Gladstone seems to have dispensed with kis armed escort. I saw hirn leave the house alone and unattended, walking stick in hand, his black frock coat unbuttoned, re• vealing a white waistcoat underneath, looking as fr esti, neat, and jaunty as a young beau bound for his lady's bower. The right lion. gentleman walked with a firm step across the square, to his official residence in Downing-street, like any other wayfarer in the streeis of London ; but he had work in plenty to touch his hat politely, as he invariably does, in acknowledg- ment of the constant salutations which matk his progress anveyhpea in the virinitv -4 of Palliament. Irish landlordism, despairing of obtaining the compensa- tion for which at one time it clamoured, arid no longer trust- ing Lord Cairn 3 to enable the lands to be sold to the State, has taken a new line, and now it proposes to ask Ministers

In-,: 'grants-in-aid as mortgages upon the property, so as to enanle owners to tide over a very bad time. Lord Castle- town celled a meeting of Irish landlords on the subject, in one of the conference rooms of the House of Comm ms, and out of it will probably arise requests to be submitted pre- sently to the Cabinet. But Mr. Gladstone is not disposed to enter into any mere schemes for lending money just at present; and Mr. Chillers is very likely indeed to send the applicants to borrow where they can in the open market: Tee question about the pryenent of £250 a year out of the Civil List to Prince Lucien Bun rperte greatly moved the Premier, on Thursday. With a vie-our unusual Er.-en for him, and with mach detail, which Ca promised, if necessary, further to enlarge upon, he dwelt upon the services ren- dered by the Prince in the unremunerative department of philology, and wound up by the declaration that he took shame to himself that the pension had not Leen earlier be- stowed. Prince Lucien is now 70 years of age, and is not likely long to remain a pensioner on the national bounty. It is a curious irony of fate that, in his old age, a nephew of the First Napoleon should become dependent on the bounty of England, his claim being established by the purshit of so harmless an occupation as philology. Mr. Bradlaugh, as might have been expected, is m the most of the opportunity provided for him by the Oppo- sition on Monday last. By way of preparing for his great performance, he is widely advertising himself by correspon- dence with the Speaker upon the resolution pissed at the instance of Sir S. Northcote: Having dexterously succeeded in fixing upon himself the eyes of the nation, he now pro- posE sto appear and endeavour to take his seat. He will certainly get no further than the door, where are posted four of the most stalwart policemen in the "A" division, one was before he joined the forced noted as a wrestler. There is something almost pathetic in this intelligent officer's con- stant apprehension that Mr. Bradlaugh my chance to turn up some time when he is off duty. To prevent surprise, instructions have been given to the police outside the Palace yard and within the precincts of the House to signal the ap- proach of the hon. member, whereupon the police in the lobby will form square and prepare to resist Mr. Bradlaugh. This is a ludicrous and undignified Position for the House of Commons to be placed in. But that is one of the least important consequences of the triumph of intolerance. A happy thought! It has occurred to Mr. Richard Paget—not the member for South Leicestershire, but the member for Mid-Somerset. Everybody knows that what makes telegrams so expensive is the need for special de- livery. One messenger has to be employed as a rule for each message. But so mach expedition is not always re- quired. A. man misses the post one slight; it is important that a communication shall be made to a client next morn- ing. But the fact that his telegram must be immediately delivered if it is sent at all is rather a nuisance than other- wise. Now, Mr. Paget wants to know whether telegrams not requiring special delivery might not, under the new bill which Mr. Fawcett intends to introduce next session, be sent at a reduced tariff. He is going to ask the Postmaster- General to consider the advisability of establishing a cheaper rate for telegrams sent from the country to London or any other populous place having two or more deliveries during the day, which must be sent to their address by the earliest available postal delivery of letters. This is a development of the sixpenny telegram which has not yet been thought of; and it would mean postal revenue. Further news from Teheran gives circumstantial details of the treaty arranged between Persia and Russia, of which oar own Government appears to know so little. Its im- portance is obvious to anyone who will take the trouble to look at a good map of the country. The object of Russia's last campaign there was to approach as near as possible the Mery oasis, and her advanced posts are as far south as A.skhahad, and her scouts have penetrated as far as Sarrakhs, about 100 miles south-west of Mery and as far east of the Persian town of Meshed. It is stated that the treaty pro- poses to advance the Russian, frontier half way between Sarrakb and Merv, but the territory is not Persia's to give, and if appropriated by Russia would be sheer robbery. But there is no power there to oppose the designs of the Mus- covites. I suppose England will regard the proposed an- nexation as "an unfriendly act," and that will be all. If, however, Russia extends her frontier in the manner des- cribed the doom of Mery is sealed, as the most of the oasis could be in the possession of the invader, who would be brought within a few days' march of Merv, which has been described as the key to Herat, which in its turn is the door of India. It may he taken for granted that the Suez Canal scheme is gone. To-night there was not a man of business in the House of Commons who approved of it; the city is in arms against it, and arrangements are being made to hold a meeting, under the presidency of the Lord Mayor, to nnmorialiee the House of Commons against it To-morrow the Council of the Chamber of Commerce will meet to draw up a protest. News comes from the North of England that the shipowners there are organising themselves to prevent the passing of the scheme. To-night the Tory leaders held a CAUCUS, anel they deter- mined to move a resolution condemning it, and there is no more chance of Mr. Gladstone curving it in face of such an opposition than of his carrying a bill for closing the canal altogether. What the shipowners asked for was a canal of English making, under English control, taking a lower tariff than the canal of M. de Lesseps, and satisfied with a smaller dividend than between 20 and 30 per cent. It will probably be impossible to avoid a discussion upon the sub- ject. A sudden withdrawal of se important a proposal

would look like weakness, but the Government is alroady i aware that its a,,,--- --` —'''' M. de T ta.eps is not worth .. I' the paper upon which ir is written. It may be, perhaps, interesting to recall the facts about the purchase of the Suez Canal shares. Mr. Gladstone ' proposes to give eight and a quarter millions Wert. as the construction of a new canal. He proposes, and asks Parlia- ment to sanction his proposition. Mr. Disraeli spent more than four millions on the purchase of shares in a canal li I already mat; ucted. He spent the money, and came 4iter-' 1 wards to Parliament with a request for an indern;;lty. air. , Gladstone will get his money according to '• i terms. 1 ..... cue usual O i Mr, Disraeli had to pay nearly .fl^- ..,,u,OOO for the loan of the i 1 iiia4" ;01' a tew da7t. on .the other hand, Mr. Disraeli 1 ' bought shares for £23 is. BJ. apiece which are now worth \ £9B. Mr. Gladstone buys nothing, and the increased value of the canal made with British capital will go to the Suez Canal Company. If Mr. Gladstone were now to sell the shares bought by Mr. Disraeli he would have more than \ , enough money to lend M. de Lesseps for a new canal. , There will be no proit on Mr. Gladstone's transaction, ok none worth speaking of ; on Lord Beaconfield's transaction the profit enables the Exchequer bonds to be paid off. Mr. Gladstone will probably plead that Mr. Disraeli's was a mere stockjobbing affair, while his own is State aid to a necessary commercial enterprise ; but the Tories hope to find justifica- tion for Lord B-aconsfield in Mr. Gladstone's agreement,and condemnation of Mr. Gladstone's agreement in the superior financial transaction of 1875. Anyhow, it is odd to find Lord Beaconsfield's Eastern policy reappearing in form, though not in substance, in the history of Mr. Gladstone's adminia- ration. The Joint Note, the calling out of the Reserves, he use of the Indian troops, and all the rest, have now the 'urther addition of money advanced for the Suez Canal.

div.head: SALTATION ARMY. PRESENTATION OF COLOURS TO THE WAR-
div.p: THE SALTATION ARMY. PRESENTATION OF COLOURS TO THE WAR-

RINGroN CORPS. In the brief space of three months' time that the recruiting officers of the Salvation Army have been in Warrington, they have succeeded in enlisting soldiers in sufficient num- bers to form a local corps. This corps will henceforth be known as the " 412th," and on Monday evening there was a public presentation of colours to the Warrington warriors. No fault could he found with the poster announcing this event, the intimation being made in the most formal phraseology; and yet it caused qaite as much stir as the former placards about which there was so much appreuen- sion in official quarters. Early in the evening people began to assemble in Buttermarket-street, and in the vicinity of the Barracks, where the Salvationists met prior to parading the town; and about seven o'clock Academy-street and a partion of Buttermarket-street were crowded with spectators. Soon after the hour above mentioned the corps commenced its march through the principal thoroughfares. The van was led by Major Taylor, of Manchester, and other officers in a carriage drawn by a pair of grey horses, then came the brass band of the Widnes corps, succeeded by the, Weil soldiers, who brought up the rear. Large numbers of persons accompanied the procession, which attracted crowds to the street corners along the route. Several hymns were ren- dered, the verses being given alternately by the band and the soldiers, but the singing of the latter could not be heard above the noise of the crowd that surrounded the corps. In the crowd were numbers of young women, innocent of bead-dress, who waved aloft their aprons and pocket-hand- kerchiefs in imitation of the Salvationists whose practice of walking backwa ds was also followed with no little dif- ficulty by several men. On arrival at the Public Hall, where the presentation was announced to take place, and to which a charge for admission was made, the Salvationists found the building putted in all parts by an interested audience, which was remarkable for its orderliness throughout the whole of the novel proceedings. In the meeting preceding the ceremony there was scarcely anything to which anyone, except the most rigid ritualist, could take objection. The service was conducted by Major Taylor, a pleasant, intel- ligent looking man, of medium height and light build. He was supported on the platform by the corps, which had there taken its stand, and in front, on one side, were the female officers attired in dresses of severe simplicity of style, while on the other side were the bandsmen enveloped in red jer- seys, inscribed across the breast with the words "Salvation Army" in yellow letters. There were also a number of soldiers, of bath sexes, in front of the platform, wearing the conspicuous uniform of the Army. The pro- ceedings commenced with the favourite hymn, "Lift up the banner on high," and then "Crown Him Lord of all" was sung. After this Captain Sheen, of MancheLter, delivered with great unction a prayer in the style characteristic of Primitive Methodist camp meetings; and ere the congre- gation had time to rise to their feet, there were heard the strains of the hymn commencing— "'Pie the old time salvation, And it's good enough for me." The hymns were sung with "fixed bayonets" (right arms raised), waving of handkerchiefs, and clapping of hands. Prayer was next engaged in by a female captain from Run- corn, and then Staff-Captain Bamford sang a solo. Major Taylor followed with an address, in which he explained the circumstances under which the Army had came to War- rington, and gave some information respecting the Army generally- which slow numbers 500 corps. His remarks were frequently greeted wan term cries of '• Amen," and "Hal- lelujah." The "sister that plays the tambourine" next spoke, and she was succeeded by a male soldier, who enlarged upon his" freedom from the devil," when the corps broke out with—
" I am a Salvation Foldier; Which nobody cut deny ; " but this was immediately changed for— For He's a mighty Saviour, Which nobody eq.n deny."

A soldier named Belsher was now put 'forward to give his experience, and he described how he used to get l drunk twice a Sunday, and "got that low he should have run away and left his family," but for the Salvation Army. It had been a good job for him and his family that the army came to Warrington, awl he meant to go on in his new course to the end, a declaration that provoked a volley of" Amens." Staff-Captain Coffin, from Arnerici, refte red to the work of the army in that country ; and then a solo was given by Irish Kitty" cLient. Hamilton). Subse- quently the progress of the army in the city of Manchester was alluded to by Captain Sheen, and an address was also delivered by Captain Osborne (176th Corps), who prefaced her observations with the remark that she " wanted every one to listen and then they would be able to hear." The time for the presentation of the colours had now arrived, and Major Taylor proceeded to perform the ceremony. Prior to doing so, however, he expressed his regret that Captain Reid, the commanding officer of the corps, who is away recruiting her health, was not present to receive the colours. In her absence, he had to present them to Captain Bamford and Lieut. Hamilton on behalf of the corps. With song the flag was then unfurled, and the Major explained that its colours were emblematical. The red was intended , to paint to the precious blood of Jesus Christ through which they believed they had forgiveness of sins ; the blue was the emblem of purity—they believed the blood of Jesus Christ could wash them and make them clean ; and the yellow was an emblem of the tire of the Holy Ghost. In the centre of the flag were the words "Blood and fire," surrounding the number of the corps, 412. The flag, the major said, was to be taken through the back streets and slums of Warrington, so that people might see the "blood and fire" on it, and be led to think about their souls. Major Taylor then presented:the flag to the officers, and Captain Bamford, in reply, said "if it cost her the last drop of her blood, she intended to bring some of the people of Warrington out of the darkness of sin into God's most marvellous light." Lieutenant Hamilton also replied, and the corps sang "The Warrington corps is bound to win. That all of you can see." After this Brothers Sambrook and Hunter gave their expe- rience, during which, as all through the meeting, the Salvationists gave expression to their feelings by firing " volleys; " and the tambourine girls distinguished them- selves so much by the energy with which they played their instruments that the major remarked that they were having " a right good time." The hymn " Lift up the banner on h;gh" was again sung, and the meeting concluded with I prayer.

WANDERING SOLDIERS.—At Prescot, on Tueslay, Wm Pratt and John Woods, two privates in the Ist battalion of the Cheshire Regiment stationed at Chester, was charged, before Mr. F. W. Earle, with absenting themselves from their regiment without leave. They had left Chester on Sunday, and on Monday they were found wandering about Prescot in a destitute condition, and locked up. The y were remanded to Walton gaol to await an escort.

A "ROARING HORSE."-At Nantwich County Court,on Wednesday, before Mr. Hughes, James Simpson, farmer, Audlem, brought an action against John Hicking, horse dealer, Chester, to recover £2, value of a horse with which a written warranty had been given.—Mr. Lisle, solicitor, Nintwich, who appeared for plaintiff, said defendant attended fairs and sold horses, which afterwards proved use- less. Plaintiff bought one of these animals, apparently sound, and the day afterwards it could be heard "roaring," according to veterinary evidence, 200 yards off. The dodge, Mr. Lislie explained, was to sell a horse as sound, and then when it was discovered to be useless to offer to re-purchase it at a considerable reduction in price. That was attempted in this instance.—The Judge said he had no doubt it was a deliberate swindle, and give an order for immediate judg- ment and all costs.

LOYAL ROCK OF HOPE LODGE (Sr. HELENS) OF ODD- FELLOWS.—Upwards of 40 members of this lodge partook of an excellent dinner at the George Hotel, George-street, St. Helens, on Saturday evening. After the cloth had been re- moved, Brother J. Lawless, D.S., was voted to the chair, from vi hich the usual loyal and patriotic toas,s were given and received with full honours. The Chairman then pro- posed " Success to the National Independent Order of Odd- fellows," coupled with the name of Brother James Ker- wick, G.M., who, in appropriate terms, referred to the bene- fits derivable by the working classes becoming members of such societies. 'Success to the Loyal Rock of Hope Lodge" was coupled with the nameee of Brother W. J. Mooney, F.G.M., secretary, and he, in response, gave a report show- ing the satisfactory condition in which the lodge was at present ; and Brother H. Carroll gave a further interesting account of the progress the lodge had made since its estab- lishment in 1863. " The health of the host" was next given, to which Mr. Eden suitably replied. The toast of "The visitors " was responded to by Mr. Wm. Fletcher in suitable terms; and songs, dm., were contributed by Brothers Bate, Harrison, Riley, Boardman, and Rowlands. The usual votes of thanks brought a pleasant evening to a close.
